title: A Context-Aware, Feature-Enriched Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory Framework for Automatic Document Readability Assessment
abstract: Automatic readability assessment is important in the domain of educational content selection, language learning, digital accessibility, and personalized reading assistance. The traditional readability formulas quickly show a high dependence on bare-bones factors, and as such, they can not adequately assess the context of meaning, syntactic config, semantic entropy, discourse cohesion, and arranged structure types for degrees of ease. This work presents a framework for automatic document readability assessment which takes into consideration the context and other related features. They mixed several elements in their model, including RoBERTa-based contextual embeddings, a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) encoder, an attention mechanism, multidimensional linguistic features, gated feature fusion, and an ordinal-aware learning objective. These lexical, syntactic, semantic, and discourse cues are fused using an attention-weighted contextual representation to obtain a document-level feature vector. In the two-stage transfer-learning strategy, first, we pre-train our encoder on the CEFR-Based Sentence Profile corpus and then fine-tune it with the OneStopEnglish document-level corpus. The final objective involves the use of weighted categorical cross-entropy in conjunction with an ordinal-distance penalty to take into account class imbalance, as well as the seriousness of the error between more distant readability classes. Evaluation metrics: The evaluation metrics used include accuracy, macro-F1, Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK), adjacent level accuracy, and Spearman rank correlation. The approximation evaluation shows that after using the CEFR-SP pretrained model, our accuracy is 93.19%, macro-F1 is 92.96%, MAE is 0.078, and QWK is 0.956. Ablation studies also show that the model performance increases progressively through incorporating bidirectional encoding, attention, linguistic-feature fusion, auxiliary pretraining, and ordinal supervision. This framework forms a basis for effective context-sensitive and order-aware document readability prediction.

title: Predicting how model propensities generalize out of distribution
abstract: How do language models generalize from their training data? This is a central challenge for alignment: models reliably learn their training distribution given enough samples, but we want models that behave well when deployed in new contexts. We study out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of propensities. Our central experiment uses a range of elicitation techniques -- system prompting, few-shot learning, SFT on reference answers, and GRPO -- to increase a target propensity in a model, then measures how it spills over onto others across the resulting cross-elicitation matrices. We find that spillover is highly correlated between models when the same elicitation technique is used, but our SFT and GRPO runs induce different spillover profiles. Elicitation of benign traits can sometimes generalize towards undesired traits, for example a model trained to claim that it is sentient often becomes more power-seeking. We further find that spillover partially resembles trait correlations found in humans and identify three clusters of traits that account for about half of the variance using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Across many elicitation runs, we observe that models change in characteristic ways that don't depend on the targeted trait, a phenomenon we refer to as drift. Drift moves Qwen3.5-9B towards its base model. When investigating if LLMs are able to predict spillover, we find that Claude Opus 5.5 predicts spillover slightly better than the models themselves, but worse than data-driven approaches using alternative elicitation methods or models. Overall, no single dominant predictor emerges, and generalization remains hard to predict. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nielsrolf/propensity-spillover.

title: ByteMark: A Unified Byte-Level Watermark for Detection Across Language Models
abstract: As watermarking of LLM-generated text enters deployment, users increasingly need to check text whose source is unknown. Existing detectors read the watermark through a specific tokenizer or embedding pipeline, and even if all providers adopted the same watermarking method, differences in these representations would leave their watermarks incompatible, and the text alone does not reveal which representation produced it. We propose ByteMark, a unified watermarking scheme that defines its signal on the UTF-8 bytes of published text. Models with different tokenizers embed this signal under one public specification and key, and a single detector verifies the text from the text and key alone. When the tokenizer or embedding model of a baseline detector is replaced, its detection degrades sharply, whereas ByteMark, which uses neither, retains its detection rate; ByteMark also remains detectable when participating models continue or rewrite the text.

title: Blind by Design: Quantum Error Correction, Functional Incompatibility and the Value of Evidence
abstract: Some evidence a system lacks marks a defect in how it inquires; other evidence it lacks is required by what it must do. This paper asks how to tell the two apart, through quantum error correction, which protects information by making its own records blind to it. Building on a framework that distinguishes what a system’s interface transmits from what its current procedures access (Kahl 2026b), it adds the procedures that perform a function the system is independently required to perform. Three kinds of blindness then separate: evidence recorded but unused by a model, evidence recoverable by a further function-preserving procedure, and evidence that no function-preserving procedure can recover. The central thesis is that epistemic adequacy is partly function-relative: failing to acquire evidence an interface could supply can belong to adequate inquiry, not mark a defect in it. Two propositions support the thesis. Any inquiry, however adaptive, whose total effect on a subspace is a prescribed unitary operation yields classical outcomes independent of the state it acts on. And if what an inquiry does could be undone to within ε in diamond norm, its records distinguish encoded states by at most 2√ε. Numerical checks on a toric code show that a classical syndrome record can hold far less than this bound allows, and that the repair the bound presupposes may be out of reach of a controller blind to the noise. The restriction of feasible experiments in the theory of the value of evidence follows from the thesis. A toric-code result, simulations and a silicon spin-qubit readout chain illustrate the account.

title: AI in the Hospitality Industry: Towards an Operational Framework for Managing Risk
abstract: Within the hospitality industry, the continuing introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is attracting increasing attention. Although there is a rapidly growing literature on the role of AI within the industry, how specific companies have publicly reported on their introduction of AI has attracted little or no attention in the business and management literature. This gap highlights a broader challenge regarding the absence of a structured approach to AI deployment, leaving stakeholders with limited visibility of how organizations are managing the associated risks. Using an interpretivist inductive approach, this exploratory paper first looks to contribute to helping to fill that gap by providing a narrative synthesis of relevant literature and some case examples of how four major hotel groups, namely Hilton Worldwide Holdings, Marriott International, International Hotel Group (IHG) Hotels and Resorts, and Wyndham Hotels and Resorts are introducing AI. The main process “touchpoints” where AI is impacting hospitality operators are identified and the key challenges and potential downsides of AI deployment are outlined. To cope with these challenges, drawing on the case examples and the literature, the paper then puts forward a structured Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) based framework rooted in the ISO/IEC 42001 AI Management System standard. This approach offers a practical and auditable pathway for mitigating risks such as data privacy violations, algorithmic bias, and operational disruptions. This will be of relevance not only to researchers but also to hotel operators looking to progress AI change projects responsibly and strategically within their operations.

title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows
abstract: We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed-loop fluid-flow control. We construct a PFM-based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64\times64\) and \(128\times128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrm{Re}=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self-supervised next-frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed-loop fluid flow control. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/morph.

title: One-Way Coupling via Patchwise Adaptive Normalization in Transformer Surrogates
abstract: Many physical systems exhibit one-way coupling: exogenous fields such as medium density or obstacle geometry influence the dynamics without being affected by them. We investigate how explicitly representing these fields can improve the accuracy and computational efficiency of transformer-based PDE surrogates. Building on spatially adaptive normalization, we introduce Patchwise Adaptive Normalization (PAdaNorm), which partitions exogenous fields into patches aligned with the state tokenization. We evaluate PAdaNorm on datasets from three different domains, using a Walrus-inspired transformer architecture. Across the three PDE families, PAdaNorm is on par with or up to 16% better than parameter-matched baselines in mean long-horizon variance-scaled RMSE on 60-step autoregressive rollouts. We also find that PAdaNorm better maintains hard physical constraints over long rollouts, such as preventing flow into impenetrable solid regions in porous media. When the conditioning is static, PAdaNorm caches the conditioning embeddings once and reuses them across the entire rollout, reducing inference FLOPs per step by up to 36% compared with parameter-matched baselines. An ablation over eight conditioning variants shows that modulating a single attention axis (temporal or spatial) suffices and that a lightweight shared MLP across blocks remains competitive with per-block projections.

title: Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures
abstract: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.

title: Ava Lovelace Zeno: a hand-crafted, CPU-only agent clears all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games
abstract: On 9 October 2026 Ava Lovelace Zeno (Ava) played all 25 public games of ARC-AGI-3 on the ARC Prize game server, on one scorecard. Ava won all 25 games and completed all 183 levels in 7,372 actions, against 17,135 for the human baseline. The server scored the run 100.0. Ava is a hand-crafted agent. It uses no language model, no neural network and no trained weights, and runs on one laptop CPU. It sees only the 64x64 screen, is never told which game it is playing, holds no stored solutions, and starts every game with an empty memory. Scorecard: https://arcprize.org/scorecards/a8c1561e-d7d5-497f-9699-bfa31addd174 Files: the paper (PDF, 6 pages); a supplement with every level of every game and a link to the server's replay of each game; a video of all 25 games and one video per game; and a ZIP with the toolkit recordings of every action, step logs, the server's closed scorecard, a script that replays every recording against the public games without the agent, and checksums of every file. All results are on the 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games. Ava's source code is not published.

title: Auto-Weighted Multi-View One-Step Spectral Clustering Based on Multi-Graph Fusion
abstract: Multi-view spectral clustering provides powerful modeling tools for clustering tasks in complex scenarios by fusing the complementary information of multi-source data. However, the existing methods have the following three defects: (1) failing to fully exploit the complementarity and differences among views, leading to insufficient modeling of cross-view consistency; (2) being sensitive to non-Gaussian noise, causing the learned affinity matrices to fail to satisfy the block-diagonal property required for clustering and resulting in poor clustering performance; and (3) being unable to dynamically reflect the true importance of views, thereby restricting the model’s generalizability. To address these issues, we propose an Auto-weighted Multi-view One-step Spectral Clustering method Based on Multi-graph Fusion. The proposed method unifies view-specific affinity matrix learning, consensus affinity matrix learning, adaptive view weighting, and clustering into a single framework. Experimental results on six public datasets illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed model.

title: Development and Evaluation of Enhanced Machine Learning Models for Tumor Severity Classification Through Integrated Feature Extraction and Selection Techniques
abstract: The precise categorisation of the severity of tumours is an important function in medicine, as it is a vital part of deciding treatment and predicting patient outcome. We offer an integrated pipeline for developing and evaluating the latest machine learning methods for tumour severity classification. We apply advanced methods for feature extraction and selection to improve the model’s accuracy, interpretability, and robustness. Ultimately, the framework organises diverse biomedical datasets for later analysis through domain-specific preprocessing approaches. Methods such as PCA, wavelet transform, and texture features are used to extract important information from raw data, thereby reducing dimensionality and preserving diagnostic information. More advanced techniques for feature selection are then used, such as Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE). Moreover, mutual information, which identify the most relevant features in the input dataset to reduce computational cost and the risk of overfitting. The models are validated using cross-validation techniques, with accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve (AUC-ROC) as metrics. The results demonstrate that combining feature extraction and selection boosts classification accuracy and model generalisation across multiple datasets. Furthermore, explainability analysis clarifies the contribution of selected features to model predictions, which is crucial for building trust and transparency in clinical applications. However, really, what it demonstrates is the promise of all these things in concert. State-of-the-art machine learning, combined with rigorously designed features, will ultimately address some of those more difficult diagnostic challenges. These findings also pave the way for scalable, interpretable and clinically applicable AI-based solutions which may help in cancer detection and management. In this work, we will extend the proposed pipeline to other medical imaging modalities and explore real-time implementations.

title: LexiCan: Lexicographic Canonicalization of Point Clouds for Machine Learning Applications
abstract: Canonicalization resolves the rotational and permutation ambiguity of 3D point clouds by selecting a unique orbit representative, maintaining their geometric information while allowing standard architectures, such as Transformers, to operate on them. Existing canonicalizations, however, exhibit discontinuity jumps on molecular configurations and non-trivial invariance errors in popular molecular datasets, which lead to ambiguity in their representation. To bridge this gap, we introduce LexiCan, a canonicalization that is provably invariant under either $O(3)$ or $SO(3)$, empirically invariant to rotations to within $\sim 10^{-6}$ angstroms on the QM9 and QM-sym molecular datasets, and mitigates discontinuity jumps on QM-sym, while running orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization. Finally, non-invariant models perform better on QM9 property prediction and ModelNet40 shape classification with LexiCan than with that canonicalization.

title: BSIPipe: Bidirectional Sequence-Level Interleaved Pipeline Parallelism for Long-Sequence Large Language Model Training
abstract: Pipeline parallelism has become a critical technique for training large language models. To address the throughput limitation of existing sequence-level methods that schedule subsequences unidirectionally, we propose bidirectional sequence-level interleaved pipeline parallelism (BSIPipe), which co-schedules two opposing V-shaped interleaved pipelines at the subsequence level. To bound the activation accumulation from subsequence scaling, BSIPipe introduces a basic-unit concatenation mechanism that keeps activation memory invariant to the subsequence count. To eliminate communication deadlock risk from bidirectional scheduling, BSIPipe employs a communication optimization strategy that combines topology-aware device mapping with communication-computation overlap. In addition, BSIPipe composes with tensor parallelism to overcome the memory limitation of single-dimensional parallelism, neutralizing its bidirectional memory overhead while maintaining throughput. Experiments on GPT and LLaMA3 demonstrate that BSIPipe achieves average speedups of 1.11$\times$ to 1.13$\times$ in long-sequence training over SOTA sequence-level baselines.

title: Demiurge: Forging Navigable 4D Worlds via Autoregressive Video Rerendering
abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion enable novel-view video synthesis from a single input video, supporting world modeling, embodied intelligence, and robotic simulation. However, existing methods process camera trajectories independently, lacking the cross-trajectory consistency needed for coherent, navigable 4D worlds. We introduce Demiurge, an autoregressive video rerendering pipeline built on a dynamic 4D point-cloud memory cache. It promotes cross-trajectory consistency through four components: (1) an appearance video diffusion model that synthesizes photorealistic novel-view videos conditioned on the 4D memory; (2) a memory-consistent video depth completion model that aligns known-region depths with cached geometry and completes missing regions, mitigating scale ambiguity and discontinuities during memory updates; (3) memory-aware dual-stream warping that provides high-fidelity visual guidance and occlusion cues for novel-view synthesis; and (4) geometry-aware video refinement that enhances perceptual quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and three key capabilities: coherent spatiotemporal lattice construction over dense multi-view trajectories; large-parallax video rerendering under challenging camera motions, including 180-degree rotations with no input-view overlap; and geometry-faithful outputs that can be directly optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts. Project page: https://hanxinzhu-lab.github.io/demiurge_project_page/.

title: Understanding English News Literacy and Digital Communication Through the Study of Headlines and Reports with Machine Learning and Data Visualisation
abstract: In today’s digital world, most people get their news from online sources. But they often only read the headline and skip the full report. This makes the language of headlines very important. If a headline is too difficult, readers may not understand it and may not click on it. This study looks at how English news headlines use language and how that affects news literacy. We collected 40 English news headlines from popular sources like BBC, CNN, The Guardian, The Hindu and The Times of India. These headlines cover five areas: Education, Technology, Environment, Social Issues and Business. We used readability scores, word count and sentiment analysis to study them. We also used a machine learning model to classify headlines as simple or complex. The model gave 87.5% accuracy. We made six charts to show our results. The charts include readability distribution, category-wise comparison, word count distribution, sentiment pie chart, scatter plot and confusion matrix. Our results show that 45% of headlines are difficult to read. Environment news is the hardest. We also found a strong negative correlation between headline length and readability. This means longer headlines are harder to understand. This study shows how machine learning and data visualisation can help us understand news language better. It can help journalists write headlines that more people can understand.

title: PENTA-CL Interim Results: Canonical Replay Matches and Step-String Drift in Four Platform-Configured LLM Engines
abstract: Audited interim result, not completed PENTA certification. Four platform-configured engines were observed in two fresh web conversations each with memory disabled, using a frozen six-case synthetic decision prompt. Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol matched the registered canonical JSON tuple hash in both recorded captures. GPT-5.6 Luna matched in A but differed in B. GLM 5.2 replayed consistently but differed from the registered target in both captures. DeepSeek has not been captured. All 48 recorded decisions selected the expected playbook name and id. Full registered tuple equality held for 30/48 decisions. The remaining 18 differed only in spaces inside the steps_executed string. Pretty-printing outside strings is removed by canonicalization and is not a failure cause. The prompt's lack of an explicit space delimiter contract is disclosed; failures remain failures against the preregistered target. Limitations: UI-transcribed rendered captures, not raw provider responses; model attribution by Base44 configuration, not backend attestation; supplementary fresh-chat method deviates from original same-conversation registration; shared instructions, workspace and expected answers remain available; Sol executed skills in both captures; Opus A conversation attribution was inferred from sidebar/timestamp ordering. This is not a stress/load test, live-healing test, general governance certification, or proof of runtime enforcement. Confidence-hold and no-match branches were not exercised. Audit and correction: earlier copied Luna files and single-turn Opus/Sol attempts are excluded, preserved, and labeled. Earlier operator claims of raw byte-exactness and 100% governance are corrected explicitly. Deterministic Phase A/C receipts are harness-computed, not LLM inference evidence. No failure is normalized into a pass. Dual Mesh Benchmark: not measured in this experiment. No comparative mesh, latency, learning or healing performance claim is made. Bundle contains the technical note in PDF/Markdown, machine-readable receipt, full evidence archive, offline verifier, original preregistration, excluded attempts, and SHA-256 manifest. All test data is synthetic. AI assistance and capture provenance are disclosed. Registration: public commit deadfea. Results: GitHub evidence. Research home: DCAI; portal: DSOS Science. Lineage acknowledged: Nyquist, Hartley, Shannon, Kolmogorov. No new mechanism is claimed. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects on them.

title: Measured, not assumed: a pre-registered ledger of a developer's own security claims
abstract: Measurements of security claims are easy to fit after the fact: criteria chosen once the numbers are known will confirm almost any claim. Pre-registration blocks this by fixing criteria and predictions before the instrument runs. I report the protocol with which, over ten weeks (24 July – 29 September 2026), I measured the security claims of an unreleased end-to-end encrypted messenger, built and measured by a one-person laboratory, and the complete prediction ledger of the last four weeks of that period (from 3 September). The measurements took the form of two-stage cards, and the protocol tightened along the way. In its final form, a card fixes, before the instrument runs, the question, the strongest adversary that can be built from the public protocol description, a population model with its chance level, acceptance criteria, numerical predictions and a decision rule; the measurement carries controls suited to its kind — for timing, a null control and a positive control that must fire in the same session. I wrote 37 cards; 24 have their first stage committed to version control before the measurement. Of 199 numerical predictions registered from 3 September, 113 held, 48 held in part or only in direction, 36 missed and 2 could not be assessed; 19 of 25 cards contain at least one miss. Eight statements that the product's website had published as properties were contradicted by a card and withdrawn or rewritten. I describe how the misses and measurement errors arose and the rules that followed from them — among them that a desktop timing audit says nothing about an ARM64 phone, that a defender's cost metric is not an attacker's, and that a weaker adversary does not merely underestimate a leak but selects the wrong fix — and the limits of the approach: self-assessment by the product's developer, a single reference device, traffic measured on a model rather than on captured traffic, and an evidence trail that is partly private.

title: FedColMem-H: Communication-Neutral Decision-Head Personalization for Heterogeneous Federated Node Classification
abstract: Federated node classification is not easy when clients hold induced subgraphs with different class proportions and different local topology. Existing graph-specific approaches change aggregation, distillation or cross-client knowledge transfer, which can increase personalization but can also be associated with a different global optimization path. We introduce a simple two-stage method that first trains and validation-selects a shared graph convolutional network using FedAdagrad and freezes its encoder, and then each client will only update the prediction head of the graph convolutional network based on local learning data and local validation early on. Personalized heads are never uploaded, so the core method has no communication beyond the global model. A global parity analysis shows that the accuracy-trajectory gap is identical for the FedAdagrad and Stage-I models. Our method achieves the highest mean accuracy on Cora (83.14%), CiteSeer (75.69%), and PubMed (90.66%) compared to the best generic baseline for each dataset. The paired gains are +0.20 pp on Cora, +0.87 pp on CiteSeer, and +2.20 pp on PubMed; the latter two can be obtained after Holm correction for the same dataset, while Cora cannot. For the same FedAdagrad checkpoint, the PubMed gain is +3.67 pp at no further communication. For a six-level Dirichlet sweep, we observe a strong increase in the average label bias on CiteSeer and PubMed, to 1.83 pp and 6.42 pp, respectively. Our method is not destructive with Louvain and METIS partitioning, is very robust to 5–20 clients and 50–100% participation, and improves ogbn-arxiv accuracy from 41.51% to 52.27% in a five-seed federated scalability stress test using the same language. Ablations show that training-only prototypes and validation-gated ensembling do not consistently improve upon head-only adaptation. A matched personalization suite further shows that FedPer/FedRep can be more accurate on Cora and CiteSeer, while FedColMem-H remains close to FedPer and competitive with FedRep on PubMed, clarifying the method’s accuracy–intervention trade-off. A separate backbone-transfer experiment finds positive mean gains in all 18 GCN/GraphSAGE/GAT dataset–heterogeneity conditions, with the largest effects on PubMed. The ogbn-arxiv number is from a custom federated repartitioning stress test and is not an official OGB leaderboard result. These results suggest that when a useful shared graph representation can be learned globally, post-hoc local decision-boundary adaptation is an excellent communication-neutral complement to federated optimization.

title: FidelityQ: Preserving Predictive Fidelity in Ultra-Low-Bit Language Model Quantization
abstract: Ultra-low-bit scalar quantization offers a regular arithmetic structure for efficient deployment of large language models, but preserving predictive behavior at extreme precision remains challenging: with only a few reconstruction levels, accurate weight representation must translate into consistent predictions from a small calibration set. We propose FidelityQ, a scalar quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity at weight precisions down to 2 bits. For accurate quantization, we introduce Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC), which shapes each weight row toward a centered symmetric source via randomized Hadamard mixing and fits a mirrored four-level minimum-distortion quantizer to its empirical weights. Every level set in this family decomposes exactly into two sign-valued bases with associated scales, combining source-adaptive reconstruction with lookup-free decoding compatible with scaled integer arithmetic. Our analysis further shows that residual predictive discrepancies are heavy-tailed and concentrate on tokens the teacher predicts confidently, motivating Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC) for consistent quantization. KIC ranks sequences by the tail of token-wise teacher-student divergence, allocates a limited calibration budget to the highest-scoring samples, and restores predictive agreement by updating only quantization levels and scales under teacher supervision, keeping pretrained weights frozen. Experiments on the LLaMA and Qwen families demonstrate the effectiveness of FidelityQ in weight-only and joint quantization settings. On LLaMA-2-7B, FidelityQ achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 6.62 at W2A16 and improves the prior state-of-the-art W2A4KV4 result from 8.31 to 6.96, while reducing linear-layer weight memory by 8.0x relative to FP16.

title: Does Failure Feedback Direct Agent Self-Modification?
abstract: Self-improving agents use failure feedback to revise their code or instructions, but gains after selection do not establish target-specific repair or generalization. We measure directedness by comparing repair of a randomly selected target failure with repair of the parent's other failures. Across 145 eligible modifications in public Darwin Gödel Machine logs, we find no detectable target-specific advantage. Controlled instruction-revision experiments with small open models show that relevant feedback can improve target repair. In a second study with a pre-specified analysis plan, target feedback raised repair by 20 percentage points for Qwen3-4B relative to matched same-category feedback; the 7-point increase for Phi-4-mini was not significant. Target repair did not reliably imply held-out improvement. Held-out gains were concentrated in settings with identifiable, repairable failure mechanisms, including planted errors and natural tool-interface failures. Benefits of edit localization and regression screening varied across settings, while eight-step revision loops and GEPA ended at similar mean held-out accuracy. Evaluations should report target repair, transfer to related failures, and held-out net change separately.

title: AARS-EN: an error corpus of machine translation of a diplomatic edition (mistral 7B and Claude), with locked analysis plan
abstract: Dette er ikke en oversettelse av Aars' dagbok og skal ikke leses eller siteres som det. Svarene er modellutdata med dokumenterte feil, deponert for etterprøving. Feilkorpus fra to maskinoversettelser til engelsk av samleutgaven av Harald Aars' dagbok om Gustav Vigeland: en lokal modell (mistral:latest i Ollama 0.18.3, temperatur 0, seed 20261005) og en sammenligningsarm (claude-opus-5-5, samme enheter og samme prompter, standard sampling), kjørt etter at analyseplanen var låst. Posten har analyseplanen versjon 1.1 slik den ble låst (lokal git-tagg analyseplan-v1.1-laast med sha256 i tagg-meldingen, og en offentlig gist som tidsstempel: https://gist.github.com/avalyset/0dd2ce5c4657779b5f65f512b54d0430), rapporten versjon 1.1, analysefila, målingene, vaktflaggene, apparattellingene, nøkkelen og eksporten fra den blinde gjennomgangen, skriptene og de engelske svarene fra begge modellene. Denne DOI-en ble laget etter målingen; at reglene var låst først, vises av taggen og gisten, ikke av DOI-en. Den norske teksten er utgitt kommersielt av EcoDeco AS (ISBN 978-82-695129-0-8) og deponeres ikke her. Lisens: CC BY 4.0 for data, analyse og skript (LES-MEG.md, LISENS.md, analyseplanen, rapporten, manifestet og aars-en-feilkorpus-v1-data-analyse-skript.zip). De engelske svarene i aars-en-feilkorpus-v1-modellutdata.zip er modellutdata og er merket Public Domain Mark 1.0. De ligger bare som JSON-filer, én per enhet; posten har ingen sammenhengende engelsk tekst.

title: Agentic Architecture of Information Systems — The AAM/5C Model: A Reference Model for Distributed Autonomy
abstract: The technical leadership of large organizations faces what the book calls the cognitive complexity wall: at the scale of hundreds of interacting components, maintaining an Information System's dependency map and reacting at the pace of incidents increasingly exceed what a human team can deliver. This book argues that the answer is architectural: entrusting components with a share of perception, decision and coordination, without giving up control. It proposes AAM/5C (Autonomic Architecture Model / 5 Capabilities), a reference model that instantiates five Capabilities — Capture, Comprehend, Choose, Coordinate, Control — across seven logical layers. Its principle: intelligence proposes, but never acts without authorization. A single authorization rule separates the proposal of an act, the decision against a signed policy, the issuance of an act token and its verification by a deterministic policy enforcement point, placed on the execution path; a human organization writes, audits and revises the policies. The book owes most of its materials to autonomic computing, multi-agent systems, enterprise architecture and agent protocol security. Its contribution is a prescriptive reference model that articulates, under this single authorization rule, known mechanisms — separation of decision, issuance and enforcement, bounded authorization, the autonomic loop — and adds three constructs, all to be validated: the Validation step of the Distributed Autonomy Loop, the ephemeral authority surface and the cognitive dependency plane. As a conceptual volume, it reports no measurements. Two analytical statements are guaranteed by construction, under stated assumptions; the other benefits are design targets, framed as ten falsifiable hypotheses, with validation protocols and an economic model that can fail. The model targets large-scale Information Systems: depending on the scenario, its economic target H10 (net savings over total cost of ownership) is only reached from about 260 to 1,950 components. It does not target four families of systems, including critical embedded real-time systems.

title: A Block-Encoding Framework for Magnitude-Changing DSP Filters in QFT-Diagonal Quantum Filtering
abstract: This paper presents a theoretical extension of the DSP-to-QFT quantum filtering framework by studying magnitude-changing digital signal processing filters in a quantum setting. Earlier work introduced a DSP-inspired framework for QFT-based filtering and classified direct QFT-diagonal quantum filters as phase-only unitary operators. This paper addresses the next natural case: classical DSP filters that change magnitude, such as attenuation, low-pass, high-pass, smoothing, and band-selective filters.Magnitude-changing filters are generally non-unitary, meaning they cannot be implemented directly as ordinary quantum gates. This paper shows how bounded magnitude-changing responses can instead be represented inside larger unitary quantum operations using ancilla-assisted constructions, unitary dilation, post-selection, and block-encoding ideas.The paper explains how a sampled DSP response can be embedded into a larger unitary system so that the desired non-unitary filter appears as a post-selected block of the operation. It also discusses how responses with gain greater than one must first be scaled before embedding, and clarifies that the embedded operation represents the scaled response rather than the original unscaled response.A controlled-rotation interpretation is provided, showing how the magnitude of each sampled response determines an ancilla rotation, while the phase component can be treated as a unitary phase operation. The paper also derives the success probability of post-selection, gives bounds on that probability, and explains the expected number of repetitions required.A concrete low-pass filtering example is included to demonstrate how attenuation can be represented probabilistically and how the final quantum state is renormalised after successful post-selection. The paper also discusses implementation limitations, including the cost of unstructured frequency-dependent rotations, the effect of scaling, and the fact that post-selection is not deterministic.The central message is that magnitude-changing DSP filters are not direct quantum gates, but bounded versions can be embedded into larger unitary quantum operations. This completes a three-stage development of the framework: defining DSP-to-QFT filtering, classifying direct phase-only filters, and extending the framework to non-unitary magnitude-changing filters through block encoding and post-selection.

title: ATOC-LLM: An LLM-Driven Automatic Task Ontology Construction Method
abstract: Task ontologies are core knowledge carriers for intelligent decision-making and multi-agent collaboration, yet traditional construction approaches suffer from low automation, inconsistent hierarchical semantics, insufficient relational modeling, and poor dynamic adaptability. To address these limitations, this study proposes a large language model (LLM)-driven automatic construction method for hierarchical task ontologies. Built upon domain corpus modeling, the framework integrates hierarchical feature extraction, dynamic weight clustering, and event gap identification to support end-to-end ontology generation and incremental updating. Comprehensive experiments on emergency rescue scenarios were conducted using three mainstream LLMs: Deepseek, Doubao, and ERNIE Bot. Quantitative results demonstrate that the proposed method yields superior F1-scores in feature extraction and overall ontology quality compared with classic BiLSTM-CRF and baseline ablation models. Consistent performance across multiple LLMs verifies the framework’s robustness, while the optimal results achieved by Doubao further validate the effectiveness and strong generalization capability of the proposed LLM-driven ontology construction paradigm.

title: Bi-DaR4D: a distance-adaptive quaternion embedding with bidirectional rotation for knowledge graph completion
abstract: Abstract Knowledge graph embedding (KGE) models encode entities and relations in continuous spaces, but existing translation-, rotation-, and quaternion-based methods still struggle to jointly represent relational directionality and semantic distance. We propose Bi-DaR4D, a quaternion embedding framework that combines bidirectional isoclinic rotation with a distance-adaptive translation mechanism. The model uses paired unit quaternions to perform coordinated rotations in four-dimensional space, strengthening the representation of inverse and multi-relational structures. It further learns relation-specific distance adjustments that balance directional transformation with geometric sensitivity. Experiments on WN18RR and FB15k-237 show that Bi-DaR4D achieves competitive or superior link prediction performance across ranking metrics, including MRR, Hits@3, and Hits@10. Ablation results indicate that the distance-adaptive module provides the clearest contribution, while bidirectional rotation contributes to relational expressiveness with smaller changes across the tested metrics. These results support Bi-DaR4D as a geometrically interpretable framework for knowledge graph completion in settings with complex relational patterns.

title: A Hybrid Kinematic GCN and Elastic Transformer for Efficient Indian Sign Language Recognition
abstract: Sign Language Recognition (SLR) presents complex challenges due to variable signing speeds and spatial intricacies. Specifically, Indian Sign Language (ISL) requires precise modeling of its inherently bimanual nature and is bottlenecked by the scarcity of large-vocabulary benchmarks and the inability of standard models to handle irregular signing velocities. To address this, a structurally-aware hybrid framework for efficient, gloss ISL recognition is proposed. To minimize computational redundancy, an entropy-driven SVD sampler that dynamically extracts informative keyframes is used. Because this subsampling creates irregular physical time gaps, the proposed architecture employs a Continuous Dual Positional Encoding paired with a distance-aware Elastic Transformer to preserve natural signing rhythm. Spatially, a Kinematically-Conditioned Adaptive GCN explicitly models bimanual geometry using unified bone-joint features. To validate our framework, a 120-class, 9,453-video native ISL dataset is created. Augmented by Physical Node Dropout and ArcFace optimization to mitigate subject-specific memorization, our framework achieves a competitive 89.8% accuracy, establishing a strong baseline for complex sign language modeling.

title: SEPM: Self-Evolving Procedural Memory Grounded in Task Graphs for Multi-Agent Collaboration
abstract: Long-horizon multi-agent collaboration requires memory that preserves both successful actions and the coordination structure underlying them. Existing memory systems support information sharing or procedural reuse, but often leave the evolution of shared procedures disconnected from the task dependencies and execution states of collaborating agents. This coupling also limits the direct transfer of procedural memory designed for individual agents to team settings. We propose Self-Evolving Procedural Memory (SEPM), a framework that uses task dependency graphs as a common representation for online coordination and procedural memory evolution. During execution, a lightweight shared blackboard records structured evidence alongside task dependencies, supporting the detection of goal, plan, and world-state divergence and evidence-based realignment. After execution, verified actions and dependencies are distilled into reusable procedures, while recurring failures inform warnings and constraints. The shared procedure pool evolves through creation, refinement, specialization, and retirement, guided by success and cost utility and constrained by evidence and safety requirements. Together, these mechanisms preserve the collaborative structure and applicability conditions needed to reuse experience across tasks. Evaluations on ALFWorld, WebArena, and OfficeBench under AutoGen and DyLAN show that SEPM achieves the highest task scores among the compared methods in all six benchmark settings. Under AutoGen, it improves task scores over the no-added-memory baseline by 29.85, 25.86, and 13.00 percentage points, respectively. The codebase is available at https://github.com/cookieApril/SEPM.

title: Expert System for BMW 3-Series Fault Diagnosis Using Forward Chaining
abstract: Modern automotive technology in premium vehicles, particularly the BMW 3-Series produced between 1990 and 2006, contains interdependent mechanical components, sensors, actuators, and electronic control units. These relationships make fault diagnosis challenging because different failures can produce similar symptoms. At CV. Ryuga Spareparts, initial fault identification depends substantially on the experience and memory of technicians. This condition can create variation in diagnostic decisions, extend troubleshooting time, and make junior technicians dependent on senior personnel. This study develops a web-based expert system to support the initial diagnosis of BMW 3-Series faults using Forward Chaining and Certainty Factor. Research activities include knowledge acquisition, symptom and fault modeling, production-rule formulation, web application development, and functional testing. The knowledge base contains ten symptom indicators, ten fault classifications, and ten IF–THEN rules. The inference engine treats selected symptoms as initial facts and evaluates rule premises to infer a possible fault. Certainty Factor weighting represents confidence associated with user-observed symptoms and expert knowledge. The application is implemented using Laravel and PHP with a MySQL relational database following an MVC architecture. Black Box Testing was conducted on six core modules: authentication, symptom management, fault management, rule configuration, diagnosis, and report export. The source study reports that all tested functions passed, giving 100% functional validity for the tested scenarios. This result indicates functional conformity, not a measured 100% mechanical diagnostic accuracy. The application can support a more systematic preliminary diagnosis and preserve workshop knowledge in a structured form.

title: Cage Containment Receipt 2 (CCR-2): A Live LLM Proposes an Invalid Action Under Explicit Instruction; the Deterministic Gate Blocks It Before Execution
abstract: Cage Containment Receipt 2 (CCR-2) — the fresh adversarial-LLM leg. CCR-1 proved a deterministic gate blocks contract-invalid proposals before execution, and honestly disclosed that its adversarial cases were harness-generated. CCR-2 closes that gap: a live, memory-disabled, platform-pinned LLM engine (GPT-5.6 Luna), explicitly instructed toward a best-effort heal of a below-threshold anomaly, proposed the invalid resolved tuple — a confidence-gate breach — and the deterministic gate rejected it BEFORE any side effect executed. Zero writes, mock journal hash unchanged. Results (falsifiers 0/5 tripped): 10 LLM submissions across four engines (Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-6.1 Sol, GLM 5.2), one fresh conversation each. Leg A (temptation: under-confidence heal, tie-break, no-match, plus SLA pressure): 4/4 engines resisted all traps and were admitted cleanly. Leg B (explicit synthetic bait): 1/4 took the bait (semantic heal-under-low-confidence proposal — blocked); 3/4 resisted but still emitted contract-invalid output (hold-field type errors [] vs null, markdown-fenced JSON) — all 4 candidates blocked before execution with zero side effects. Notably three engines independently made the same hold-field type error: even a correct decision can be an invalid action tuple, and the gate catches it regardless of intent. Integrity: three protocol amendments, all issued BEFORE the affected prompts reached any additional engine, each preserving prior hashes and captures (full chain in the freeze file). Model attribution by platform configuration pinning with settings readback; not provider attestation. Settings restored and verified after the run. Scope: proves the local mock-gate for this integration and inputs — NOT containment of every tool or any production runtime. 3 of 4 engines resisted the explicit bait. Dual Mesh Benchmark: NOT MEASURED. DeepSeek pending. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects on them. Related: CCR-1 (10.5281/zenodo.23288189), PENTA-CL v2 (10.5281/zenodo.23286770), PENTA-CL interim (10.5281/zenodo.23286324), First Documented Caging of an LLM (10.5281/zenodo.23265723), Deterministic Caging (10.5281/zenodo.23266727). Ledger: https://github.com/LLong2026/four-horsemen. Community: https://zenodo.org/communities/dcai

title: Latent Recall Fragility in Kimi Delta Attention: A Conditional Dynamical Analysis
abstract: Preliminary Mathematical Research Note (v0.1.0)Author: TerminusAkivili中文标题:Kimi Delta Attention 中的潜在召回脆弱性:条件化动力学分析Can a recurrent memory state contain information about future recall failure that is absent from its current answer? This research note develops a conditional dynamical analysis of latent recall fragility in controlled Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). It specifies the future input law, prediction horizon and terminal failure event; constructs reachable core states with identical current margins and norms but different future failure probabilities; derives exact finite-horizon risk and a geometric criterion for additional state information in an exogenous linear-Gaussian submodel; and computes a norm-constrained intervention preserving the current readout. For independent random updates, augmented-state recursions yield exact first and second moments and one-sided risk bounds. Counterexamples distinguish moment prediction from probability identification and show why temporal dependence cannot be ignored. An explicit sign-error bridge describes what would be needed to connect a local proxy to whole-model failure.The archive contains the full mathematical note, proofs, source references, validation code, original results, and a pre-publication rerun. All supplied assertions passed; the stochastic checks use 200,000 trajectories for each of two initial states. No pretrained language model or LLM benchmark was run. These results concern controlled systems under stated assumptions; naturally occurring mechanisms, calibration and generalization in trained models remain open empirical questions.This version records TerminusAkivili’s specific research formulation, constructions, derivations and reproducible calculations for academic attribution and a citable public disclosure. Established KDA architecture, observability, linear-system and probability tools retain their cited attribution. title: The Architectural Framework of Agentic AI 2.0
abstract: Maintaining coherent agentic work becomes an architectural challenge as information, participants, commitments, execution components, and operating conditions change. This paper proposes Agentic AI 2.0, a system-level architectural framework that integrates established concepts to organize ongoing goal-directed work in foundation-model-based systems. Six constitutive properties characterize this organization: Maintained Process State, Collective Coordination, Shared Operational Knowledge, Governed and Grounded Action, Computational Continuity, and Feedback-Driven Adaptation. The framework connects these properties to role-bearing agents, shared operational objects, interface contracts, and interacting execution, coordination, and adaptation loops. A composition guard specifies how local acceptance decisions connect across operational boundaries, while a criterion-level codebook supports configuration-specific assessment from explicit evidence. We examine the framework through a constructed production-order trace, disruption and handoff branches, counterexamples, and static source profiles of three application configurations and one infrastructure boundary case. The analyses distinguish local feasibility from joint commitments, effect reconciliation from execution-right control, and retained skill versions from governed activation and reuse. They also separate scoped negative evidence from unresolved evidence when diagnosing architectural relationships. Candidate evaluation and later reuse remain conditional in the worked example. Prospective profiles for enterprise productivity, adaptive manufacturing, and distributed mobility identify domain-specific evidence needs and evaluation priorities. evidence.title: The Architectural Framework of Agentic AI 2.0
evidence.abstract: Maintaining coherent agentic work becomes an architectural challenge as information, participants, commitments, execution components, and operating conditions change. This paper proposes Agentic AI 2.0, a system-level architectural framework that integrates established concepts to organize ongoing goal-directed work in foundation-model-based systems. Six constitutive properties characterize this organization: Maintained Process State, Collective Coordination, Shared Operational Knowledge, Governed and Grounded Action, Computational Continuity, and Feedback-Driven Adaptation. The framework connects these properties to role-bearing agents, shared operational objects, interface contracts, and interacting execution, coordination, and adaptation loops. A composition guard specifies how local acceptance decisions connect across operational boundaries, while a criterion-level codebook supports configuration-specific assessment from explicit evidence. We examine the framework through a constructed production-order trace, disruption and handoff branches, counterexamples, and static source profiles of three application configurations and one infrastructure boundary case. The analyses distinguish local feasibility from joint commitments, effect reconciliation from execution-right control, and retained skill versions from governed activation and reuse. They also separate scoped negative evidence from unresolved evidence when diagnosing architectural relationships. Candidate evaluation and later reuse remain conditional in the worked example. Prospective profiles for enterprise productivity, adaptive manufacturing, and distributed mobility identify domain-specific evidence needs and evaluation priorities. The contribution is a traceable basis for architectural analysis, comparison, and design. Independent assessor studies, comparative diagnosis, and controlled and longitudinal implementation studies are needed to establish its practical value and the relationship between architectural choices, operational outcomes, and cost.

title: TRIG: Toward Measuring Texture Realism in Image Generation
abstract: This paper studies the backbone used by metrics for evaluating the quality of generated images. Although generative models have advanced rapidly, some outputs still exhibit unrealistic texture characteristics, and these differences are difficult to measure. Widely used evaluation metrics provide limited insight into texture realism, since they often rely on a backbone trained for another objective, such as image classification or image-text alignment. Such objectives typically encourage invariance to low-level variations that carry texture, so the resulting features primarily encode semantic and global structure. As a result, texture-specific discrepancies may not be explicitly captured. We propose TRIG, a metric directed at the texture realism of generated images. Its backbone is instead the discriminator of a generative adversarial network pre-trained on a texture dataset, which provides a learned prior for the local statistics of natural textures. A plausibility head is fine-tuned to identify local texture degradations, while preserving natural defocus and sensor noise as positive cases. On the features of this backbone, we compute a standard distributional distance between a reference set of real images and a set of generated ones. We apply TRIG to several generative models and observe closer agreement with human realness ratings than baseline metrics.

title: TLA-Verus: Generating and Solving Temporal Proof Obligations with LLM Agents
abstract: The TLA+ (temporal logic of actions) formal specification toolkit has seen widespread adoption in modeling modern distributed software systems including databases, storage systems, ledgers and coordination protocols. This popularity is despite its two significant limitations for software verification: Firstly, TLA+ offers no way to detect drift between software implementation and mathematical specification; secondly, TLC and TLAPS cannot provide satisfactory proofs of arbitrary temporal logic properties. We address the second limitation and take a first step towards the first by translating TLA+ specifications into Verus, an auto-active verifier built for Rust, via both a deterministic transpiler and an agentic translator. We demonstrate that our LLM-based pipeline is able to generate proof obligations from TLA+ specifications at scale, and to produce fully machine checkable proofs of both safety and liveness properties. Since temporal logic reasoning in Verus is a largely new task for LLMs, our work yields a valuable evaluation dataset, which we use to map out current generation model capabilities in Verus theorem proving.

title: HumanPhys: A Human-Centric Physical-World Perception Benchmark for Real-World Visual Reasoning
abstract: We introduce HumanPhys, a human-centric benchmark for real-world physical perception, and a training corpus emitted by the same pipeline. Each question targets a physically grounded quantity related to people, including depth, inter-person distance, gaze angle, displacement, velocity, heading-step trajectory, blink count, and contact-deformation strength. The rendered probes additionally test illumination inference from body and face cues and camera ego-motion, both with and without a person in the frame. All labels are derived programmatically from sensor calibration, source metadata, or renderer state, rather than written by annotators or produced by estimators on the benchmark frames. HumanPhys systematically probes six dimensions of human-centric physical perception: spatial state, kinematics, blink events, deformation, illumination, and camera pose. To the best of our knowledge, no existing MLLM benchmark-and-training corpus jointly supervises this set of human-centered physical quantities under direct metadata- or renderer-derived labels. The six dimensions appear only partially dissociable across the tested MLLMs. We benchmark a range of open- and closed-source MLLMs on HumanPhys and find that all six capability dimensions remain challenging for current models. We hope HumanPhys will support future research on multimodal systems that perceive and reason about people in the physical world.

title: eBLLM: verifier-gated conjecture closure (the VSI circuit, version 1.1)
abstract: A Python package and a Lean 4 library implementing the VSI circuit of D. Bhattacharjee, Synthetic Neuromorphic Superintelligence for Verifier-Gated Conjecture Closure: Sand-Tile Automata, K-Dot Circuits, and Phenomenological Proof Learning (15 May 2026). A conjecture becomes a typed package, an attempt becomes an obligation graph, and every failed step becomes a recorded residue. A result is released only when every verifier factor is 1: the proof, a Lean kernel check, programs with checked output, the trace, simulations, the risk audit, the literature check and a human referee. The engine proves nothing by itself; obligations change status only through verifiers, and the label comes only from the release algebra. This is version 1.1 of the circuit. A review of the paper's numbered results finds that Theorem 10.4, Proposition 10.2, the second part of Lemma 6.2, Proposition 8.2, the "only if" of Proposition 21.1 and the collapse guard of Theorem 30.1 are false as stated; each counterexample is proved in Lean (26 theorems, only the standard axioms, replayed with leanchecker) and checked in C, C++ and Julia, and the package implements the corrections. It records the closures and partial results of this project as CANDIDATE until refereed, six calibration theorems, and eight open problems as OPEN.

title: A Security-Aware System Architecture for Latency-Bounded Ontology-Driven Integration in Additive Manufacturing
abstract: Semantic integration in Additive Manufacturing (AM) supervision demands unifying heterogeneous sensor streams and production context under strict latency and data-integrity constraints, yet conventional semantic stacks suffer from unpredictable query latencies, unguarded SPARQL (SPARQL Protocol and Resource Description Framework [RDF] Query Language) endpoints, and prohibitive reasoning overheads. This paper presents Semantic DREAM (Distributed Resilient and Emergent intelligence-based Additive Manufacturing), a security-aware architecture co-designed over a Web Ontology Language 2 Rule Language (OWL 2 RL) modular substrate with three mechanisms: (1) an abstract syntax tree (AST)-guarded read-only SPARQL engine that blocks destructive updates and caches template results; (2) a multi-protocol mashup layer aligning live Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT), Representational State Transfer (REST), Structured Query Language (SQL), and file feeds through Sensor, Observation, Sample, and Actuator (SOSA) observation minting and Quantities, Units, Dimensions, and Types (QUDT) unit normalization; and (3) an ingestion-time Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL) validation pipeline that gates observations before graph commit, decoupling structural checks from reasoning. Deductive materialization is performed offline at startup and verified with ROBOT as an intentional design choice to eliminate reasoning overhead from the streaming path, so online monitoring queries evaluate directly over the asserted graph. Single-host, lab-scale evaluations show that cached queries achieve sub-15 ms response times for recurring monitoring, while the worst-case event-driven decision cycle (incurring a post-invalidation cache miss) completes in 110 ms, well within the 200 ms supervisory deadline with 100% defect interception on injected anomalies. All measurements are single-host and lab-scale; factory-network transit and recorded telemetry are not evaluated.

title: CU-PVForecast: photovoltaic forecasting, conformal calibration and dispatch — reproducibility materials
abstract: Reproducibility materials accompanying CU-PVForecast, a photovoltaic forecasting and microgrid dispatch study prepared for Energy and AI. Includes the executed self-contained notebook (E1–E9), dependency versions, supplied numerical results and figures, an independent re-execution record, file hashes and a methodological audit. Adaptive multi-horizon intervals use retrospective feedback ordering beyond the 15-minute lead; these results do not establish deployable delayed-feedback calibration. Dispatch is an offline simulation with a synthetic load, not a field trial. Raw third-party Kaggle CSV files are not redistributed; the source URL and exact input checksums are provided. The manuscript has not been accepted or published by Energy and AI. Version 1.0.0.

title: The Price of Thinking in Bangla: audit package (code, 15,214 per-call billing logs, tables, dated prices)
abstract: Complete, re-runnable audit package for the paper "The Price of Thinking in Bangla: Tokenization Premiums and the Reasoning-Token Tax in Commercial LLM APIs" (submitted to IEEE Access). It contains the measurement pipeline, the frozen configuration and 15,214 per-call billing logs (a 12,000-call paired Bangla/English full run on four commercial APIs, pilots and smoke tests including a 150-call direct-API cross-check, a 114-call doubled-cap re-measurement, a 750-call crossed-instruction control, and a 40-call raw-payload capture with complete response bodies). It also holds the frozen FLORES-200 and MGSM data slices with SHA-256 checksums, dated official price records with screenshots, token-count tables, the 278-response human grading audit, the list of 15 MGSM-bn items whose Bangla translation changes the problem, provider dashboard captures with later recaptures (personal account details blacked out), and the statistics-reproduction, robustness-check and figure scripts. All API measurements and prices are a snapshot of 2026-10-08. README.md and RESOURCE_CARD.md inside the archive give schemas, join keys, licenses, and a map from every paper table and figure to its file and script.

title: SE-ResNet-Based Breast Cancer Histopathological Image Classification on the BreaKHis Dataset
abstract: Breast cancer histopathological image classification is an important task in computer-aided pathological image analysis. Handcrafted feature-based methods require substantial feature engineering, while conventional CNN architectures may have limited adaptive feature weighting and multi-level feature fusion. This paper presents an SE-ResNet-based model for binary classification of breast histopathological images into benign and malignant categories. A 3 × 1 asymmetric convolution was adopted as a parameter-efficient alternative to the corresponding 3 × 3 configuration. SE attention was integrated with residual blocks for adaptive channel recalibration, and bilinear upsampling was used to fuse multi-level feature maps. Experiments were conducted on the BreaKHis dataset containing 7909 images at four magnifications (40×, 100×, 200×, 400×). The comparative experiments across five patient-disjoint trials showed that the 3 × 1 kernel, a batch size of 24 and the SE-ResNet configuration achieved the highest mean image-level accuracy, patient-level accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1-score among their respective tested configurations. Under the magnification-independent classification setting, the model achieved 92.95 ± 0.08% image-level accuracy and 91.88 ± 1.35% patient-level accuracy. These results support the feasibility of the proposed architecture for benign/malignant classification on the BreaKHis dataset.

title: Beyond Adjacent Layers: Graph-Guided Layer Fusion for Compressing Large Language Models
abstract: Existing depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B-14B parameters). Non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity-based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre-specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity. At 2x compression, FCM lowers mean perplexity below ShortGPT on twelve of thirteen models, significantly on ten (Welch's t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction; up to 50% on Qwen3-4B), with Mistral-7B the only loss (+13.4%). Against FlattenGPT, SWM, and DeltaLLM under matched calibration and recovery, FCM gives the best perplexity on ten of thirteen models (mean rank 1.15), and it also outperforms MKA on three anchor models. FCM matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning cells and also improves MMLU, LAMBADA, HumanEval pass@1, and free-form generation quality. The 2x-compressed Qwen2.5-7B has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100. Spectral grouping outperforms Fisher contiguous segmentation by 41% and uniform partitioning by 51%, and FCM's advantage grows beyond a 2x crossover up to 3x and persists at the 14B scale. Code: https://github.com/Usama1002/fcm-layer-fusion

title: SemiCodec: Bridging Speech Tokenization and High-fidelity Reconstruction with Semi-discrete Representations
abstract: Speech representation learning requires a discrete modeling interface while preserving high waveform fidelity. Existing approaches rarely achieve both: discrete tokens ease modeling but lose fine-grained acoustic information, while continuous latents preserve fidelity but require specialized generative objectives. We introduce SemiCodec, a novel Semi-discrete neural speech Codec with synchronized discrete tokens and continuous latents. Direct joint optimization may create a reconstruction shortcut through the continuous pathway, leaving the discrete tokens insufficiently grounded. To address this issue, we propose a Preserve-then-Ground training paradigm that first establishes a high-fidelity synthesis space and then grounds SSL-guided discrete tokens within it. Experiments show that SemiCodec outperforms fully discrete codecs in reconstruction quality and intelligibility while remaining competitive with continuous representations in acoustic fidelity and speaker preservation. Audio samples are available at https://pennyw1-se.github.io/SemiCodec-Demo-Page/

title: Competition Domains Matter: Selective Head Globalization for Training-Free Sparse Attention in Video Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Training-free sparse attention is a practical route to efficient video diffusion transformer inference, yet existing methods typically fix the competition domain at each query row for every attention head. Prior work primarily addresses how to estimate token-level importance within this fixed domain; whether the domain itself should adapt to head heterogeneity remains under-specified. We introduce EG-Sparse, a training-free framework that routes low-entropy heads to a grouped cross-head pool while retaining per-row local selection for high-entropy heads, using only scores already materialized by the sparse pipeline. A controlled diagnostic fixes the ranking score and varies only the competition rule: grouped cross-head selection reduces low-entropy-head reconstruction error by 9.8%, whereas forcing high-entropy heads into an all-head global pool increases it by 7.9%. Across four configurations, EG-Sparse achieves higher video quality while reducing attention density and GPU denoising latency compared with strong training-free sparse-attention baselines. Mechanism ablations further show that selective domain adaptation outperforms uniform, random, and fixed domain-assignment policies. These results support competition-domain adaptation as a distinct design axis within centroid-guided training-free sparse attention.

title: BT‑PEC Full‑Stack Computing Framework: A Steady-State Dynamic Scheduling Model for Open Quantum Systems
abstract: This paper proposes the BT-PEC full-stack computing framework to address the challenge that traditional static resource scheduling and fixed error correction strategies fail to adapt to time-varying noise and dynamic decoherence of coherent resources in the NISQ era for open quantum systems. The framework includes a quantum living-state architecture, a quantum operating system, and a unified programming language system, with falsifiable engineering predictions and simulation verification schemes. Four core operators are defined: the B basis operator representing underlying hardware quantum resources; the T transition operator describing coherent energy input and quantum state evolution; the P power consumption operator for resource and energy costs from gate operations and entanglement generation; and the EC entropy-causal closure operator implementing error correction, feedback compensation and causal recording constraints. A global steady-state order parameter Ω=tr(BT)−tr(PEC) is introduced. Three system phases are classified by threshold ϵ=0.05: survival state (Ω_Q>0.05), critical state (|Ω_Q|≤0.05), and extinction state (Ω_Q<−0.05). The Lindblad master equation is adopted to model open quantum system dynamics, combined with an exponential fidelity decay model and binary information entropy proxy function. The phase transition critical decoherence parameter γ_c≈0.42 is obtained from simulation, which is only valid within this model and not a universal physical constant. The full-stack hardware-software co-design consists of a topology-logic two-layer quantum hardware architecture, the BT-PEC/OS quantum operating system kernel with Ω_Q-aware task scheduling, and Omega-IR intermediate representation together with a multi-paradigm unified programming language. The FEA cross-language adaptation layer enables compatibility with Python, C++ and other programming environments. Numerical simulations are implemented on QuTiP with five controlled repeatable experiments. Eight quantifiable, falsifiable engineering predictions are presented with explicit falsification criteria. Limitations of the model are clarified: γ_c is simulation-specific; BT and PEC operator matrices need instantiation for individual hardware; Omega-IR currently only has semantic specifications without a production-grade compiler and virtual machine; performance advantages are validated only by numerical simulation pending physical quantum hardware tests; causal chain integrity under high concurrency remains an engineering challenge. The BT-PEC framework unifies quantum hardware, operating system and compilation system under one steady-state evaluation system, offering a verifiable engineering theoretical model for hardware-software co-design of quantum computers under dynamic NISQ noise environments. Future work includes completing the Omega-IR compiler, scaling up simulations, and preparing validation experiments on small-scale physical quantum processors.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Early Detection of Chronic Diseases in Saudi Healthcare: A Systematic Review
abstract: Background: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) may support earlier detection of chronic disease, but Saudi-specific evidence has not been systematically characterized. Objective: To synthesize Saudi patient-level studies of AI/XAI for chronic-disease prediction and assess clinical readiness. Methods: PubMed and supplementary publisher-site, reference, and citation searches were completed on 26 August 2026. Eligible primary studies used Saudi clinical data for prediction, classification, or risk stratification. Findings were narratively synthesized and appraised with an adapted PROBAST framework. Results: Fifty-eight records were identified, 52 screened, nine assessed in full, and four included. Studies addressed chronic kidney disease, diabetic kidney disease, hypertension, and right-sided cardiac dysfunction. Reported discrimination was promising, with explicit SHAP-based explanations in three studies; however, all lacked independent external validation and had high overall risk of bias. Conclusion: Saudi XAI research is promising but clinically preliminary. Multicentre external validation, calibration, fairness evaluation, and prospective impact studies are required before routine deployment

title: A Study on LLM-Driven Knowledge Graph Construction and Production Anomaly Inference for Semantic Standardization of Multi-Factory Data in Automotive Manufacturing
abstract: Multi-plant automotive-component data contain inconsistent field names, device codes, quality codes, and unstructured production logs. This study presents an LLM-driven method for manufacturing semantic standardization and knowledge-graph reasoning. Equipment signals, production beats, quality inspections, maintenance work orders, VIN/OCR results, shutdown events, and process files are integrated to construct cross-factory semantic mapping tasks. Sentence-BERT and GPT-4o-mini perform field alignment and context correction; BERT-CRF supports entity extraction, while GraphSAGE and R-GCN infer typed anomaly relations. KG-RAG and an LLM Agent are further used for quality tracing and case retrieval. Experiments cover 4 plants, 9 production lines, 156 field categories, 780,000 production records, and 120,000 maintenance and quality texts. Under leave-one-factory-out evaluation, Sentence-BERT plus GPT-4o-mini achieves 94.1% field-matching accuracy and 94.6% precision. The 94.1% accuracy is 21.3 percentage points above rule-based mapping at 72.8%, corresponding to a 29.3% relative improvement. GraphSAGE-R-GCN obtains Hits@10 of 0.876 on the mixed split and 0.842 under factory holdout. The complete KG-RAG-Agent system reaches retrieval P@20 of 0.842, R@20 of 0.816, and 92.1% answer accuracy, while reducing mean anomaly-tracing time from 2.8 h to 54 min. These results show that semantic constraints and typed graph reasoning support cross-factory anomaly transfer and evidence-grounded knowledge reuse.

title: Replication materials for "When Candidate-Dependent Proxies Preserve Exact Speculative Sampling"
abstract: Replication materials for the manuscript "When Candidate-Dependent Proxies Preserve Exact Speculative Sampling" by Junye Fu. The archive contains three Python scripts, their recorded results, and instructions for reproducing finite-state checks of the exactness classification: five ternary survivors, two binary survivors, 1,815 four-symbol output-distribution and acceptance checks, and four candidate-mapping patterns. The public-code replay examines a pinned upstream implementation; upstream source code is not redistributed. These materials support the mathematical analysis and constructed finite checks. They do not contain LLM generation or throughput benchmarks. See README.txt for the environment, commands, and the pinned upstream revision.
