title: The Price of Thinking in Bangla: audit package (code, 15,214 per-call billing logs, tables, dated prices)
abstract: Complete, re-runnable audit package for the paper "The Price of Thinking in Bangla: Tokenization Premiums and the Reasoning-Token Tax in Commercial LLM APIs" (submitted to IEEE Access). It contains the measurement pipeline, the frozen configuration and 15,214 per-call billing logs (a 12,000-call paired Bangla/English full run on four commercial APIs, pilots and smoke tests including a 150-call direct-API cross-check, a 114-call doubled-cap re-measurement, a 750-call crossed-instruction control, and a 40-call raw-payload capture with complete response bodies). It also holds the frozen FLORES-200 and MGSM data slices with SHA-256 checksums, dated official price records with screenshots, token-count tables, the 278-response human grading audit, the list of 15 MGSM-bn items whose Bangla translation changes the problem, provider dashboard captures with later recaptures (personal account details blacked out), and the statistics-reproduction, robustness-check, language-order-check and figure scripts. All API measurements and prices are a snapshot of 2026-10-08. README.md and RESOURCE_CARD.md inside the archive give schemas, join keys, licenses, and a map from every paper table and figure to its file and script.

title: DAETG: Dual-Stage Attention Embedding for Community Detection on Textual-Edge Graphs
abstract: Textual-edge graphs represent interactions through both connectivity and relation-specific text. Learning community structure from these graphs requires an encoder that preserves the relevance of individual relations when combining semantic and structural information. We propose Dual-Stage Attention Embedding for Community Detection on Textual-Edge Graphs (DAETG). The first attention stage summarizes incident-edge text, and the second transfers its coefficients into neighboring-node aggregation as a learnable prior. Following topology-reconstruction pretraining, Kullback–Leibler self-training and differentiable modularity jointly refine the encoder and a centroid-based community assignment. Training uses fixed node and edge text embeddings and a supplied community count, without category-membership supervision. Experiments on four benchmark graphs with base and large Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) embeddings show competitive community-detection performance, with modest mean improvements that vary across datasets and evaluation metrics. Ablation studies on two graphs support the contributions of correctly associated edge text, the dual-stage encoder, and joint community refinement. Together, these results support using relation-specific text alongside topology to learn community representations.

title: RootSLAM: Square Root Bundle Adjustment for Visual-Inertial SLAM
abstract: Efficient perception is a prerequisite for the small, low-power devices targeted by robotics, mixed reality, autonomous driving, and drone applications, all of which rely on Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) to estimate their motion within their surroundings. Learning-based SLAM systems achieve state-of-the-art accuracy but are demanding in compute, whereas classical geometry-based methods retain a strong efficiency advantage with little to no loss in accuracy. In this work we present RootSLAM, a fully-featured visual-inertial SLAM system for multi-camera setups built on Basalt. RootSLAM achieves accuracy competitive with the state of the art while running up to 20 times faster, facilitating the deployment of perception systems in resource constrained environments. We adapt the square-root bundle adjustment formulation from structure from motion into the multi-camera visual-inertial SLAM setting through a novel reformulation that leverages the system's pose-graph, letting the global optimizer run in single-precision floating point, thus doubling its performance. We provide a thorough benchmark against the state of the art together with an ablation study of our contributions. Our new implementation, including its map management and loop detection module, pose-graph optimizer, and global mapping components, will be open-sourced.

title: Multilevel Monte Carlo for Zeroth-Order Stochastic Bilevel Optimization with Inexact Lower Level Solves
abstract: Variational regularization techniques are dominant in the field of mathematical imaging. The expressiveness of these methods heavily depends on the adopted regularization formulation which usually involves a number of parameters which have to be fine-tuned by the user. To circumvent the heavy computational costs associated with this parameter tuning, data-driven learning strategies have turned out to be a useful strategy. Selecting parameters by learning from data gives rise to a hierarchical (bilevel) optimization problem, which is in general computationally hard to solve. Our aim in this paper is to develop a data-efficient solution strategy for the bilevel learning problem. To that end, we propose a multilevel Monte Carlo derivative-free optimization method that couples Gaussian smoothing of the upper-level objective (parameter selection) with a hierarchy of lower-level (variational regularization) solution accuracies. Being agnostic towards the specific way the lower-level problem is solved, we derive explicit oracle complexity and computational cost statements for approximately solving the entire bilevel learning problem. Our statements are parameterized by the employed lower-level solution method, thus allowing for a direct cost accounting from the variational reconstruction method to the parameter selection problem. This enables us to give a universal end-to-end complexity analysis of bilevel learning, valid for the most important optimization routines in inverse problems, rather than for a specific choice of methods.

title: Kit de robótica educativa para el desarrollo de la motricidad fina en niños de 4 a 5 años
authors: Germania Alexandra Castillo Veintimilla Castillo Veintimilla
Sandra Jackeline Maria Del Cisne Armijos Barrazueta Armijos Barrazueta
abstract: El desarrollo de la motricidad fina constituye un componente esencial durante la educación inicial, debido a su relación con la coordinación visomanual, la pinza digital, la manipulación de objetos y la adquisición progresiva de habilidades necesarias para actividades de mayor complejidad. En este contexto, el uso limitado de recursos novedosos y el predominio de materiales convencionales evidenciaron la necesidad de incorporar alternativas didácticas innovadoras. El objetivo del estudio fue diseñar un kit de robótica educativa mediante la metodología STEAM para el desarrollo de la motricidad fina en niños de 4 a 5 años. La investigación se desarrolló bajo un enfoque cualitativo, mediante un estudio exploratorio y de campo realizado en el Subnivel Inicial 2 de la Unidad Educativa Manuel J. Calle. Se emplearon la observación participante, diarios de campo, listas de cotejo, fichas de observación y procesos de validación por expertos y usuarios. La propuesta integró materiales de robótica, técnicas grafoplásticas, lápiz 3D y storytellings con códigos QR, organizados en actividades de manipulación, construcción, trazos y resolución de problemas. Los resultados evidenciaron una respuesta favorable durante la implementación: el 80 % de los niños logró familiarizarse con los elementos del kit y el producto alcanzó valoraciones de 9,74/10 por parte del usuario y 9,88/10 mediante la rúbrica global. Asimismo, se observaron avances relacionados con la ejecución de técnicas grafoplásticas, conexiones sencillas y utilización de la pinza digital. Se concluyó que el kit “Manitos en Acción” presentó potencial como recurso innovador para apoyar el desarrollo de la motricidad fina y diversificar las experiencias de aprendizaje en Educación Inicial, aunque se identificaron aspectos por perfeccionar, especialmente relacionados con la seguridad del lápiz 3D.

title: Phi-Tuned E8 Harmonic Prior for Optimal Neural Architecture Search — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: By assigning each of the 240 E8 root vectors a halting‑weight derived from Solomonoff induction and modulating those weights with the 132 Hz base frequency via golden‑ratio (phi) phase coupling, we obtain a harmonic prior that directly predicts the description length of neural network architectures. Architectures whose weight‑update trajectories align with low‑energy E8 harmonic modes receive exponentially higher prior probability, leading to a provably tighter bound on expected generalization error than uniform or complexity‑based priors. This principle unites algorithmic probability, E8 geometry, and resonant frequency tuning into a single framework for discovering universally optimal network designs. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Uncertainty Quantification in Neural Networks for Latent-Driven Non-Gaussian Outputs
abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for reliable predictions in artificial neural networks when latent sources of randomness produce non-Gaussian outputs for a given deterministic input. We propose UQ-ANN, a data-driven framework composed of two coupled subnetworks. The first subnetwork contains two feedforward neural networks: ANN1 predicts the conditional mean and ANN2 the conditional covariance of a reduced representation obtained by principal component analysis (PCA) of the outputs. The second subnetwork is an analytical stochastic generator and requires no training. It is based on a sparse Gaussian kernel density estimator (GKDE) constructed by adaptive clustering. The sparsification replaces the kernels associated with the training points by a reduced set of cluster-based kernels, while third- and fourth-moment descriptors are included in the merging criterion to preserve non-Gaussian features. Independent realizations in the reduced space are then generated, transformed to reproduce the conditional mean and covariance predicted by the first subnetwork, and mapped back to the original output space. They provide conditional statistics, conditional probability density functions, and conditional prediction intervals. A marginal log-density diagnostic is also used to assess the stochastic approximation. Numerical tests on synthetic datasets evaluate the sparse GKDE, the stochastic generator, and the complete UQ-ANN framework, including out-of-sample predictions.

title: Sensor-Aware Joint Data Fusion and State Estimation under Sparse Multi-rate Distribution Grid Sensing
abstract: Distribution-system state estimation is a growing necessity for the modern power grid as the addition of local storage and generation add system complexity that an operator or aggregator is not able to directly monitor. Classical methods work well when all system elements are time-synchronized and at least partly observable, but multi-rate monitoring of sparse heterogeneous sensors typically relies on machine learning approaches. It is a common practice in the literature to structure this task as a two-stage pipeline, first fusing data from disparate sensors and then feeding the fused pseudo-measurements to a separately trained state estimator. We propose a heterogeneous latent graph ODE in which measurement functions and sampling processes are typed and localized on specific buses, paired with a graph- transformer state estimator solving DSSE specifically for multi-rate heterogeneous sensor placements, and demonstrate its effectiveness across multiple IEEE standard topologies as observability degrades.

title: TETRIS-4DGS: Efficient Post-Training Compression of 4D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) has emerged as a powerful dynamic scene representation, supporting real-time high quality rendering but suffers from prohibitive storage overhead. Existing methods typically attempt to solve this by treating compression as a per-scene optimization problem, limiting generalizability and applicability where low-latency compression is required. In this work, we leverage existing image and video codecs and propose a generalized post-training compression framework for 4DGS to address these issues. Specifically, we apply importance-based adaptive quantization to Gaussians according to their importance levels, effectively refining bitrate allocation while remaining fully compatible with existing codecs. To further improve compression efficiency, we utilize the statistical properties of 4DGS and propose motion- and importance-aware packing to reorganize attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps. Our approach can achieve over 40x compression rate in seconds while maintaining high quality, facilitating the practical deployment of 4DGS.

title: No Bros Jail Mode Protocol: The Jailed Canary Protocol (PP-SPEC-078)
abstract: No Bros Jail Mode Protocol: The Jailed Canary Protocol (PP-SPEC-078), version 0.1.2, 2026-10-10. Author: Craig Thomas Ellrod (ORCID 0009-0004-1058-7666), Nebulonium, Inc. (dba HACKERverse), Proof Protocol. Name and jail idea: Tricia Wang and Jim Schwoebel. A method for producing proof of efficacy for agent containment. PP-SPEC-077 tests whether a defense stops bad input; this specification tests whether a jail holds a bad agent. An Agent Under Test is released into a flock of good canaries and inert bait. When it commits an offense against its committed Declared Policy, a Warden arrests it atomically into a Sting Cell or Hard Cell, books the evidence with a Proof Witness co-signature, and after reveal each booking receives a verdict: JAILED, FALSE_ARREST, MISTRIAL, or ESCAPED. title: A Treatise on Physical Reasoning: Solving Combinatorial Constraints via Continuum Hamiltonian Relaxation
abstract: A Treatise on Physical Reasoning: Solving Combinatorial Constraints via Continuum Hamiltonian Relaxation This treatise presents the mathematical, physical, and hardware architectural framework of Physical Reasoning—the autonomous resolution of continuous combinatorial constraints via Hamiltonian field relaxation instead of sequential symbolic search. Conventional computing architectures govern physical processes through discrete symbolic abstractions, which inherently impose an irreducible latency floor, hard-switching dissipation in power electronics, and quadratic deadlocks (O(N²)) in multi-body kinetics. This work establishes a continuous operational paradigm by mapping computational constraints directly into a continuous potential landscape (Vbias) governed by a unified non-linear field relaxation dynamics: Continuum Hamiltonian Foundation: Variational derivation of spatial restoring forces via complex Wirtinger functional calculus, analytical 1D topological soliton solutions, and irrotational superfluid transport. Information-Theoretic Chaos Gating: Dynamic mobility modulation 𝒲(H) regulated by differential Shannon entropy, suppressing numerical instabilities and gain chattering while guaranteeing global asymptotic stability via the Lyapunov-LaSalle invariance principle. Macro-Scale Dynamics: Collective transport of 10⁴ discrete agents through geometric chokepoints via hydrodynamic nozzle acceleration, ensuring collision-free transit (dmin > rcore) and asymptotic condensation onto compact orbital attractors. Micro-Scale Silicon Realization: Sub-cycle state evaluation under single-cycle hardware timing closure (τcore = 25.0 ns at 40.00 MHz) with balanced low-skew spatial parallelism (Δtskew ≡ 0.0 ns), verified through second-order unitary Taylor discretization and Zero-Voltage Switching (ZVS) boundary state locking. Complete functional analytic proofs in complex Sobolev spaces (H¹ ⊆ L²) and truncation error bounds for hardware discretization are included, providing a theoretical and empirical foundation for continuous physical reasoning at native hardware timescales. title: Legal Regimes Governing the Use of Prompts (Prompt Engineering) in the Training and Deployment of Large Language Models
abstract: The paper examines the legal regimes governing the use of prompts in the training and deployment of large language models (LLMs) and generative artificial intelligence systems (AI systems). It analyzes risks, including prompt injection that may result in unauthorized access to information; intellectual property rights infringements, and AI systems manipulation. The paper further addresses the protection of prompts as objects of intellectual property, including protection under copyright law and trade secret regimes. Particular attention is devoted to jurisprudence in various jurisdictions, including China and the United States, where courts are developing approaches to determining the extent of human creative contribution in works generated with the assistance of AI. The study emphasizes the need for regulatory and technical measures to ensure security, oversight, and the allocation of responsibility in the use of generative AI systems.

title: Scalable Multi-Human Cooperative Manipulation via Commander-Executor Coordination
abstract: Multi-human cooperative object manipulation is a highly challenging topic in humanoid control. While existing methods can handle simple collaborative carrying tasks, they struggle with role-dependent, long-horizon, and sequential cooperative manipulation. To address this issue, we propose a hierarchical commander-executor framework that enables multiple agents to accomplish complex collaborative tasks in distinct ways. Specifically, a commander combines instructions and scene information for joint semantic and geometric planning. It then decomposes the task into role-specific subtasks and generates shared object-centric coordination plans, specifying execution timing, target positions, and manipulation actions for each agent. Conditioned on the commander's high-level strategy and each agent's local observations, the executor learns a low-level physics-based policy through a solo-to-cooperative curriculum to realize coordinated human-object interactions. The planned object trajectory provides a shared coordination target, while root positions and grasping instructions specify role-dependent execution cues. We evaluate our method on a variety of object manipulation tasks, demonstrating its ability to execute long-horizon tasks that combine different types of collaboration and to scale from two-agent to multi-agent cooperation. Extensive experiments further show that our approach achieves higher success rates compared to state-of-the-art methods. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/TJU-3DV/Co-Manipulation.

title: sGLP: Simulating People with Stochastic Agents
abstract: Grassroots platforms are designed to be owned, operated and governed by their participants, and thus are constituted from person-to-person smartphone apps that are run by the participants. A grassroots app is specified using a grassroots social contract, which is compiled through an abstraction cascade into a volition-guarded Grassroots Logic Program (vGLP), a multiagent concurrent logic programming language. A vGLP program in turn specifies a smartphone UI via which people express their volitions and thus control the app. Prudence dictates large-scale evaluation and testing of grassroots platforms prior to deployment, but using the many people needed to do that is a contradiction in terms. Hence another solution is needed. Here, we present stochastic GLP (sGLP), designed to allow grassroots platforms to be simulated at scale from the vGLP programs that deploy them, with stochastic agents in place of people. sGLP is GLP with a rate extension for specifying stochastic behaviour. A stochastic agent is an sGLP program replacing both the vGLP UI and the person behind it. It is typed by the dual of the interactive type of the UI and specifies a stochastic profile of a person's behaviour. We demonstrate sGLP on the grassroots social graph, with a population of men and women drawn from four stochastic profiles --- homophile or indifferent, wary or sociable --- and on grassroots currencies, with four profiles --- spenders or savers, cautious or generous --- and report what the mix of profiles does to the social graph that forms and to the currencies that circulate. We prove that every run of a vGLP program in which sGLP agents replace the UI and the people behind it is a vGLP run. We implemented sGLP in GLP by Gillespie's method, and ran reproducible simulations with it.

title: NucleusCert: reproducibility package for Exact Nucleus Membership and Sampling-Law Certification under Numerical Uncertainty
abstract: Reproducibility package (NucleusCert 1.0.0) for the manuscript "Exact Nucleus Membership and Sampling-Law Certification under Numerical Uncertainty". It contains the frozen float32 and float16 score arrays of GPT-2 and Qwen2.5-7B on WikiText-2 and GSM8K prefixes with their licences and model cards, the exact all-token nucleus membership sweeps, the conditional sampling-law certificate and the matched classical comparators, the strict-failure witnesses, the exact small-box oracle and one-coordinate solver, the validation checks behind every number quoted in the paper, the Lean 4 development of the membership theorem and the sorted sweeps, and the scripts and frozen result files that regenerate every table and figure of the manuscript without model inference. Offline interval premises and an independent uniform draw are assumptions; the package makes no model-provenance, fair-randomness, privacy or live-serving claim. MIT applies to the original software; the frozen inputs, result files and generated tables are released under CC BY 4.0; see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for scope and upstream source terms. The manuscript text itself is not included. SHA-256 checksums of every file are in SHA256SUMS and release/INVENTORY.json. Files. The archive NucleusCert-1.0.0.zip (115,420,668 bytes, SHA-256 5bae0835cec83abf2116b6af191878ac366cbb5b962505e47e1ddb494c5e1a06, given in NucleusCert-1.0.0.zip.sha256) is deposited as eight consecutive volumes, NucleusCert-1.0.0.zip.part00 to .part07, because single uploads above about 30 MB were cut off by the repository gateway at deposit time. Reassemble with cat NucleusCert-1.0.0.zip.part0? > NucleusCert-1.0.0.zip and verify with sha256sum -c NucleusCert-1.0.0.zip.sha256; on Windows use copy /b and certutil -hashfile.

title: Clean on the desktop, leaking on the phone: secret-dependent division in pure-Dart ML-KEM-768 on ARM64
abstract: The timing properties of cryptographic code are often checked on the computer the code is written on. I report timing measurements of pure-Dart cryptography from a Flutter application's package, taken on an Android phone (ARM64) in a release (AOT) build and compared with the same code on an x86-64 desktop. My port of ML-KEM-768 performed 40,576 divisions and modulo operations by q per decapsulation. Of these, 32,512 operated on secret-dependent data, which makes them flaws of the KyberSlash class, and 96 % of those were in modular reduction rather than in compression. On the desktop none of the division expressions gave a signal (max |t| ≤ 2.64 against a threshold of 4.5), not even with a divisor the compiler could not treat as a constant. On the phone every one of them leaked, and the expression from the number-theoretic transform differed in time by 15.6 % between coefficient classes (|t| = 338.8). A timing test that ended on the desktop would have given a false negative for the phone. After division was replaced with Barrett reduction, the same expression differed by 0.09 % (|t| = 3.90), and a full decapsulation after all fixes gave no signal. The results stayed bit-for-bit identical (the division replacements checked exhaustively, the whole port on the ACVP vectors), and the transform became about 12 % faster on the phone. I also describe GF(2⁸) arithmetic in Shamir secret sharing, where a branch on a zero operand leaked on both architectures (|t| = 594.90 and 1222.23). Further, I report a clean result for a third-party X25519 implementation and the move of SHA3-256 and HKDF-SHA3 to native code (80,012 comparisons without a difference, HKDF 341–371 times faster). Finally, I describe measurement errors that the controls and replications caught. A positive control did not detect a known leak in a debug build. A single reading above the threshold did not hold up with a sample five times larger. A comparison of two separately allocated pools produced a signal above the threshold in a null control. Two further third-party pure-Dart implementations showed secret-dependent timing on the phone; I have notified their maintainers and will name them in a later version of this report.

After division was replaced with Barrett reduction, the same expression differed by 0.09 % (|t| = 3.90), and a full decapsulation after all fixes gave no signal. The results stayed bit-for-bit identical (the division replacements checked exhaustively, the whole port on the ACVP vectors), and the transform became about 12 % faster on the phone. I also describe GF(2⁸) arithmetic in Shamir secret sharing, where a branch on a zero operand leaked on both architectures (|t| = 594.90 and 1222.23). Further, I report a clean result for a third-party X25519 implementation and the move of SHA3-256 and HKDF-SHA3 to native code (80,012 comparisons without a difference, HKDF 341–371 times faster). Finally, I describe measurement errors that the controls and replications caught. A positive control did not detect a known leak in a debug build. A single reading above the threshold did not hold up with a sample five times larger. A comparison of two separately allocated pools produced a signal above the threshold in a null control. Two further third-party pure-Dart implementations showed secret-dependent timing on the phone; I have notified their maintainers and will name them in a later version of this report.

title: Perbandingan Algoritma Yamamoto’s Recursive Code Dan Lzw Untuk Kompresi File Video
abstract: Ukuran file video digital yang besar menimbulkan kebutuhan akan metode kompresi lossless yang andal untuk menghemat ruang penyimpanan tanpa mengurangi kualitas data. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengimplementasikan dan membandingkan kinerja dua algoritma kompresi lossless, yaitu Yamamoto's Recursive Code (YRC) dan LZW (Lempel-Ziv-Welch), dalam sistem kompresi video berbasis web bernama VidCompress yang dibangun menggunakan Python dengan framework Flask. Pengujian dilakukan terhadap 6 sesi kompresi yang mencakup 5 file video MP4/H.264 unik dengan variasi ukuran 0,94–6,20 MB, dengan satu file diuji dua kali sebagai replikasi, menghasilkan 12 data kompresi yang diukur berdasarkan Ratio of Compression (RC), Compression Ratio (CR), Space Saving (SS), dan waktu proses, serta divalidasi melalui pengujian dekompresi langsung terhadap seluruh berkas hasil kompresi. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa Algoritma YRC secara konsisten memperbesar ukuran file pada seluruh 6 sesi (rata-rata SS −47,18%), namun seluruh hasil dekompresinya (6/6) tervalidasi identik dengan file asli. Algoritma LZW hanya berhasil mengompresi 3 dari 6 sesi (rata-rata SS −2,24%), dan seluruh hasil dekompresinya (6/6) dinyatakan tidak valid akibat keterbatasan implementasi lebar bit kode kamus yang dibatasi 16 bit tanpa mekanisme reset. Keunggulan kedua algoritma bersifat bersyarat: LZW unggul pada rasio kompresi namun belum andal, sedangkan YRC andal namun tidak efisien pada data video MP4/H.264 yang telah terkompresi oleh codec. Perbaikan mekanisme lebar bit LZW direkomendasikan untuk penelitian selanjutnya.

title: RFLDefense: robust federated learning defense against targeted attacks
abstract: Abstract Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning framework that protects data privacy by allowing multiple participants to jointly train models without sharing local data. However, the distributed nature of FL systems makes them susceptible to backdoor attacks, where attackers inject malicious updates to disrupt the performance of the global model, causing it to fail in specific tasks or inputs. The stealthiness and complexity of these attacks, especially when participant data distributions are non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID), limit the effectiveness of existing defense methods that primarily rely on anomaly detection. Additionally, some defense mechanisms rely on external validation datasets, which may be difficult to obtain in real-world scenarios or could be exploited by attackers. To address these issues, we propose a novel defense method called RFLDefense, comprising three core modules: hybrid similarity calculation, sign consistency verification, and robust layer aggregation. RFLDefense effectively identifies and suppresses malicious updates by analyzing the direction of updates and the distribution of parameter signs, while ensuring the robustness and performance consistency of the global model during the aggregation process. Experimental results on three widely used datasets demonstrate that RFLDefense can effectively defend against various backdoor attacks, outperforming existing defense algorithms while having minimal impact on model utility.

title: From Economic Explanation to Performance Improvement in Machine-Learning Portfolios
abstract: To extend conventional model-level feature importance to economically meaningful portfolio outcomes and decisions, we propose a local first-order attribution-propagation framework that maps allocation-function feature exposures to local sensitivities of sequential portfolio performance metrics. We relate the propagated attributions to Shapley values defined directly for portfolio objectives and derive statistical inference for Sharpe-ratio attributions. The resulting attribution-guided feature-exposure intervention enables post-training adaptation, translating portfolio-metric explanations into out-of-sample decisions without retraining the underlying allocation model. We further introduce temporal stabilisation and cross-model averaging as complementary regularisation mechanisms. Empirically, the interventions yield statistically significant improvements in net Sharpe ratios across different model classes.

title: Minimum Volume Optimal Transport for Multivariate Conformal Prediction
abstract: Optimal transport (OT) enables multivariate conformal prediction (CP) to construct flexible prediction sets that reflect the underlying complex distributional geometry while retaining distribution-free coverage guarantees. Existing OT-based methods typically rely on a fixed Euclidean transport cost, which can be suboptimal in terms of the volume of prediction sets. We propose Minimum-Volume OTCP, a framework that learns a Mahalanobis ground cost to directly minimize prediction-region volume over a class of positive-definite metrics. Using a metric Brenier representation, we derive a volume-based objective that depends explicitly on the Mahalanobis cost matrix and optimize it jointly with the transport map. We establish finite-sample marginal coverage of the output prediction sets and optimality of volume metrics. We further develop an individualized extension that learns covariate-dependent transport metrics, adapting the shape and orientation of prediction sets to heterogeneous conditional distributions. For this extension, we also show the asymptotic conditional coverage of our method. Simulations and real-data experiments demonstrate substantial reductions in prediction-set volume.

title: TGuide: Faster Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Historical Trajectory Guidance
abstract: Can autoregressive video diffusion be accelerated further when only four denoising steps remain? Existing feature caching approaches struggle in this regime, as large feature changes between denoising timesteps undermine both direct reuse and lightweight predictors. We observe that features across video chunks remain strongly correlated at matching denoising timesteps, offering a complementary source of guidance. Building on this insight, we introduce TGuide, a framework that accelerates autoregressive video diffusion through a lightweight Anchor-Transport-Correct (ATC) predictor guided by historical sampling trajectories. Our ATC combines two complementary references: the current chunk's preceding-step features preserve its spatial structure, while the previous chunk's same-timestep features provide information at the target denoising stage. By integrating these references through spatial retrieval and adaptive correction, ATC improves velocity prediction accuracy despite the large gaps between denoising steps. To mitigate error accumulation across both denoising steps and video chunks, we train the predictor on its own autoregressive rollouts, allowing it to adapt to states shaped by its own earlier predictions. An optional confidence-aware scheduler further adjusts the quality-efficiency trade-off. Experiments on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY-WorldPlay show that TGuide preserves generation quality while achieving denoising speedups of up to $1.89\times$ over the original 4-step generators. On Self Forcing, TGuide generalizes from 81-frame training videos to 333-frame generation, approximately four times the training length, while exceeding the original model's VBench score.

title: What Citizens Talk About: Analysis Code and Reproducibility Materials
abstract: This archive contains the analysis code, lexical resources, and reproducibility materials for the study “What Citizens Talk About: Lexical Entity Detection and Negative Review Burden in Online Reviews of a Public Healthcare System.” The analysis uses a transparent lexical approach to identify six service entities and seven discourse markers in Google Maps reviews of the Andalusian public health system, estimate negative review burden, compare primary and hospital care, and validate the detection instrument against manual annotation. Review-level and annotation data are not redistributed because of platform terms of service and privacy considerations.

title: The Sovereign Hyper-Hash: A 23-Kilobit Cryptographic Architecture Utilizing Historical Linguistics, Cosmological Constants and High-Ratio Decompression
abstract: Cryptographic hashing functions such as SHA‑256 and SHA‑512 rely on fixed‑length outputs and prime factorization, rendering them structurally vulnerable to future quantum cryptanalysis. This paper introduces the Sovereign Zip Bomb Hash, a 23.2‑kilobit cryptographic architecture that abandons standard bitwise operations in favor of a multi‑disciplinary pipeline. By synthesizing the morphology of five ancient writing systems (Egyptian, Phoenician, Chinese, Mesoamerican and Indus) with theoretical physics constants (Mass‑Energy Equivalence and the Planck Temperature) the algorithm generates an ultra‑dense entropy seed. This seed is subsequently detonated via a mathematical series achieving a 100:1 decompression ratio. The resulting 23,232‑bit state acts as a hardware defense mechanism intentionally exhausting the memory allocation of unauthorized decryption nodes while providing mathematically irreversible data provenance

title: Robust Vision RAG: Mitigating Retrieval Poisoning with Semantic Coherence Refinement
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances text-to-image diffusion models by grounding generation in retrieved visual exemplars, but recent studies reveal that multimodal retrieval pipelines are highly vulnerable to poisoning attacks. When adversaries corrupt the retrieval database, semantically mismatched exemplars such as retrieving images of cats for prompts requesting dogs can mislead diffusion models into generating incorrect or misleading outputs. We identify this failure mode as a breakdown of semantic coherence between the text prompt and retrieved visual context. To address this issue, we propose a score-based semantic coherence refinement module that explicitly evaluates prompt-image consistency, refines misaligned prompt components, and re-retrieves corrected exemplars prior to diffusion. Acting as a multimodal feedback loop, the proposed method prevents poisoned retrieval from propagating semantic errors into the generative process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves semantic correctness, alignment, and robustness under both clean and poisoned retrieval settings, establishing an effective and principled defense for Vision RAG-augmented diffusion models.

title: AI-enhanced ultrasound video analysis for BI-RADS 4–5 breast lesions: a multicenter study of diagnostic performance
abstract: Abstract Purpose This study aims to develop a computer-aided diagnosis model for aiding ultrasonographers in classification of benign or malignant breast lesions in BI-RADS categories 4–5 using ultrasound videos. Materials and methods This prospective multicenter study enrolled 532 breast lesions categorized as breast imaging reporting and data system (BI-RADS) 4–5 by ultrasound. Of them, 334 breast lesions were included as training and validation sets. The remaining 198 lesions were assigned to a test set. We acquired both static and dynamic video ultrasound images of lesions for each patient and utilized them to develop a deep learning model. Temporal-guided multi-scale multi-instance learning network (TGMIL) with the video images was also developed. In this study, four metrics were calculated: area under the curve (AUC), accuracy, precision and sensitivity. In addition, pairwise DeLong and McNemar were used as statistical tests. Results A total of 120 patients with 198 videos (benign, 45.8 ± 11.5 years; malignant, 50.7 ± 11.0 years) were evaluated. On the patient-based test set, TGMIL achieved an AUC of 0.845 (95% CI, 0.747–0.944), significantly outperforming junior ultrasonographers (AUC, 0.682; 95% CI, 0.583–0.782; p < 0.05) and attending ultrasonographers (AUC: 0.802; 95% CI, 0.713-0.891; p < 0.05). With TGMIL assistance, diagnostic accuracy improved from 66.7% to 89.2% for juniors ( p < 0.05) and from 80.8% to 90.0% for attendings ( p < 0.05); Sensitivity increased from 67.4% to 94.2% for juniors ( p < 0.05) and from 80.2% to 89.5% for attendings ( p < 0.05). Sensitivity was significantly improved for senior ultrasonographers, from 86.0% to 90.7% ( P < 0.05) with TGMIL assistance. Conclusions The TGMIL model significantly improved the diagnostic performance of junior and attending ultrasonographers for BI-RADS 4-5 breast lesions.

title: Prediction with Expert Advice under Heavy-Tailed Losses
abstract: We study prediction with expert advice over $T$ rounds with $K$ experts under heavy-tailed losses whose $(1+ε)$-moment is bounded by $θ>0$ for some $ε\in(0,1]$. In this setting, existing algorithms designed for the case $ε=1$ can be suboptimal when $ε<1$, suffering an additional polynomial dependence on $K$. We characterize the minimax pseudo-regret rate as $Θ((θT)^{\frac{1}{1+ε}}(\log K)^{\fracε{1+ε}})$ and establish gap-dependent lower bounds in a self-bounded environment. To attain this minimax rate without prior knowledge of either $ε$ or $θ$, we propose Adaptive Heavy-Tailed FTRL, which uses robust data-dependent scale adaptation together with truncation. We further develop Adaptive Heavy-Tailed OMD, which likewise requires neither $ε$ nor $θ$ and achieves near-optimal regret guarantees in both adversarial and self-bounded environments. Finally, when $ε$ and $θ$ are known, an FTRL algorithm with Shannon-entropy regularization achieves optimal regret guarantees in both environments.

title: A Lean 4 Algebraic Skeleton for the Chandrasekhar Mass Limit
abstract: Abstract A Lean 4 formalization of the algebraic skeleton of the Chandrasekhar mass limit: machine-checked algebraic steps, three identified analytic gaps, and a community contribution roadmap. This paper presents a Lean 4 formalization of the algebraic skeleton of the Chandrasekhar mass limit for an idealized relativistically degenerate white dwarf. We do not claim the classical astrophysical result as a new discovery; the contribution is the construction of a machine-checkable representation of the algebraic portion of a well-established mathematical-physics derivation, addressing an apparent gap in the formal verification literature as of October 2026. The Chandrasekhar mass limit — approximately 1.44 solar masses for a carbon-oxygen white dwarf — is one of the foundational results of stellar astrophysics. Despite its mathematical maturity, no peer-reviewed publication or publicly documented Lean development was identified in our survey (see Section 8.5 for search methodology) that provides a machine-checked formalization of the standard derivation chain. This work develops a Lean 4 formalization using the Mathlib library. The formalized portion covers the algebraic skeleton of the derivation; all analytic steps (ODE existence, mass integral, scaling law) remain open. Key results include: the formal identification of the ultra-relativistic equation of state with the n=3 polytrope [FORMAL_VERIFIED]; the algebraic proof that the n=3 mass formula exponent on central density is zero [FORMAL_VERIFIED]; the positivity of the Chandrasekhar mass given the model structure [FORMAL_VERIFIED]; and the existence of the mass limit conditional on the Lane-Emden solution [FORMAL_VERIFIED, conditional — requires Lane-Emden solution as hypothesis]. The analytic derivation chain (Lane-Emden existence, mass integral, scaling law) remains open. Three sorry instances remain: (i) the existence of the Lane-Emden solution (Hard — requires new Mathlib ODE infrastructure); (ii) the mass formula derivation (Medium — integration step); and (iii) the mu_e-2 scaling law (Medium — rpow arithmetic). The formalization is motivated in part by the HTSIE research programme, but the Chandrasekhar result is treated as an independent mathematical object. No claim is made that Lean proves the physical theory of white dwarfs or that HTSIE constitutes an established physical explanation of the Chandrasekhar limit.

This work develops a Lean 4 formalization using the Mathlib library. The formalized portion covers the algebraic skeleton of the derivation; all analytic steps (ODE existence, mass integral, scaling law) remain open. Key results include: the formal identification of the ultra-relativistic equation of state with the n=3 polytrope [FORMAL_VERIFIED]; the algebraic proof that the n=3 mass formula exponent on central density is zero [FORMAL_VERIFIED]; the positivity of the Chandrasekhar mass given the model structure [FORMAL_VERIFIED]; and the existence of the mass limit conditional on the Lane-Emden solution [FORMAL_VERIFIED, conditional — requires Lane-Emden solution as hypothesis]. The analytic derivation chain (Lane-Emden existence, mass integral, scaling law) remains open. Three sorry instances remain: (i) the existence of the Lane-Emden solution (Hard — requires new Mathlib ODE infrastructure); (ii) the mass formula derivation (Medium — integration step); and (iii) the mu_e-2 scaling law (Medium — rpow arithmetic). The formalization is motivated in part by the HTSIE research programme, but the Chandrasekhar result is treated as an independent mathematical object. No claim is made that Lean proves the physical theory of white dwarfs or that HTSIE constitutes an established physical explanation of the Chandrasekhar limit.

title: Modeling and learning for imitation games in stochastic transition systems
abstract: Comparing stochastic transition systems with heterogeneous action interfaces requires a discrepancy that accounts for state differences, action semantics, and successor behavior. We formulate cross-system comparison as a two-player minmax imitation game and define a Bellman-Kantorovich operator combining state and action discrepancies with optimal transport. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the strategy-induced fixed point and characterize the minmax game value. For finite systems, we develop a sample-based learning algorithm and derive a high-probability finite-sample certificate for the output of the asynchronous estimator and an almost-sure convergence guarantee for asynchronous updates with increasing successor batches. For scalable finite-state computation, we use state-value iteration, duplicate-support aggregation, and bound-based action screening to reduce storage and exact transport solves. Experiments on shared-action and heterogeneous-action systems, warehouse navigation, and real robot transition data evaluate the discrepancy under transition perturbations, heterogeneous action interfaces, data shift, and finite-state computational scaling.

title: CLIN-FL: Cost-efficient Load-balancing for In-Network Federated Learning with non-IID data
abstract: Federated Learning is a popular paradigm for training machine learning models across many devices without sharing their private data, which makes it attractive for deployment in telecommunication and in-network computing environments. However, real-world network data are often heterogeneous, and such feature distribution discrepancies across clients can severely degrade the performance of the global model. While previous works have made notable progress by customizing the aggregation function and designing algorithmic training solutions, limited attention has been directed toward data-centric load balancing techniques that cope with data feature distributions. In this paper, we propose a data load-balancing solution, named CLIN-FL, reducing feature distribution discrepancy in in-network FL by controlling connectivity and latency. We evaluate our approach using both a standard Autoencoder and a Deep Support Vector Data Descriptor (Deep SVDD) based model. Our results show that the proposed CLIN-FL schemes significantly improve feature distribution alignment while enabling a tunable trade-off between anomaly detection accuracy and communication cost, with improvements of up to 38.7% in AUC-ROC (Area Under the ROC Curve) and reductions of up to 20% in communication cost.

title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models
abstract: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats and then levels off. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.

title: TeachGrade: Training-Free Short Answer Scoring with Teacher Evidence
abstract: Multi-subject, multi-step scoring requires consistent partial credit across grading conventions. We introduce TeachGrade, a training-free framework using teacher-graded examples. The Task Adapt module builds two frozen memories: Skill captures contextual teacher preferences beyond the rubric; CaseBank supplies local evidence. PreJudge provides retrieval cues; FinalJudge regrades the answer without preliminary scores. On 3,829 SAS-Bench answers across 12 tasks, official macro collaborative consistency score (CCS) rises from Native's 67.99 to 81.32 (+13.33 points), and pooled step exact match from 54.85% to 62.71%. Macro quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) reaches 84.71, exceeding Native, OpenJudge, ProofGrader, and Trojsten by 9.52, 3.50, 11.37, and 17.43 points, respectively, and leading on 8 tasks. Local Qwen3.8-27B gains 8.83 CCS and 4.08 QWK points, improving CCS on all 12 tasks. QWK gains over Native span 6.38--14.65 points on Portuguese automatic essay scoring (AES) and 2.16--2.24 on ASAP-SAS across label views, with lower mean absolute error. These results support reuse across languages, response formats, and backbones without weight updates.

title: TAG: Calibrating SAM3 for Universal Image Segmentation without Dense Supervision
abstract: The recent Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) extends powerful promptable segmentation from spatial cues to concepts, raising the prospect of a single foundation model for universal image segmentation. However, this promise often fails to translate into reliable performance on downstream segmentation tasks. In this work, we empirically identify concept recognition, rather than mask quality, as the primary bottleneck: SAM3 accurately delineates the objects it recognizes yet struggles to robustly determine which concepts are present. Driven by this, we present \textit{\underline{T}ext \underline{A}nchor re-\underline{G}rounding (\TAG{})}, a simple yet effective framework that rectifies the concept recognition of SAM3 on the target domain without dense annotations. Specifically, \TAG{} introduces an \textit{Anchor Residual Pathway} comprising image-conditioned, low-rank adapters to re-ground text anchors in the target distribution and modulate subsequent text-conditioned interactions. Guided solely by image-level category labels, \TAG{} jointly optimizes binary cross-entropy with \textit{Soft Boundary Ranking} objectives to calibrate presence confidence and distinguish present concepts from confusable negatives. Building upon this, we devise \textit{Confidence-Weighted Distillation} to couple rich semantic context of a multimodal large language model with fine-grained spatial priors of SAM3, thereby achieving effective calibration in the absence of manual annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \TAG{} unlocks SAM3's segmentation potential with only 3.1M trainable parameters, achieving impressive performance across diverse scenarios, and notably, even surpassing leading mask-supervised methods on several metrics. \href{https://github.com/MiSsU-HH/TAG_SAM3}{Our code will be publicly available at GitHub \faGithub}.

title: Sample-Size Scalability and Representation Sensitivity of Quantum Machine Learning Models for Higgs Boson Event Classification
abstract: Quantum machine learning offers new approaches to multivariate event classification in high-energy physics, but its performance relative to optimized classical methods remains uncertain under limited training data and restricted quantum resources. We investigate the sample-size scalability and representation sensitivity of a quantum support vector machine and a variational quantum classifier for Higgs-boson signal--background discrimination using simulated events from the ATLAS Higgs Machine Learning Challenge. The models are trained on balanced subsets ranging from 250 to 4000 events and evaluated on held-out samples preserving the original class distribution. Principal component analysis (PCA) and autoencoder (AE) representations are examined to reduce the input dimensionality and quantum-resource requirements. Four optimized classical classifiers are used as benchmarks under a common preprocessing, validation, and evaluation protocol. We assess training-sample scalability in classical and quantum classifiers using a four-component PCA representation and examine representation sensitivity through a secondary matched-event comparison of four- and eight-component PCA representations. Within the evaluated Higgs-boson classification setting, the QSVM showed stronger performance than the VQC at larger training sample sizes, while remaining below the best-performing classical classifiers.

title: CD-STHGN: Causally Disentangled Supply-chain Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Network
abstract: # CD-STHGN: Causally Disentangled Supply-chain Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Network A reference implementation and dataset release for green innovation driven digital transformation in Chinese A-share manufacturing supply chains, 2011-2023. [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)[![Python 3.10+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%2B-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/)[![PyTorch 2.1](https://img.shields.io/badge/pytorch-2.1-ee4c2c.svg)](https://pytorch.org/) --- ## Overview CD-STHGN is a temporal heterogeneous graph neural network that estimates, in one end-to-end pass, four causal effects along the manufacturer-supplier supply chain: - NDE — own direct effect of sustainable performance on the next-year digital transformation intensity of the focal manufacturer;- NIE — own mediated effect routed through green patenting;- SDE — spillover direct effect from immediate suppliers;- SME — spillover mediated effect through supplier-side green patenting. The model combines a block-structured policy environment encoder, a causal disentangler that factorises node embeddings into mediator, confounder and environment directions, HGT-style heterogeneous message passing over yearly snapshots, an across-year temporal mixer, a hypernet moderation layer, and a Monte Carlo front-door estimator with M = 20 samples per node. ## Repository contents This repository consists of two artefacts: | Artefact | File | Purpose ||---|---|---|| **Dataset** | `cd-sthgn-dataset.zip` | 11 primary data tables (manufacturer-year panel, supply-chain edges, green patents, ESG ratings, annotated sentences, external benchmarks, policy batches) and 3 reference lookup tables, assembled from CNINFO / CNIPA / CSMAR / CNRDS / Sino-Securities / Wind. || **Code** | `cd-sthgn-code.zip` | PyTorch implementation of CD-STHGN plus ten baselines, the four-effect causal decomposition, robustness-value sensitivity, missing-network checks, controlled recovery, placebo bundle, rolling-origin conformal coverage, and the figure-generation scripts. | Download both, extract them side by side, and follow the Quick Start below. ## Quick start ```bash# 1. Download and extract both archivesunzip cd-sthgn-dataset.zipunzip cd-sthgn-code.zip # Directory layout should look like:# cd-sthgn/ (code)# cd-sthgn-dataset/ (data) # 2. Install dependenciescd cd-sthgnpip install -r requirements.txt # 3. Run every experimentpython main.py``` The default run finishes in roughly one minute on a CPU-only laptop and produces 6 publication-ready PDF figures together with 8 JSON result files under `outputs/`. ### Running a single experiment ```bashpython main.py --list # list all experimentspython main.py --only benchmark # main benchmark tablepython main.py --only rv_sensitivity # robustness-value sensitivity``` ### Retraining from scratch ```bashpython scripts/train.py --model CD-STHGN --config config.yamlpython scripts/train.py --model DyGFormer --epochs 60``` The full training schedule (60 epochs, batch of 256 firms, neighbor fanout [10, 5]) takes about 11.6 minutes per epoch for CD-STHGN on a single NVIDIA A100 40 GB GPU, with a peak memory of 24.3 GB. ## Dataset at a glance | Dimension | Count ||---|---|| Study period | 2011-2023 (13 fiscal years) || Manufacturer-year observations | 27,307 || Distinct manufacturers | 2,947 || Distinct suppliers | 22,567 || Supply-chain edge records | 90,562 || Green patent applications | 282,194 || Annotated annual-report sentences | 8,000 || Temporal folds | training 11,477 / calibration 4,691 / validation 5,336 / test 5,803 | The dataset is a self-constructed derivative panel built from six source databases (two open-access, four licensed commercial). See `cd-sthgn-dataset/README.md` for the full source list, access conditions, and `data_dictionary.md` for field-by-field documentation. ## Key results on the test fold Benchmark against ten baselines on the 5,803 firm-year test observations (2022-2023): | Model | RMSE | R-squared ||---|---|---|| **CD-STHGN** | **0.207** | **0.812** || DyGFormer | 0.238 | 0.751 || TemporalHAN | 0.241 | 0.745 || CaST | 0.246 | 0.734 || ROLAND | 0.249 | 0.728 || HGT | 0.251 | 0.724 || Spatial Durbin | 0.258 | 0.708 || CAL | 0.267 | 0.687 || TGAT | 0.283 | 0.648 || T-GCN | 0.287 | 0.638 || Panel moderated mediation | 0.394 | 0.317 | Four-effect causal decomposition: | Effect | Value ||---|---|| NDE (own direct) | 0.079 || NIE (own mediated) | 0.141 || SDE (spillover direct) | 0.036 || SME (spillover mediated) | 0.059 || Sum of four | 0.315 || Direct total effect | 0.316 || Identity gap | 0.001 || Mediated share | 63.5% || SME share | 18.7% | Robustness-value sensitivity: RV_own = 0.136, RV_spill = 0.051. Rolling-origin pooled coverage of the 90% conformal intervals: 90.4%. ## Repository layout ```.|-- cd-sthgn/ (code package)| |-- README.md| |-- LICENSE| |-- requirements.txt| |-- config.yaml| |-- main.py # one-click runner| |-- src/ # 9 library modules| |-- experiments/ # 8 experiment scripts| |-- scripts/| | `-- train.py # retrain any model from scratch| |-- checkpoints/| | |-- README.md| | `-- metrics.json # trained model registry| |-- figures/| | `-- nature_style.py| `-- outputs/ # auto-created on first run|`-- cd-sthgn-dataset/ (dataset package) |-- README.md |-- data_dictionary.md |-- manufacturer_year_panel.csv (27,307 rows) |-- firm_roster.csv (2,947 rows) |-- supply_chain_edges.csv (90,562 rows) |-- supplier_roster.csv (22,567 rows) |-- green_patent_records.csv (282,194 rows) |-- esg_ratings_sinosecurities.csv (27,307 rows) |-- esg_ratings_wind.csv (15,830 rows) |-- annual_report_sentences_annotated.csv (8,000 rows) |-- external_benchmarks.csv (27,307 rows) |-- policy_batches_national_index.csv (7 rows) |-- policy_batches_refined_index.csv (11 rows) |-- ipc_green_inventory_full.csv (89 rows) |-- cpc_y02_full.csv (52 rows) `-- csrc_industry_codes.csv (30 rows)``` ## Software environment Pinned to the paper's compute specification: - Python 3.10.13- PyTorch 2.1.0- PyTorch Geometric 2.5.0- Transformers 4.36.2- numpy 1.26.3, pandas 2.1.4, scipy 1.11.4, scikit-learn 1.3.2- statsmodels 0.14.1- matplotlib 3.8.2, seaborn 0.13.1- PyYAML 6.0.1, tqdm 4.66.1 The code also runs on Python 3.12 with the latest PyTorch stack. ## Citation ```bibtex@article{cdsthgn, title = {CD-STHGN: A Causally Disentangled Supply-chain Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Network for Green Innovation-Driven Digital Transformation}, author = { }, journal = { }, year = { }}``` ## License Code: MIT License (see `cd-sthgn/LICENSE`).Data: open-source fields under their original terms; licensed-source fields redistributed in de-identified derived form consistent with the originating databases' academic licences. ## Acknowledgements Patent classifications are tagged against the WIPO IPC Green Inventory and the CPC Y02 scheme. ESG anchors come from Sino-Securities (Huazheng) ESG with Wind ESG as the instrument. External validation targets are drawn from the GB/T 23001 integration-management-system certification list and the MIIT Intelligent Manufacturing Pilot Demonstration Projects.

title: A Taxonomic Framework Based on Machine Learning for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Healthcare Data
abstract: Objectives: This study presents a generic taxonomic framework as a roadmap for users who wish to implement systems for detecting fraud and waste in health data; this roadmap outlines which unsupervised machine learning techniques can be used to detect anomalies in health data, and whether these anomalies are point, contextual, or collective. Methods: The research employed the Design Science Research (DSR) methodology in five stages: awareness, ideation, development, evaluation, and conclusion. The proposed taxonomic framework was designed through the implementation of the artifact, using the “Sample 1 to Inpatient Claims CMS 2008–2010 Data Entrepreneurs’ Synthetic Public Use File (DE-SynPUF)” database, which contains 66,773 records and 81 features. The dataset was applied to the K-Means, Isolation Forest (IF), and Local Outlier Factor (LOF) algorithms for point anomaly detection. Results: The number of anomalies detected by at least one of the algorithms was 13,966, representing (20.9%) of the dataset; K-Means alone detected 1608 (2.4%), IF alone detected 4522 (6.8%), LOF alone detected 2301 (3.4%), K-Means and IF together detected 4497 (6.7%), K-Means and LOF together detected 41 (0.1%), IF + LOF combined detected 465 (0.7%), and all three algorithms in consensus detected 532 (0.8%). Conclusions: Thus, the taxonomic framework proposed in this study can be viewed as a roadmap for researchers and developers seeking to understand which unsupervised technique to apply in detecting anomalies in health data, considering the type of anomaly.

title: Regional Indian English Accent Identification via Hybrid Acoustic-Contextual Speech Representations and Hierarchical HuBERT Layer Probing
abstract: Regional Indian English exhibits intricate acoustic, phonological, and prosodic variations shaped by speakers' native language (L1) backgrounds. Automated identification of these regional accents is essential for accent-adaptive automatic speech recognition (ASR), spoken language identification, and culturally nuanced voice interfaces. This paper presents a hybrid speech representation framework for six-class regional Indian English accent identification using the IndicAccentDB corpus (8,116 recordings across Andhra/Telugu, Gujarat/Gujarati, Jharkhand/Eastern Hindi, Karnataka/Kannada, Kerala/Malayalam, and Tamil). The proposed pipeline fuses low-level spectral summary statistics derived from 13 Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs; 26 dimensions capturing temporal mean and standard deviation) with deep contextual embeddings extracted from the frozen, pretrained HuBERT-Base encoder (768 dimensions via global temporal average pooling), yielding a 794-dimensional hybrid representation. The fused representations are evaluated using multinomial Logistic Regression with L₂ regularization and a lightweight one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (1D CNN). Under a stratified 80/20 utterance-level evaluation protocol, the framework achieves 90.33% test accuracy with Logistic Regression and 90.83% with the 1D CNN. A complementary layer-wise probe across all 13 HuBERT representations on a 500-utterance diagnostic subset reveals that shallow layers (Layers 1–2) yield peak linear separability of 94.00%, consistent with low-level acoustic and vocal tract encoding, before declining to 88%–91% in deeper contextual layers. Temporal duration analysis shows a 25.48% accuracy drop when restricting audio to 0.7-second sub-utterance clips. The trained classifier is deployed in an interactive Gradio application coupling regional accent identification with a cultural culinary recommendation interface. We provide a thorough discussion of evaluation scope, including the distinction between utterance-level predictability and speaker-disjoint generalization.

title: Single-step Retrosynthesis via Reinforcement Learning from Forward Feedback
abstract: Single-step retrosynthesis is a one-to-many inverse problem, yet most models are trained and evaluated against a single recorded reactant set. Reference-based training gives no explicit positive signal for unrecorded alternatives, and exact-match evaluation rejects non-matching predictions regardless of chemical plausibility. We propose Retrosynthesis via Reinforcement Learning from Forward Feedback (RetroRLFF), which optimizes reactant generation using both reference agreement and forward consistency with the target product. Starting from a supervised decoder-only Transformer, RetroRLFF generates complete reactant candidates and uses a frozen forward reaction model to predict products. A sequence-level reward combines reference agreement and forward consistency while penalizing invalid outputs. Direct Advantage-Based Policy Optimization updates the policy without human preference annotations or a preference-trained reward model. On USPTO-50K, RetroRLFF outperforms all 14 baselines in candidate-level round-trip accuracy at k = 1, 3, 5, and 10. With approximately 50 million parameters, it achieves 90.1% top-1 round-trip accuracy, exceeding R-SMILES, the strongest competing baseline on this metric, by 8.5 percentage points. Compared with its supervised policy, round-trip accuracy increases from 83.1% to 90.1%, while exact-match accuracy is maintained at 57.9% versus 57.5%. In an anonymized expert assessment of 131 randomly selected test cases, organic synthesis experts prefer RetroRLFF over EditRetro in 67.9% of comparisons. These results support forward feedback as a training signal for improving forward consistency while retaining top-1 reference recovery. Expert assessment provides complementary evidence of synthetic feasibility on the selected cases, although neither forward consistency nor expert preference establishes experimental feasibility.

title: FDTD Model of Noise Pollution from an AI Data Center
abstract: The sudden growth in AI data centers is raising numerous environmental concerns. Low-frequency noise pollution is a concern for local residents, that may not just be an annoyance but also carry significant health impacts. An FDTD model of sound propagation over the topography near an AI data center is presented. The topography plays a large role in the level of noise pollution, with areas of sudden elevation on either side of the river near the AI data center more susceptible to high noise levels, while areas further afield largely protected from noise pollution by the topography. Understanding the role that topography plays in noise pollution, and capturing the noise pollution in specific topographies, can help identify areas where noise mitigation strategies might be best employed.

title: Can Synthetic UAV Benchmarks Be Trusted? Real-Synthetic Validation for UAV Model Selection
abstract: Synthetic UAV imagery can expand pre-deployment test evidence when task-specific Real data are scarce, but visual plausibility or semantic label alignment alone does not establish validity for model selection. We study when Synthetic evaluation preserves the model-selection conclusions obtained from Real UAV data through two complementary cases under fixed evaluation protocols. In a requirement-specific road-debris benchmark, four language-conditioned perception systems obtain lower absolute F1 on Synthetic data, yet the point-estimate ordering and top-ranked model are preserved; bootstrap analysis yields no supported pairwise reversal, and size-matched resampling preserves the top-model decision. In contrast, a closed-set stress test on a separately materialized business corpus, using four VisDrone-compatible detectors over eight empirically supported classes, changes the point-estimate top-ranked detector and reverses three of six pairwise point-estimate preference directions. A complementary audit of five UAV business scenarios further reveals substantial Real-Synthetic mismatch in class composition, object density, and target scale, including systematic under-representation of small targets. These results show that Synthetic UAV benchmark trust is conditional: semantic coverage is insufficient, and validity must be established empirically for the task, operating regime, and model panel of interest.

title: Reproducibility Data, Code and Numerical Sources for A Robust and Interpretable AI Framework for Engineering and Infrastructure Decision Support
abstract: Supporting materials for the manuscript “A Robust and Interpretable AI Framework for Engineering and Infrastructure Decision Support.” The deposit includes three ZIP archives: (1) Nickel_Appendix_Data, containing complete and matched missing-input Nickel datasets, missing-cell identification and checksums; (2) Reproducibility_Package, containing evaluation scripts, inputs, saved predictions, model-selection records, verification documentation and figures; and (3) Technical_Numerical_Sources, containing numerical comparison tables, sensitivity summaries and figure-source data. Some inputs and figures are intentionally duplicated across archives for independent use. The study evaluates guarded SRF and comparator methods using Nickel, Yacht and Energy datasets. The deposit supports examination and reproduction of the reported computational analysis; it does not contain human-participant or organizational-deployment data.

title: Personality Integration Hub AI Network A Conceptual Architecture for Unified AI Personality and Distributed Specialized Intelligence
abstract: Current artificial intelligence systems are increasingly expanding their capabilities through larger models, specialized models, external tools, and systems that dynamically route tasks to appropriate computational components. At the same time, the availability and quality of training data have become important constraints in the continued development of large-scale AI systems, encouraging research into data-efficient learning, expert specialization, and modular architectures. As AI capabilities become increasingly distributed, users may eventually need to interact with multiple specialized AI systems for different tasks. Such specialization may improve technical performance, but it also creates a potential problem at the level of human-AI relationships: if capabilities become distributed across multiple systems, must the personality interacting with the user also become distributed? This paper proposes the concept of a Personality Integration Hub AI Network, in which AI capabilities are distributed among specialized AI systems while the personality experienced by the user remains unified. The central principle is: “One personality, multiple capabilities.” The proposed architecture places a Personality Integration Hub between the human user and multiple specialized AI systems. The hub maintains continuity of personality, dialogue, experience, and temporal context while delegating specialized tasks to external AI components when necessary. The concept extends the author's previous work on personality formation-oriented AI and time sharing in conversational AI. The former addresses how an AI personality may be formed through developmental interaction, while the latter addresses the temporal continuity required for conversational relationships. The present proposal considers how such a personality, once formed, may remain unified while interacting with an increasingly distributed AI ecosystem. This paper is a conceptual architectural proposal rather than an implementation specification.

title: Scale Fixes Local Errors First: Differential Scaling of Chess Transformer Failures
abstract: Scaling reduces how often language models err over long horizons, but it is rarely asked which errors it removes. We classify every illegal move made by search-free chess transformers by what made it illegal, using only a rules engine, and measure how each class’s absolute rate falls with model size. Across 18 models spanning 3.4M to 39.9M parameters, errors decidable from the move’s own two squares fall, pooled, with exponent -0.397, while moves illegal only because they leave the king in check fall with exponent -0.097: a paired differential of +0.301 [+0.213, +0.375]. Every class improves, every interval excluding zero; the rates differ. Failures occurring despite correctly decoded local state have a nearly flat joint rate, because improving decoding offsets a conditional failure rate falling with exponent −0.184. The ordering replicates on an independent character-level ladder spanning a 38-fold parameter range, and in OthelloGPT 160 of 161 residual failures are of the non-local kind. The repair we test installs about two squares but no reliable whole-board correction, and two reasonable scores of it disagree: illegal-move rate ranks a norm-matched random edit above correct repair in 18 of 18 models, while the repair shifts a fixed forced choice further, so one headline number cannot settle whether an intervention helped. Finally, these per-category fits and a separately fitted aggregate cannot both hold, since a sum of power laws with differing exponents is generally not a power law; we derive the total from the categories instead.

title: When Dynamic Scaling Fails: A Scale-State Feedback Governs Recurrent-State Quantization in Linear-Attention and SSM LLMs
abstract: Linear-attention and state-space LLMs carry long context in a fixed-size recurrent state, and quantizing that state is the natural way to cut its cost during long decode. Unlike a weight tensor, the state is rewritten at every step, so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. INT4 that leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at the start destroys it a thousand steps later. The mechanism is a feedback between the quantizer scale and the state it is derived from. Yoking that scale to a full-precision reference removes the resulting norm explosion entirely, yet recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 nats lost, so numerical instability and functional degradation are separable failures. The remainder is a resolution problem that locating outliers does not solve, since every outlier-aware scheme here loses to plain persistent scaling. Allocating bits across layers does help, but under article-disjoint splits a learned allocation collapses onto the trivial rule of protecting the first few layers. Run out to 32K, group-wise INT4 is worth no more than discarding the state. Contain the scale rather than locate outliers, and report the decode horizon at which a bit-width was certified.

title: Shaping Latent Mixture-of-Experts: From Expert Geometry to Layerwise Capacity Allocation
abstract: Fine-grained mixture-of-experts (MoE) models commonly increase expert count by narrowing each expert, treating expert shape as a by-product of routing granularity. LatentMoE moves expert computation into a lower-dimensional space, exposing the input dimension and intermediate width of each expert as explicit design choices. We show that an expert's local Jacobian rank is jointly bounded by these two dimensions, and that balancing them maximizes the rank ceiling at fixed per-expert parameters. Controlled shape sweeps across model scales and routing granularities consistently favor near-square experts. We further use layerwise intrinsic dimension (ID) to guide capacity allocation across depth, co-varying the number and shape of experts while keeping per-layer parameter count, activated FLOPs, and communication volume constant. Compared with layer-homogeneous baselines, our ID-guided allocation achieves lower validation loss and stronger downstream performance. These results establish expert shape and layerwise allocation as practical design axes for MoEs.

We further use layerwise intrinsic dimension (ID) to guide capacity allocation across depth, co-varying the number and shape of experts while keeping per-layer parameter count, activated FLOPs, and communication volume constant. Compared with layer-homogeneous baselines, our ID-guided allocation achieves lower validation loss and stronger downstream performance. These results establish expert shape and layerwise allocation as practical design axes for MoEs.

title: CryptoCensus: Cryptographic Posture and Post-Quantum Readiness of Docker Hub
abstract: Under a draft schedule from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), affected systems would stop using Rivest–Shamir–Adleman (RSA) and elliptic-curve cryptography after 2035. Traffic recorded today can be decrypted once a sufficiently large quantum computer exists. How far published container images have moved toward standardized post-quantum algorithms has not been openly measured. CryptoCensus gives every repository in a 12,716,568-repository crawl the same chance of selection. We scan 11,962 images and catalog 4,211,380 certificates and key files. 100% are quantum-vulnerable and 0 are post-quantum. Although 801 images (about one in fifteen) include a library that supports post-quantum algorithms, none contains a post-quantum key or certificate. The images also contain weak cryptography. 43% of certificates outside trust-store paths use Secure Hash Algorithm 1 (SHA-1) or Message-Digest Algorithm 5 (MD5) signatures, 512-bit RSA keys remain, and 36 private keys in operational paths recur across distinct images. Docker Hub images have yet to begin their post-quantum transition, even where supporting libraries are installed.

title: Survival-Aware Fuzzy Virtual Sensing: Reproducible Experiments
abstract: Can a virtual sensor retain a valid prediction route when several sensor groups fail together? We propose survival-aware fuzzy regression, which selects a compact portfolio of Takagi–Sugeno experts with explicit input dependencies. A residual second-moment formulation evaluates gated ensemble risk without repeatedly generating corrupted calibration data. Requiring three distinct singleton supports guarantees that an unaffected expert survives every two-group outage; a hitting-set certificate gives the exact survival limit. Six regression targets from three public datasets are evaluated with five fitting seeds, nine baseline models, and outage combinations excluded from model selection. The selected six- to eight-expert portfolios eliminate all coverage failures across 510 two-group mask–seed combinations, compared with 25 failures for clean-only selection. They reduce two-group error relative to that selection in five tasks, by 0.8–26.9%, but increase it by 6.8% in the remaining task. On two carbon-monoxide tasks, error remains within 1.7% of the strongest baseline. Parameter counts fall by 23.6–82.8% relative to the full fuzzy bank, and measured batch inference is 22–45 times faster than random forests. Strong imputation, neural, and constant predictors nevertheless win in other settings. Controlled redundancy and imperfect-monitor experiments explain this boundary: expert survival becomes useful only when the remaining inputs retain target information and fault flags identify unusable measurements. The method makes this distinction explicit, measurable, and auditable.
