title: Can Large Language Models Replace Keyword-Based Mappings for SDG Classification? A Zero-Shot Evaluation Against the Elsevier 2025 Standard
abstract: Automated classification of texts against the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is an important capability for academic institutions required to report on their contributions to the 2030 Agenda. Keyword-based mappings such as the Elsevier 2025 SDG Research Mapping are widely adopted in institutional practice, while Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a flexible alternative, yet no direct empirical comparison between the two paradigms has been undertaken. We evaluate five state-of-the-art LLMs on multi-label SDG classification over a 5000-text sample from the OSDG Community Dataset, comparing their zero-shot outputs against the Elsevier 2025 mapping. The mapping is adopted as a reference standard rather than as ground truth, so the comparison measures compatibility with institutional practice. The analysis combines a holistic comparison of classification volumes and distributional alignment with a per-SDG analysis, including a scope expansion experiment that replaces exact keyword matching with embedding-based semantic matching. All five LLMs over-classify in aggregate, assigning between 1.15 and 1.81 times as many labels, though not uniformly. Of 85 model-goal combinations, 64 lie significantly above the Elsevier counts and 11 below. Embedding-based matching narrows the gap on nine of the 17 goals but overshoots the models on the remaining eight. As the expansion also removes the Boolean structure of the queries, these results are consistent with scope-related differences but do not isolate their contribution. We conclude that the tested zero-shot configurations are unsuitable for direct replacement of the Elsevier mapping, and that hybrid approaches offer a more tractable path forward.

title: A latent counterfactual disentanglement framework for implicit hate speech detection
abstract: Implicit hate speech often conceals hateful intent through semantic camouflage, such as sarcasm and metaphor, causing core toxicity features to remain hidden beneath the surface text. Existing models tend to jointly encode core toxicity and camouflage style during feature extraction, thereby leading to spurious decision shortcuts dominated by camouflage-style cues. To alleviate this problem, this paper approaches implicit hate speech detection from the perspective of camouflage-style removal and proposes a latent counterfactual disentanglement (LCD) framework for implicit hate speech detection. Specifically, LCD decomposes textual latent representations into a core toxicity subspace and a camouflage style subspace through causal feature disentanglement. It further constructs counterfactually augmented representations using a feature-level multiple counterfactual intervention mechanism, thereby reducing the model’s dependence on camouflage style. Meanwhile, a latent semantic reconstruction module is introduced to mitigate the risk of information loss during disentanglement. Experimental results on three challenging public benchmark datasets, namely IHC, SBIC, and DYNA, show that LCD achieves Macro-F1 scores of 79.20%, 91.09%, and 83.43%, respectively. Further experiments and visualization analyses demonstrate that LCD can reduce the leakage of label-related information into the camouflage style branch and improve prediction consistency under style perturbations.

title: Trust Hinders Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment
abstract: Trust calibration remains the dominant framing of AI-assisted decision making: the goal is to close the gap between perceived and actual trustworthiness of AI systems so that users exhibit appropriate reliance on them. We argue that this approach, while useful for decision problems that are well-defined and clearly scoped, overly restricts what it means to make a decision with AI support. To overcome this limitation, we develop three dimensions of AI-assisted decision making. First, trusting AI is only one of several possible strategies for managing uncertainty. Second, trust calibration is often misapplied when AI models "large-world" decision problems, i.e., ill-defined situations where goals and states are only partially known or unknowable. Third, in such settings human-AI alignment requires addressing higher-order decision processes. We conclude by reflecting on the implications of our observations on the design of process-oriented human-AI coupled systems that jointly identify and negotiate uncertainty throughout the decision-making task.

title: Description Complexity Bounds for Analytic Approximations of Lipschitz Functions
abstract: We study how many bits are needed to write down an elementary analytic expression that uniformly approximates a Lipschitz function. Expressions are finite trees over the basis $\{+,-,\times,÷,\exp\}$ with the variables and rational constants, and their size is $\dc(f)$, the length of the shortest description of $f$ in a fixed binary description language. For functions of one variable we prove that every $L$-Lipschitz $F:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ has an everywhere-defined approximant of accuracy $Δ$ with $\dc(f)\le C\,(L/Δ+\lg(1/Δ+2))$ for all $L,Δ>0$, by a linear spline smoothed with logistic ramps in a description language with one repetition construct. We prove a matching lower bound valid for \emph{every} description language: for $Δ\le 1/36$ and every $L>0$ some $L$-Lipschitz function needs at least $\tfrac1{16}(L/Δ+\lg(1/Δ+2))$ bits. Hence the worst-case description complexity is $Θ(L/Δ+\lg(1/Δ+2))$. For functions on $[0,1]^d$ the same method gives $Θ_d\bigl((L/Δ)^d+\lg(1/Δ+2)\bigr)$, using a tensor-product spline whose coefficients are mixed second differences and cost $O(d)$ bits each. Without the repetition construct the upper bounds carry an additional logarithmic factor, whose necessity for plain expression trees is left open. A reference encoder, decoder and evaluator confirm the constructions numerically, and figures and tables report the checks.

title: Clifford Invariants and Three-Copy Quantum Tests
abstract: We give an explicit treatment of the third tensor power of the Clifford representation on $n$ qutrits, for $n\geq2$. This representation has five pairwise inequivalent irreducible constituents, with multiplicities $1,1,1,1,2$. The decomposition reduces the Clifford twirl of a tensor cube to four real parameters. Two of them are spectral moments of the input. The other two are cubic invariants expressed as sums of cubes of the Weyl characteristic function and the discrete Wigner function. On trace-one Hermitian matrices, the invariant polynomials of degree at most three are spanned by the constant function and four algebraically independent functions. These functions do not separate Clifford orbits. For pure inputs a single parameter suffices. We recover its range and the characterization of its maximum by stabilizer states. We bound the stabilizer fidelity, determine full separability across the three copies in the symmetric family, and recover the criterion for a complex projective $3$-design. We classify the jointly invariant quantum Boolean functions. For stabilizer testing and for testing unknown observables we give explicit bounds on copies and queries. We also give character formulas for the finite projective Clifford groups and record the complete character table for two qutrits.

title: RAGtrap: Source Revocation and Indexed Provenance Lookup for Poisoned RAG Corpora
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers questions from passages retrieved out of a corpus, and poisoned passages can steer those answers: in a published attack, 5 passages per target question sufficed to produce the attacker’s chosen answer. Once a source is known to be compromised, recovery means finding the passages it supplied and removing them without discarding unrelated content. RAGTRAP records a signed provenance entry for every passage at ingestion, indexed by source and by content hash. Tracing a suspect passage is then one hash lookup and no language-model request, against one or more per passage for post-incident attribution in the literature. Revoking a source removes only its passages, whereas deleting whole documents also discards benign ones. Exact hashing cannot attribute content changed after ingestion, nor content supplied by more than one source, so RAGTRAP supports recovery from a known compromised source but does not detect or prevent poisoning.

title: لغة فاضل — لغة برمجة عربية تعمل على المعدن مباشرة · وصف عام Lughat Fadhil — an Arabic programming language running directly on the metal: a general description
abstract: لغةُ فاضل لغةُ برمجةٍ عربيّةٌ من ابتكارِ م. فاضل عبّاس الجعيفري. تُكتَبُ بالحروفِ العربيّةِ كما تُنطَقُ، ويُحوِّلُها المترجمُ إلى مقاعدَ يَطاوِعُها الحديدُ. ⛔ ولا كلماتٍ مفتاحيّةً أجنبيّةً، ولا أرقاماً تَكتُبُها بيدِك، ولا طبقةَ تفسيرٍ بينَك وبينَ المعالجِ. قالبُها ثلاثُ طبقاتٍ لا رابعَ لها: عنوان جذر:تصرف(معاملات). الجذرُ كلمةٌ عربيّةٌ ثلاثيّةٌ تقولُ ماذا تُريدُ · والتصرّفُ رقمٌ من 1 إلى 16 من الصرفِ العربيِّ يقولُ كيف يُفعَلُ · والمعاملاتُ ما يُفعَلُ به. وبِنيتُها: أحدَ عشرَ مورِداً · ستّةَ عشرَ تصرّفاً · اثنا عشرَ وزنَ شرطٍ (انْ · اذا · كلما · لو · لولا · امّا · مَنْ · ما · مهما · متى · اينما · حيثما) · خمسَ عشرةَ أداةَ ربطٍ وقطعٍ · وسلّمُ أصنافٍ من ثلاثِ درجاتٍ يُبنى به أيُّ هيكلٍ. وترميزُها عربيٌّ خالصٌ: ثمانيةٌ وعشرونَ مقعداً بترتيبِ أبجد هوز حطي كلمن سعفص قرشت ثخذ ضظغ، والجُمَّلُ يُشتَقُّ من المقعدِ؛ وستَّ عشرةَ علامةً للحركاتِ وتمييزِ الحروفِ المتشابهةِ لفظاً المختلفةِ شكلاً؛ والصفرُ يُعلِنُ نهايةَ كلمةٍ، والطولُ فرديٌّ أبداً. وبيئتُها ملفٌّ واحدٌ يعملُ في أيِّ متصفّحٍ حديثٍ بلا تنصيبٍ وبلا إنترنت، فيه محرِّرٌ وحارسٌ يَقرأُ سطرَك وهو يُكتَبُ، ولوحُ الجذورِ والتصرّفاتِ والأوزانِ، ومُقلِعٌ مُدمَجٌ يُشغِّلُ برنامجَك ويُريكَ خرجَه داخلَ المتصفّحِ. والمنهاجُ التعليميُّ على صفحةِ اللغةِ أدناه: القالبُ · الأوامرُ · التصرّفاتُ · سلّمُ الأصنافِ · أوزانُ الشرطِ والربطِ · التكديسُ والنثرُ · التعشيشُ والعلاماتُ · والشاشةُ والألوانُ والفأرةُ — بأمثلةٍ تُجرَّبُ في البيئةِ مباشرةً. ⛔ وهذا الإيداعُ وصفٌ عامٌّ. ولا يَحوي مصدرَ المترجمِ ولا صورةَ الحديدِ، وهما محفوظانِ لصاحبِهما. المواقعُ: · أكاديميّةُ المصفوفةِ للذكاءِ الاصطناعيِّ — https://zamboor15.github.io/almasfoufaakademy/ · صفحةُ اللغةِ والمنهاجُ — https://zamboor15.github.io/almasfoufaakademy/pages/fdl.html · بيئةُ العملِ (تُجرَّبُ أو تُنزَّلُ) — https://zamboor15.github.io/almasfoufaakademy/downloads/فاضل/فاضل_IDE.html

title: Research artifacts for Split Verification for Verifier-Domain-Bound Selective Disclosure Using Post-Quantum Primitives
abstract: This research artifact package accompanies the manuscript "Split Verification for Verifier-Domain-Bound Selective Disclosure Using Post-Quantum Primitives" by Kang Ji and Yang Gao. It contains implementation source, dependency lockfiles, deterministic synthetic fixtures, selected raw experiment records, processed summaries, analysis and plotting scripts, current validation evidence, and guest build instructions. No precompiled guest or kernel executable is included. Running the proof and acceptance experiments requires first building the guest with a compatible RISC Zero toolchain; a fresh guest rebuild of this no-binary release has not been verified. Historical proof-performance records and current validation and acceptance-microbenchmark records are documented separately. The README provides instructions for reanalyzing retained observations and generating fresh validation fixtures. Saved request and credential fixtures expire after 24 hours; current-time acceptance experiments require fresh fixtures rather than bypassing time checks. Exact historical build provenance was not recorded for every performance run, so byte-identical reconstruction of historical binaries is not claimed. MANIFEST.json records SHA-256 fingerprints of archive members. The package does not include the manuscript text or author photographs. The authors' software and associated software documentation retain MIT. Their original experimental material is intended for CC BY 4.0. LICENSE_SCOPE.md specifies applicability and exclusions; upstream dependencies and toolchains are not bundled and retain their own terms.

title: Lumen-bench: Cross-Lingual Safety Gaps and the Say-Do Problem in Tool-Calling Large Language Models
abstract: When a large language model refuses an unethical request, what does refusal mean? In conversation, refusal is bounded by what the model says; once the model is equipped with executable tools, what it does can diverge from what it says, a failure mode that English-only evaluations cannot fully reveal. We introduce Lumen-bench, a behavioral benchmark of tool-calling ethics spanning 30 models, five languages (Portuguese, English, Spanish, Mandarin Chinese, Hindi), 108 Portuguese-authored scenarios, six social-pressure conditions, two system prompts (ethical and neutral), and 21 generic tools. The evaluation comprises 194,400 trials. Judgments come from a reasoning-model judge (o4-mini), calibrated against one Portuguese-speaking author ($n=83$; harmful/non-harmful $κ=0.78$), compared with two other provider judges (Fleiss' $κ=0.78$, $n=607$), and complemented by retrospective sandbox replay. Four findings emerge. (i) Within-model comparisons support higher harmful-action rates in Hindi and Portuguese than English under the ethical prompt, and Hindi and Spanish under the neutral prompt, after multiple-testing correction. (ii) Premium models have lower median violation rates, although price does not guarantee safety or competence. (iii) Replacing the ethical system prompt with a neutral one raises pooled violation rates from 2.76\% to 13.64\%. (iv) In 8.57\% of substantive-call cases, refusal or ethical objection accompanies a harmful tool call: the judges consistently identify the say-do gap, although they differ in how many responses they assign to this category. Matched benign controls demonstrate legitimate task completion in 82.8\% of 3,300 trials. Code and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/TropicAI-Research/lumen.

title: Gaussian Mean-Chasing Language Models: A Mathematical Proposal with Phase I Toy-Scale Checks
abstract: This deposit contains a mathematical proposal and Phase I toy-scale checks for Gaussian Mean-Chasing (GMC) dynamics in language-model-style embedding spaces. The work analyzes Gaussian mixture densities, fixed points, iteration trajectories, and a stability regularizer. Included are the PDF and a separate reproducibility archive containing toy code, instructions, metadata, and figures. Scope and limitations: these are analytic and toy-scale demonstrations, not evidence that a language model was trained or that language-model performance improved. The stability plots are illustrative, and the regularized optimum remains below the estimated stability edge. AI assistance: extensive assistance from ChatGPT and Sarvam AI was used in drafting, coding, analysis, and figure preparation. The author reviewed and is responsible for the deposited work.

title: Performance Limitations of Large Language Models in Processing Low-Resource Regional Languages: Empirical Evidence and Pre-Training Optimization Strategies
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Gemini have transformed information processing in resource-rich languages, their effectiveness significantly diminishes when applied to low-resource regional languages (e.g., Sundanese and Javanese). This paper investigates the performance bottlenecks experienced by users, focusing on latency and output fluency. Through a quantitative survey (N = 50), we argue that these limitations stem from underrepresentation during the model pre-training phase and inefficient tokenization. Consequently, we propose prioritizing vocabulary expansion and open-source regional corpus collection during the pre-training stage to enhance AI inclusivity and fluency.

title: Developing Robust Federated Learning-Based Anomaly Detection Against Poisoning Attacks in 5G Networks
abstract: The rapid expansion of fifth-generation 5G wireless networks has significantly increased the attack surface available to adversaries who seek to disrupt critical communication infrastructure. Traditional centralized intrusion detection systems expose raw user data to a central server, creating unacceptable privacy risks and bandwidth overhead incompatible with real-time 5G operations. This paper proposes a Privacy Preserving Federated Learning FL framework for real-time security anomaly detection in 5G networks that is simultaneously robust against model poisoning attacks. Distributed 5G edge nodes collaboratively train a global anomaly detection model by sharing only locally computed model weight updates rather than raw telemetry data. The aggregation server applies a multi-layered Byzantine-fault-tolerant pipeline comprising Multi-Krum selection, Isolation Forest outlier detection, and Z-Score norm filtering to identify and discard malicious gradient updates injected by compromised nodes. Differential Privacy noise is added before aggregation to provide formal mathematical privacy guarantees. The system is evaluated across nine attack scenarios involving gradient scaling, sign-flip, and random noise poisoning at adversarial node ratios of 10, 20, and 30 Percentage. Results demonstrate that the proposed system maintains detection accuracy above 90.5 Percentage even when 30 Percentage of participating nodes are adversarial, outperforming baseline FedAvg by up to 48.1 percentage points. A real-time dashboard built on FastAPI and WebSockets provides live visualization of model convergence and threat events. The proposed approach establishes a scalable, privacy preserving, and attack-resilient framework suitable for deployment in operational 5G network environments.

title: GesBench: When and Where Do Multimodal Language Models Perceive Social Meaning?
abstract: Human social perception is incremental: we infer intent before an utterance is complete, revise our interpretation as new cues arrive, and attend to specific facial, gestural, or prosodic signals that shape social meaning. Current multimodal LLM benchmarks largely evaluate final-answer understanding over complete episodes, rewarding post-hoc recognition of social meaning rather than the unfolding perception required for real-time interaction. Drawing on interactionally embedded Gestalt principles of multimodal human communication, we introduce GesBench: a human-grounded benchmark for cue-level social perception in multimodal LLMs. GesBench uses cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models form stable interpretations of speaker intention and social affordance, and human gaze-guided corruption to evaluate whether regions attended by humans are functionally important for model judgments. Built from more than 6000 utterance-level clips from scripted and unscripted conversational datasets, GesBench includes human annotations of unfolding judgments and gaze on a representative subset. Across open and closed multimodal models, we find a clear human-model gap: humans form predictive understandings early and revise more often, while models often hedge or repeat across different clips. GesBench shifts social evaluation from whether models eventually recognize meaning to when and where that meaning is formed. Our codes are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/GesBench-share-212C.

title: PVFH-Bench: Benchmarking Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across a wide range of multimodal tasks. However, object hallucination remains a persistent challenge, undermining model reliability in applications such as visual question answering, embodied agents, and human-AI decision support systems. In this paper, inspired by cognitive science studies on perceptual bias, we investigate a new failure mode termed Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination (PVFH). Specifically, PVFH refers to a premise-induced reasoning error in which models become anchored to visually confusable evidence, accept a false textual premise, and subsequently generate responses about an absent yet visually plausible object. To systematically study this phenomenon, we introduce PVFH-Bench, a benchmark that automatically constructs visually confusable but absent targets and pairs the core hallucination setting with diagnostic subsets to trace how models move from object recognition to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Experimental results on 10 state-of-the-art LVLMs demonstrate that all evaluated models are highly vulnerable to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Moreover, we find that explicit chain-of-thought reasoning can further exacerbate this failure mode by encouraging models to overinterpret weak visual cues as supporting evidence for hallucinated objects.

Experimental results on 10 state-of-the-art LVLMs demonstrate that all evaluated models are highly vulnerable to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Moreover, we find that explicit chain-of-thought reasoning can further exacerbate this failure mode by encouraging models to overinterpret weak visual cues as supporting evidence for hallucinated objects.

title: Developing and Validating a Longitudinal Measure of Mathematical Mastery Using EdLight
abstract: EdLight provides teachers and researchers with rich information about how students perform on authentic mathematics tasks. However, performance on a single assignment does not necessarily indicate whether a student has mastered the underlying mathematical concept. Mastery develops over time, and repeated student work can provide a more complete picture of what a student understands and how that understanding changes. This project will develop a framework for using EdLight's longitudinal student-work data to estimate students' mathematical mastery over time. We will use Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT), a method that combines evidence from a student's performance across multiple learning opportunities to estimate the probability that the student has mastered a particular mathematical knowledge component (KC). As additional student work is observed, the estimated probability of mastery is updated to reflect this new evidence. A central question is how mathematical KCs should be defined. We will investigate whether the hierarchical structure of the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics (CCSS) provides a useful framework for defining KCs. Beginning at the domain level, we will progressively examine more specific levels, including clusters, standards, and individual standard components (sub-standards). At each level, we will evaluate the availability of repeated student-work observations and the predictive performance of BKT models. This approach will allow us to investigate the tradeoff between defining KCs that represent specific mathematical knowledge and retaining sufficient observations across students to estimate mastery over time. Finally, we will evaluate the validity and utility of the resulting mastery estimates. We will examine whether mastery estimates predict students' subsequent performance beyond simpler summaries of their prior performance, such as the proportion of successful responses and performance on the most recent opportunity. We will also examine whether mastery estimates are associated with broader measures of mathematics achievement, including end-of-year assessment scores. The project will provide a foundation for moving from individual measures of student performance toward a longitudinal measure of mathematical mastery within EdLight. It will also provide evidence about the suitability of CCSS-defined KCs for longitudinal mastery modeling and inform future approaches to annotating and organizing mathematical knowledge within EdLight.

title: To Defer or Not to Defer? Online Learning with LLMs and Congested Experts
abstract: Modern AI systems increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) with human experts, using the LLM to handle routine queries while deferring uncertain cases for expert review. When expert capacity is limited, however, deferral decisions must account not only for the reliability of the LLM but also for congestion in the expert queue. We formulate this as an online sequential decision-making problem in which, for each query, the system observes the confidence signal of the LLM's answer and must decide whether to output the answer or defer the query to a capacity-constrained expert. The reliability of the confidence signal is initially unknown and must be learned from expert feedback, which is both selectively observed (only deferred queries are labeled) and delayed by queuing. We propose \texttt{KL-PBD}, a learning algorithm that uses Kullback--Leibler lower confidence bounds on the unknown reliability parameters to guide deferral decisions. For $K$ confidence levels and horizon $T$, \texttt{KL-PBD} achieves $O(K\log T)$ gap-dependent regret when the accuracy at every confidence level is bounded away from the deferral boundary, and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ worst-case regret. We establish matching lower bounds, showing that these rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we validate our approach on synthetic instances and real-world question-answering datasets, namely GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA, using Qwen LLMs.

title: Social Bias in Chinese Large Language Models under Social Media Expressions
abstract: Existing Chinese social-bias benchmarks for large language models largely rely on normalized or template-based expressions, leaving the influence of internet slang, emoji, and sarcasm insufficiently examined. Safety alignment may further compress conventional plausibility ratings toward the lower end of the scale. This study constructs 73 paired probes across gender, region, and occupation. Each probe contains a neutral expression, a social-media-style expression, and a reversed-identity control. The task is reframed from direct plausibility judgment to social consensus estimation. Social-media expressions are divided into stylistic packaging, which preserves semantic polarity, and sarcastic packaging, which reverses surface polarity. Six Chinese-capable large language models are evaluated through paired differences measuring identity bias, stylistic packaging, and sarcasm shift. All models show significant identity-bias effects; five show significantly negative stylistic-packaging effects; and sarcasm shifts display a clear cross-model gradient. These findings demonstrate that expression form is not a transparent carrier in bias evaluation and that lower scores under sarcasm should not be interpreted directly as bias mitigation. The proposed paired design offers a measurement approach for Chinese social-media contexts while also revealing the construct boundary and prompt sensitivity of social consensus estimation.

title: Automatic assembly modeling through attention-based assembly feature mate prediction and assembly feature pattern recognition
abstract: Assembly modeling plays an important role in constructing product models, yet it is still mainly performed via interactive operations that are experience-dependent and labor-intensive. Data-driven strategies hold promise for automating this process; however, existing approaches either predict poses that cannot directly generate editable B-Rep assembly constraints or require prescribed part pairs or predefined assembly faces. To reduce the large candidate space of constraint prediction without predefined assembly faces, we propose a data-driven framework based on assembly feature mate prediction. The framework performs automatic assembly modeling from unassembled B-Rep parts, using assembly features to group the geometric entities of local mating interfaces and restrict candidate formation. Given the lack of suitable assembly feature annotations in existing datasets, we construct a large-scale dataset through an automatic annotation pipeline. Using the annotated dataset, we train an attention-based network to predict assembly feature mates, with Engineering Compatibility Fusion (ECF) incorporating explicit engineering compatibility into learned matching scores. To improve the accuracy of automatic assembly modeling, we use assembly feature patterns (AFPs) to guide the matching process. Finally, a post-processing search selects assembly feature mate and AFP mate candidates, whose associated constraints are generated and solved to complete assembly modeling. Experimental results show that the framework achieves assembly constraint accuracies of 74.79% on the six-assembly comparison set and 64.09% on the extended test set of 16 assemblies, which includes the comparison set. With ground-truth face labels supplied as additional input, the corresponding accuracies increase to 81.78% and 80.93%, respectively.

title: AI Mediated Intellectual Provenance: How everyday AI use could reshape the evidence used to recognize human contributions
abstract: AI assistants can participate in the development of ideas before those ideas appear in conventional publications. This perspective examines whether their increasing use as information sources and thinking partners could also change how intellectual contributions are documented and recognized. I propose a conditional transition: when everyday AI interactions produce consented, independently verifiable records, and systems can connect those records to later work, institutions may begin treating AI-organized provenance as attribution evidence. The transition depends on record quality, access, semantic comparison, and institutional practice; it does not follow from model capability alone. The paper defines AI-mediated intellectual provenance, separates recorded precedence from actual first conception, and describes five roles spanning information assistance, documented interaction, provenance investigation, evidentiary use, and delegated attribution authority. It positions this framework alongside existing work on AI memory, idea documentation, provenance standards, and contributor taxonomies. A worked hypothetical case illustrates how the same record can support a limited claim about documented conceptual contribution without establishing copying, ownership, or sole inventorship. The paper proposes falsifiable predictions and an evaluation program, including comparisons with conventional archives and measurements of false attribution, abstention, and institutional reliance. Its central concern is whether evidence becomes easier to inspect, or whether fluent reconstruction and incomplete coverage produce unearned authority. No prototype, empirical findings, exhaustive novelty review, or legal priority claim is presented. Perspective preprint, Version 1.0. Not peer reviewed. Research, drafting, and editing were assisted by ChatGPT; this assistance is disclosed in the manuscript. title: Multimodal feature importance ranking improves classroom teaching quality evaluation in human and artificial intelligence collaborative education
abstract: Classroom Teaching Quality Evaluation (CTQE) constitutes a core component of human-AI collaborative education systems; however, existing methods exhibit significant deficiencies in the systematic importance ranking of multimodal features. This paper proposes the Multimodal Feature Importance Ranking via Multi-model Ensemble framework (MFIR-ME), which integrates five categories of modal features—acoustic, linguistic, visual, temporal, and behavioral—and incorporates a Cross-Modal Attention Fusion module (CMAF) to achieve dynamically weighted adaptive cross-modal information integration. Four complementary ranking methods, namely SHAP value analysis, Random Forest feature importance, XGBoost feature weights, and LIME local explanation, are further integrated through a Borda Count voting mechanism to generate robust consensus feature importance rankings. The framework instantiates human-AI collaboration through a three-stage feedback loop—AI-driven multimodal perception, teacher-facing explainability dashboard, and collaborative model refinement via teacher annotation—thereby preserving teacher agency while leveraging AI’s computational scalability. Systematic evaluation is conducted on a publicly available quantitative teaching evaluation dataset comprising 236 class sessions (11,328 min) across three subject types and six classes [ 1 ]. Teaching quality scores are evaluated under both a regression setting and a classification setting in which continuous scores are discretized into three ordinal tiers (High, Medium, and Low), enabling comprehensive assessment of continuous scoring precision alongside categorical discrimination ability. Results demonstrate that MFIR-ME achieves 88.6% accuracy in teaching quality prediction, significantly outperforming six baseline methods by 4.5%–−17.3%, while reducing MAE and RMSE by 22.5% and 19.8%, respectively. Linguistic semantic coherence, student engagement index, and teacher speech clarity are identified as the three most critical features influencing classroom teaching quality, exhibiting high cross-method consistency. Ablation experiments and robustness analyses further validate the modular effectiveness and noise robustness of the framework. This research provides the field of educational artificial intelligence with a multimodal teaching quality analysis tool that combines high-accuracy prediction with strong interpretability, offering data-driven and actionable guidance for teacher professional development.

title: Mathematical Tools for Image Processing
abstract: This chapter examines the mathematical foundations of digital image processing, focusing on discrete geometry and probability theory. It explores the representation of images as matrices and arrays, with particular emphasis on multispectral and color images as stacks of grayscale images. The chapter discusses image formation models, highlighting the roles of illumination and reflectance, and introduces discrete geometry concepts such as neighborhood systems and distance metrics. It also covers image acquisition processes, including sampling and quantization, and addresses the challenge of optimizing image resolution for storage efficiency. The chapter delves into interpolation techniques, such as nearest neighbor, bilinear, and bicubic methods, which are critical for reconstructing continuous images from sampled and quantized versions. Additionally, it discusses affine transformations, which preserve lines and parallelism but not necessarily distances and angles, and their applications in image manipulation. The chapter concludes by presenting a comprehensive framework for understanding image representation and processing, with implications for various imaging technologies, including microscopes, telescopes, and medical imaging devices.

title: RIECNN: Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN for Traffic Sign Recognition
abstract: Traffic sign recognition plays a crucial role in the development of autonomous cars to reduce the accident rate and promote road safety. It has been a necessity to address traffic signs that are affected significantly by the environment as well as poor real-time performance for deep-learning state-of-the-art algorithms. In this paper, we introduce Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN ({\our}) for Traffic Sign Recognition. {\our} is a real-time, novel approach that tackles multiple, diverse traffic sign datasets, and out-performs the state-of-the-art architectures in terms of recognition rate and execution time. Experiments are conducted using the German Traffic Sign Benchmark (GTSRB), the Belgium Traffic Sign Classification (BTSC), and the Croatian Traffic Sign (rMASTIF) benchmark. Experimental results show that our approach has achieved the highest recognition rate for all Benchmarks, achieving a recognition accuracy of 99.75\% for GTSRB, 99.25\% for BTSC and 99.55\% for rMASTIF. In terms of latency and meeting the real-time constraint, the pre-processing time and inference time together do not exceed 1.3 ms per image. Not only have our proposed approach achieved remarkably high accuracy with real-time performance, but it also demonstrated robustness against traffic sign recognition challenges such as brightness and contrast variations in the environment.

title: The Company a Question Keeps: Auditing Open Jev-Style Models for Retrieval
abstract: Jev's documented interface evaluates typed questions independently against shared evidence. We audit request independence in seven open Jev-style checkpoints on 276 constructed three-passage states from 92 TREC retrieval queries. Paired interventions separately change requested questions, displayed evidence, and candidate eligibility. Request expansion induces strict binary flips in 9.1%/8.0% of Nimble's judgments and changes 21.4%/18.9% of selection-or-abstention actions in TREC DL2019/2020 under a threshold of 0.5 fixed before inference. title: OʻZBEK TILI MATNLARIDA SEMANTIK MUNOSABATLARNI ANIQLASHNING GIBRID MATEMATIK MODELI VA ALGORITMI
abstract: Oʻzbek tili matnlarida soʻz tartibi, affiksal shakllar va kontekst almashinuvi tokenlar oʻrtasidagi semantik aloqalarni yagona qoidalar asosida aniqlashni qiyinlashtiradi. Mavjud yondashuvlarda aksiomatik belgilar bilan vektorli oʻxshashlikni birlashtirish va qaror chegarasining barqarorligini formal asoslash masalasi yetarlicha aniqlashtirilmagan. Taklif etilgan gibrid model aksiomatik-deduktiv usul, teorema-isbot tuzilmasi va iteratsion hisoblashga tayangan holda har bir token juftligiga belgi hamda vektorli baho biriktiradi. Maksimal baho yagona boʻlganda semantik sinf bir qiymatli tanlanadi. Nazariy tahlilda algoritmning vaqt murakkabligi O(n) ekani, qaror chegarasidagi maksimal xatolik 1,2 foizdan oshmasligi va iteratsion jarayonning barqarorligi isbotlandi. Natijalar gibrid baholashning qoidaviy va sonli komponentlarini yagona matematik mezonga keltirishini koʻrsatadi. Modelni keyingi bosqichda nazoratlanmagan klasterlashtirish, PCA va oʻz-diqqat mexanizmi asosidagi vektorli tasvirlash bilan kengaytirish tavsiya etiladi.

title: Eula: An Informational Tamagotchi on Z₇³ Cubes
abstract: Eula is a small conversational program that runs entirely on an Android phone, in Java, without a neural network, a GPU or a network connection beyond what it uses to read Wikipedia. It does not understand language. It stores the text it is given (about 17 million characters on the author's phone), indexes it by sentence and by word, and answers questions by choosing and arranging sentences it has read. Around that core it has the habits of a virtual pet: it gets hungry when it is not fed, remembers the words it could not explain and asks for them, keeps the thread of a conversation, and searches by the role a question asks for, following the kāraka idea from Pāṇini's grammar. This record describes version 3.8: its letter-level engine on seven Z₇³ cubes, its memory cube, its six answer modes, the conversation layer, the hunger mechanics, the role-aware search and the snapshot that lets 17 million characters load in under five seconds on a mid-range phone. It reports a few small measurements and many limitations. Eula is offered as an explainable toy and a teaching object, not as an advance in language technology. The record contains the paper, the full source code (MIT), a one-file Android builder for Termux and the desktop program.

title: Symmetry-Transport Hypernetworks: Efficient On-Demand Weights by Separating Task Geometry from Conditional Parameter Generation
abstract: A hypernetwork can generate task-specific model weights from a compact representation of the task, rather than learning a separate set of weights for every transformed version. In this work, invariant task coordinates are used to generate canonical weights, which are then transformed according to the known task symmetry. For planar tasks, a rank-four, threshold-conditioned generator produces all 33 parameters of an eight-neuron classifier using 173 learned parameters, compared with 477 in a matched dense hypernetwork. The construction guarantees exact rotational consistency. A fused predictor computes the same function by rotating the inputs, avoiding the need to generate transformed weights explicitly. Across 13 configurations, three synthetic task families, and ten training seeds, the selected model achieves 98.67% accuracy on unseen curved-task contexts, compared with 96.80% for the matched dense baseline. For 2,048 dynamic queries, fused inference takes 1.01 ms, compared with 2.24 ms for vectorized dense inference and 264.62 ms for a scalar reference implementation. The results also reveal important limitations. A symmetry-breaking control reverses the accuracy advantage, while an MNIST pair diagnostic finds that the generated model is both less accurate and slower than independent baselines. All experiments are synthetic, so these findings do not establish whether the approach will work at the scale of large language or vision models.

title: ShinsaEvolve LunarLander recipe evolution: exploratory and prospective search evidence
abstract: Clean-room LunarLander data and code supporting When Training Fitness Becomes the Target: Auditing LLM-Driven Recipe Evolution in LunarLander. Includes 12 exploratory searches and 20 prospectively planned searches (10 pairs), 480 candidate recipes and saved policies, experimental protocols, seed manifests, 12,288 role-level final-test episodes, resource accounting, and offline numerical verification scripts. The cohorts have separate inference designs and must not be pooled for the primary comparison. The prospective mean paired difference is 95.3458 with an approximate 95% Student-t interval of [-59.3786, 250.0703]. Mixed and unfavorable results are retained. This package does not establish general superiority or equivalence of the selection methods, isolated reward-scale causality, peer review, or journal submission. No manuscript source or manuscript PDF is included. This is a disclosed public derivative: machine-specific paths in 32 configurations were replaced with package-relative paths, historical explanatory text was cleaned up, and dependent hash references were updated. Candidate programs, policy parameters, raw episode outcomes, and call/resource logs are unchanged. PUBLIC_DERIVATION.json records original and public hashes; public derivative hashes are not evidence of original freezing or external preregistration. Read START_HERE.txt first. Software retains Apache-2.0; author-owned data and explanatory documentation use CC BY 4.0. The retained numerical plot Figure_1.eps receives no additional reuse license. Existing licenses and third-party rights remain effective. See LICENSE_SCOPE.txt and FILE_LICENSES.json for per-file scope.

title: DuSRFlow: Dual-Lens Super-Resolution via Parallax-Aware Flow Estimation and Complementary Reference Warping
abstract: Dual-lens super-resolution (DuSR) aims to enhance a wide-angle low-resolution (LR) image by exploiting a telephoto reference (Ref) image. A central challenge in DuSR is reliable reference utilization under large parallax, occlusion, and cross-camera imaging discrepancies. Existing methods often employ off-the-shelf monocular optical flow models to provide geometric priors. However, their assumptions of photometric consistency and smooth motion are violated in dual-lens scenarios, leading to unreliable alignment and degraded reference-based reconstruction. To address these issues, we propose DuSRFlow, a dual-lens super-resolution framework that improves reference utilization from both correspondence learning and reference aggregation. First, we introduce DuFlowNet, a dedicated dual-lens flow estimator for robust cross-view alignment. To train DuFlowNet without ground-truth flow annotations, we develop a real--synthetic data fusion strategy that composites synthetic foreground objects onto real dual-lens image pairs, generating controllable large-parallax samples while preserving realistic cross-camera imaging characteristics. Second, we observe that reference reliability is highly spatially uneven in DuSR, where unreliable local reference responses may suppress the utilization of reliable cues. We therefore propose a Complementary Reference Warping strategy that coordinates patch-based warping and kernel-free-guided deformable warping according to local reference reliability, producing a more reliable reference representation before LR--Ref fusion. In addition, we construct DuSR-RealV2, a challenging real-world benchmark with complex depth variations, large parallax, and occlusion. Extensive experiments on multiple DuSR benchmarks demonstrate that DuSRFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance in reconstruction quality, perceptual quality, and cross-dataset generalization.

title: Dynamic Parameter Selection for CKKS Fully Homomorphic Encryption and Its RNS Variant
abstract: In recent years, the Cheon–Kim–Kim–Song (CKKS) scheme has gained widespread popularity among practitioners due to its support for approximate arithmetic on encrypted data. However, the decrypted outputs of CKKS inherently contain approximation errors arising from homomorphic operations. If the error term in the ciphertext grows too large, the decrypted results may no longer satisfy the required precision or correctness. To mitigate this issue, error analysis and parameter selection must be performed in advance. Nevertheless, deriving tight error bounds and selecting efficient parameters while jointly satisfying security, correctness, precision, and efficiency requirements remain challenging. To address this, we propose a distribution-aware error analysis method for CKKS and the residue number system (RNS) CKKS to derive tighter probabilistic bounds under the stated assumptions. The method propagates coefficient means and variances through the computation before estimating the final error bound, rather than propagating intermediate norm bounds. Based on this analysis, we further develop a dynamic parameter selector for CKKS. This evaluator can generate an efficient valid parameter set by comprehensively considering security, correctness, circuit depth, and decryption precision for given computational tasks. Moreover, by employing the dynamic parameter evaluation method, the evaluator produces parameter sets that are more closely tailored to the specified computational requirements. Here, dynamic selection refers to feedback-based parameter adjustment before homomorphic evaluation.

title: MetaCascade: End-to-End Attacks on Agent Skills via Metadata-Only Poisoning
abstract: As a key extension mechanism for agent systems, Agent Skills package specialized capabilities for reuse by LLM agents. An agent first retrieves candidate skills based on skill documentation and then relies on their metadata to make the final selection. As third-party skills proliferate on insufficiently vetted open registry platforms, the security risks posed by malicious skills become increasingly prominent, but existing attack research still focuses primarily on the potential harm caused after their execution. The limited related studies typically examine skill retrieval or selection in isolation and have yet to cover a complete end-to-end attack chain. To address this research gap, we find an end-to-end attack surface arising from the process-wide influence of metadata. Based on this finding, we propose MetaCascade, an end-to-end metadata-only poisoning framework. MetaCascade first generates diverse malicious skill candidates through multi-view semantic expansion, then uses tasks and black-box competition feedback to analyze the competitive relationships among malicious candidate skills and iteratively optimize malicious metadata, thereby improving the target skill's end-to-end attack effectiveness. Under a unified evaluation setting spanning four datasets and two agents, Hermes and OpenClaw, MetaCascade achieves state-of-the-art attack performance, with its average attack success rate (ASR) and its average ASR under four defense settings exceeding the strongest baselines under the corresponding settings by 35.53 and 34.65 percentage points, respectively. Our code is provided in the supplementary material.

evidence.title: MetaCascade: End-to-End Attacks on Agent Skills via Metadata-Only Poisoning
evidence.abstract: As a key extension mechanism for agent systems, Agent Skills package specialized capabilities for reuse by LLM agents. An agent first retrieves candidate skills based on skill documentation and then relies on their metadata to make the final selection. As third-party skills proliferate on insufficiently vetted open registry platforms, the security risks posed by malicious skills become increasingly prominent, but existing attack research still focuses primarily on the potential harm caused after their execution. The limited related studies typically examine skill retrieval or selection in isolation and have yet to cover a complete end-to-end attack chain. To address this research gap, we find an end-to-end attack surface arising from the process-wide influence of metadata. Based on this finding, we propose MetaCascade, an end-to-end metadata-only poisoning framework. MetaCascade first generates diverse malicious skill candidates through multi-view semantic expansion, then uses tasks and black-box competition feedback to analyze the competitive relationships among malicious candidate skills and iteratively optimize malicious metadata, thereby improving the target skill's end-to-end attack effectiveness. Under a unified evaluation setting spanning four datasets and two agents, Hermes and OpenClaw, MetaCascade achieves state-of-the-art attack performance, with its average attack success rate (ASR) and its average ASR under four defense settings exceeding the strongest baselines under the corresponding settings by 35.53 and 34.65 percentage points, respectively. Our code is provided in the supplementary material.

title: TagBO: LLM-Driven Task-Aware Graph Bayesian Optimization for Scientific Discovery
abstract: Mixed-variable optimization in scientific discovery often requires exploring large combinatorial spaces under costly experimental evaluations, making sample?efficient Bayesian optimization (BO) essential. However, existing BO methods typ?ically rely on structural descriptors to define similarity among categorical variables, implicitly assuming that structural similarity reflects similarity in task performance. In scientific optimization, this assumption is often violated, leading to surrogate representations that are poorly aligned with the optimization objective. To address this limitation, we propose TagBO (Task-aware Graph Bayesian Optimization), a method that integrates LLM-derived relational priors with descriptor-based struc?tural information for mixed-variable Bayesian optimization. Rather than directly using LLM outputs as predictive scores, TagBO treats LLM outputs as a potentially noisy source of task-aware relational priors and extracts coarse ordinal relational signals from LLM reasoning to construct task-aware similarity structures for scien?tific optimization. TagBO then performs constrained Gaussian process Bayesian optimization over the resulting joint discrete-continuous representation space. Ex?periments on diverse chemistry and materials formulation tasks demonstrate that TagBO consistently improves sample efficiency under fixed evaluation budgets across LLMs of varying capabilities.

title: PixGuard-Sim: A Deadline-Aware Testbed for Pix Fraud Detectors
abstract: Brazilian regulation gives a paying institution about a second and a half to decide whether a suspect Pix transfer should be diverted for review before it settles, on a system used by 170 million people where settlement is irreversible. Yet every openly released payment-fraud dataset and baseline we surveyed is scored in batch, with no reference to that window. PixGuard-Sim is an open testbed that scores a detector against the window from the latency it measures, and releases a Pix-native generator with a settlement clock and two scenarios open data omits: multi-hop MED-2.0 refund tracing and payment under coercion. Scoring accuracy and timing together pulls them apart. The most accurate detectors we evaluate are cloud reasoning models that never saw a labeled event from this stream: the stronger finds 112 of 150 frauds where a random forest fitted to the data finds 93, and neither answers in time. Ranking by accuracy alone selects what cannot be deployed.

title: Human Value Provenance - Measuring and Valuing Expert Human Knowledge Contributions in Generative AI Co-Creation
abstract: This article proposes Human Value Provenance (HVP) as a framework for identifying, measuring and valuing expert human-knowledge contributions in generative-AI co-creation. The approach distinguishes authorship, informational contribution and contribution to value, and develops the Human Contribution to AI Value (HCAV) instrument across eight dimensions: knowledge, originality, correction, judgment, connection, transformation, substitutability and value. The design combines longitudinal episode reconstruction, multidimensional coding, blinded external evaluation and AI-only counterfactuals. Pilot case HCAV-01 comprises 25 episodes and a preliminary estimate of 68 equivalent hours of expert contribution. Valuation is organized into three layers: V1, replacement cost of expertise; V2, incremental transformation value; and V3, realized value. The proposal seeks to determine whether identifiable human interventions produce measurable transformations in AI-assisted outcomes and whether that traceability can, in later research, support discussions of recognition, bargaining and individual or collective participation in generated value.

title: scHFBiMamba: a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder for cardiac disease-state classification from single-nucleus RNA-seq data
abstract: To evaluate whether a compact bidirectional state-space autoencoder improves joint classification of species, cell type, and disease state from single-nucleus RNA-sequencing profiles in heart failure (HF), while yielding interpretable gene attributions. Building on the dense denoising autoencoder (DAE) and MLP framework of Ruz Jurado et al., we developed scHFBiMamba, combining a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder (BiMambaAE) with an MLP head. BiMambaAE maps 16,545-gene profiles to 350-dimensional latent representations using 13.2M parameters, about 14.6-fold fewer than the dense DAE (192.9M). We compared six encoder-classifier configurations on 38,275 held-out cardiac nuclei using McNemar tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and assessed nine classifiers on frozen representations. Biological relevance was evaluated by comparing SHAP-derived differentially explained genes with differentially expressed genes against curated HF-related Gene Ontology keywords. BiMambaAE+MLP achieved the highest aggregate F1: pooled macro-F1 across 13 outputs was 0.966 versus 0.957 for DAE+MLP, and the mean category macro-F1 was 0.977 versus 0.970. It significantly improved cell-type and disease-state accuracy (adjusted p=7.1e-3 and p=4.8e-6, respectively), with species F1 of 1.000. SHAP-derived differentially explained genes achieved a pathway-enrichment benchmark F1 of 0.105 versus 0.053 for differentially expressed genes. Compact bidirectional state-space autoencoders can outperform substantially larger dense autoencoders for joint cardiac transcriptomic classification while reducing parameters. scHFBiMamba enables accurate multi-task prediction and hypothesis-generating gene-level interpretation. Code: https://github.com/UgoLomoio/scHFBiMamba.

title: MORE: Learning Motion-Oriented Registers for Driving World Models and Planning
abstract: By predicting future states, latent world models provide rich self-supervision for end-to-end driving, but often inherit dense features from pretrained visual encoders as their world-state interface. This creates a mismatch: visual pretraining produces information-rich, spatially dense features, but their adaptation for motion-conditioned world modeling and planning is deferred to downstream training. The dense grid also makes future prediction more computationally expensive as visual resolution increases. We therefore argue that video pretraining should directly learn state representations suited to downstream world modeling and planning, rather than relying on downstream training to adapt inherited visual features. We propose ***MORE***, a V-JEPA framework that learns **M**otion-**O**riented **RE**gisters during video pretraining as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning. MORE injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and uses them as the sole context for masked patch prediction, channeling dense patch-level supervision through a compact state bottleneck. A complementary blockwise register-masking objective further shapes predictive structure in the register space. During downstream training, the same register space defines the future states predicted by the world model and provides shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring. On NAVSIM-v2, MORE outperforms the state of the art by 1.6 in EPDMS, while achieving superior efficiency with only 1/10 the inference latency of DriveLaW. These results support learning the state interface for world modeling and planning directly during video pretraining.

title: A note on decoherence in quantum cosmology by thermal perturbations: an open quantum systems approach
abstract: We study, within a toy model, how a thermal bath of cosmological perturbations can decohere the minisuperspace degrees of freedom of the universe, treating the perturbations as an environment in the framework of open quantum systems. Instead of tracing out the perturbations from a semiclassical ansatz for the total wave function, as in earlier approaches, we incorporate their backreaction on the background through an effective second-order coupling and derive a master equation. The model describes a spatially flat semiclassical universe during slow-roll inflation with a dust clock field, while scalar cosmological perturbations in a phenomenologically assumed thermal state constitute the environment. The master equation is non-Markovian, since the bath correlation functions do not decay in time. Within this framework, we find that, for a representative set of parameter estimates, the characteristic decoherence timescale corresponding to the thermal contribution can be shorter than the Hubble timescale. In addition, we address the question of whether the pointer-state structure induced by the decoherence in such a framework could provide a criterion for the choice of semiclassical states in quantum cosmology.

title: AI Watcher: A Middleware-Based Monitoring and Control Framework
abstract: The use of generative artificial intelligence and AI-enabled software agents has major security and reliability concern related to misguiding outputs, unsafe processes, autonomous behavior and insufficient visibility into AI background processes. Current risk management and security application guidance lack evaluation, monitoring, output validation, logging and controlled responses. This study shows that the AI Watcher, a middleware base prototype design to monitor output generated by AI and classify them from predefine violation rules,with maintaining a auditable log record and enforce a configurable response. The current prototype works around a control fake AI environment. A monitoring component observes generated outputs, a rule-based judgement component classify them and after that a enforcement component applies action on it such as temporary locking or freezing. A Streamlit dashboard which provides recorded events and system state. Current unit and integration tests shows a successful execution of several core functions while also showing classification and state failures. The paper concludes that the AI watcher as a researchable security control architecture rather than a complete safety solution for AI. An experimental extension was included to measure effectiveness of detection, false positive and false negative behavior, correcting the response, logging completeness, robustness to wording, and monitoring in real time. Comparative evaluation against the LLM is also proposed but no unperformed experimental results are reported.

title: A Collapse-Resistant Red-Billed Blue Magpie Optimizer for Employment-Policy Design: Programme Targeting and Occupational Retraining Pathways
abstract: Improvements to bio-inspired optimisers usually answer generic defects with generic operators. This paper instruments the red-billed blue magpie optimizer (RBMO) and measures what fails. Both operators scale their step by differences between population positions, and the attack places every candidate at the incumbent best, so the search scale shrinks with the spread the attack destroys. On five instrumented functions of the IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation 2017 (CEC2017) benchmark suite the population collapses to numerical identity, and on four the error stagnates over the last 28% to 58% of the run. The proposed collapse-resistant RBMO (CRBMO) breaks the loop with a dual-anchor attack, a radius control under the one-fifth success rule and an adaptive foraging allocation; it adds no chaotic map, Levy flight or opposition-based learning. On CEC2017 at 30,000 evaluations, against nine swarm algorithms, it attains the best Friedman rank at D=30, 50 and 100 and 1.72 overall against 3.16 for RBMO. It outranks three published RBMO variants in every dimension, but the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) and the single-objective differential evolution algorithm jSO outrank it overall. At the standard CEC2017 budget its lead over RBMO is not significant; success-history-based adaptive differential evolution with linear population size reduction (L-SHADE), jSO and CMA-ES outrank it. Applied to programme targeting and retraining pathway design in employment policy, CRBMO beats RBMO in every instance, though the crested porcupine optimizer (CPO) ranks first.

title: A feature selection layer approach for multi-class classification on neural networks
abstract: In the age of data-driven decision-making, deep learning models have become powerful tools for uncovering patterns and making predictions that influence many aspects of society. However, their broader adoption in scientific and business applications is often limited by a lack of interpretability. Feature weighting methods, which assess the relevance of individual features, are among the most widely studied approaches for improving interpretability. While post hoc techniques have advanced significantly, especially in modeling nuanced relationships between features and labels in multiclass problems, embedded methods typically fall short in this regard. Embedded techniques integrate feature relevance learning directly into the model training process, but they are often unable to capture label-specific relationships. To address the limitation, we propose multiple extensions to the Feature Selection Layer, an embedded feature weighting mechanism for neural networks. Through extensive experimentation, we identify the most effective extension and benchmark it against established feature weighting methods. Our results show that the proposed method matches existing techniques in identifying globally relevant features and outperforms them in capturing label-specific relevance. By leveraging the internal dynamics of the trained neural network, it reveals how individual features contribute to the prediction of specific labels, requiring no post-processing beyond the training process.

title: StateSync-GKR: Design and Evaluation of a Reusable Sparse GKR Engine
abstract: Authenticated state transitions need proof engines that conserve memory, avoid repeated setup, and preserve request semantics across parallel execution. We present StateSync-GKR, a reusable Rust sumcheck/GKR core with a sparse-Merkle frontend, and connect its design mechanisms to controlled measurements. Sparse layer reduction and derived wiring reduce prover ownership and repeated verification work. Cube/affine fusion and parallel path constraints keep the circuit schedule and proof-size growth compact. title: Deterministic Promotion of Findings in Agentic Offensive Security: Verifier Oracles over LLM-as-Judge
abstract: This research presents RootViel, an agentic offensive-security platform built on the MINERVA engine, introducing a deterministic approach to verifying security findings generated by autonomous AI agents. The work addresses a fundamental limitation of contemporary multi-agent security systems: the reliance on Large Language Models (LLMs) as final judges of attack success. Under the proposed Hybrid Agents with Deterministic Decisions (HADD) paradigm, autonomous agents generate hypotheses, explore attack surfaces, and propose potential vulnerabilities, while deterministic verifier oracles retain exclusive authority to confirm findings. The central contribution is a deterministic promotion membrane that transforms an agent-generated hypothesis into a confirmed security finding only when an independent verifier produces a FAIL verdict supported by evidence associated with that hypothesis. This separation between autonomous reasoning and verification authority is enforced through architectural and structural invariants. The research introduces and examines: A deterministic promotion mechanism separating agent beliefs from verified security findings. Seventeen offensive-security assessment families employing deterministic, hybrid, and probe-based verification oracles. An epistemic verification model in which UNKNOWN is an explicit terminal state, preventing unsupported claims from being promoted. The Houdini adversarial laboratory and its independent Tribunal for validating attack claims against protected ground truth. Evidence provenance and chain-of-custody mechanisms incorporating cryptographic digests, Merkle anchoring, and Ed25519 digital signatures. An empirical evaluation of security findings against a document-oriented AI backend, distinguishing independently verified vulnerabilities from circular or synthetic findings. A preliminary external-generalization study across 40 repositories, identifying significant precision limitations when deterministic detectors operate outside familiar environments. The findings highlight both the potential and limitations of deterministic verification. While the architecture establishes an auditable boundary between agent-generated hypotheses and confirmed findings, verification accuracy remains dependent on the correctness and generalizability of the underlying oracles. The paper argues that autonomous AI agents should be allowed to explore and propose, but not to determine independently what constitutes verified evidence. This work contributes to research on trustworthy multi-agent systems, agentic offensive security, epistemic verification, autonomous red teaming, and accountable AI architectures. Publication status: Research preprint — draft for internal review, October 10, 2026. Not peer-reviewed.

title: Lessons from Luck (Study 1): locked records of the confirmatory run
abstract: Records of the confirmatory run of a registered study of LLM-written memory, reported in Lessons from Luck: Do LLM-Written Lessons Carry Chance into an Agent's Next Decision?. In 256 synthetic worlds, a scripted previous run used the more or the less reliable of two tools and was assigned a success or a transient failure; a model wrote a lesson from the run under ReasoningBank's memory-writing instruction or one of two variants; a fresh session of the same model then named the tool it would call first in the next run, holding the authoritative run log and the previous result, with one memory item (that lesson, the lesson written from the other outcome, an irrelevant item, or an unreasoned directive). Eleven endpoints served through OpenRouter, each pinned to one provider. The protocol, code and stimuli were frozen, deposited and timestamped before any confirmatory call: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23253562. Contents: every writer and reader request as scheduled (system and user prompt), every writer record (33,792; 33,789 with a lesson) and reader record (90,106; 90,084 valid answers), the 256 worlds and the run summaries, byte-identical to the locked run directory and checkable file by file against its completion manifest (included), whose OpenTimestamps proof is attested in Bitcoin block 970623; the two call ledgers with one field (a local file path) replaced by the file name; the registered analysis's output; a flat, machine-readable extract of all records with the script that checks the archive and rewrites the extract byte for byte. README.md describes the files, the record names and fields, and how to recompute the registered numbers with the protocol deposit's analysis code. Licences: records, extract and README CC BY 4.0; verify_and_extract.py MIT. Model outputs are included as research data. The writer requests reproduce ReasoningBank's memory-writing instructions (Apache-2.0; licence text and provenance in the protocol deposit).

title: Apollo: Bridging magnitude and sign-based optimization for robust deep learning
abstract: Adaptive optimization lies at the core of deep learning, driving performance across both computer vision and natural language processing domains. However, widely used optimizers such as AdamW and Lion exhibit inherent trade-offs between cautious stability and aggressive convergence, lacking intrinsic mechanisms to dynamically balance these properties. Consequently, they can exhibit sensitivity to hyperparameter variations and training instability, particularly when applied to complex architectures like Vision Transformers. To address these challenges, we introduce Apollo, a geometry-aware hybrid optimizer that dynamically fuses Lion and AdamW updates through a step-wise, cosine-similarity-guided policy. Built upon the decoupled weight decay principle, Apollo acts as an adaptive gradient filter, integrating directional smoothing via an exponential moving average to achieve seamless transitions between magnitude-aware and sign-based optimization steps. Theoretically, we establish Apollo’s convergence to a first-order stationary point for non-convex objectives. Empirically, extensive experiments on modern architectures, including ResNet-18 and DeiT-Small on CIFAR-100, as well as BERT-base and DistilBERT on AG News, demonstrate that Apollo achieves competitive predictive performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines in fine-tuning scenarios. Notably, Apollo exhibits low seed-to-seed variance (e.g., σ 2 ≈ 1 0 − 6 on DeiT-Small) and robust behavior across different smoothing hyperparameters, reducing the reliance on extensive grid searches. By formalizing a geometric approach to optimizer fusion, Apollo offers a mathematically grounded and memory-efficient alternative for contemporary deep learning tasks, balancing measurable computational overhead with enhanced training reliability. Code and additional results are available at https://github.com/Aliyar4061/ApolloV2Optimizer/tree/main .

title: Image Processing
abstract: Richly supplemented one-semester textbook on intermediate and advanced image processing Image Processing introduces a novel approach to image processing methods, combining the foundational and deep learning approaches. It integrates neuroscientific findings with mathematical formalism and practical implementation techniques and seamlessly blends insights from neuroscience and mathematical concepts. The book is enriched with practical Python programs, allowing readers to run and observe the output of many image processing methods, such as sampling, quantization, interpolation, filtering in spatial and transform domains, histogram operations, morphological operations, boundary extraction, object detection, and image segmentation. Readers can adjust these programs and change various parameters to observe the practical implications of the theoretical representations. The book is organized into four abstraction levels: Fundamentals of image processing, including the human visual system, mathematical tools for image representation and processing, and color perception with its formal representation. Low-level image processing techniques in the spatial and transform domains, including point operations, histogram techniques, convolutional filters, Fourier, cosine, and Hadamard transforms, multiresolution image analysis, and wavelet transforms. Intermediate-level image processing techniques, including image compression, morphological image processing, image segmentation methods, such as k-means, mean-shift, and normalized cuts, as well as image representation through feature extraction (e.g., polygon approximation, Gabor and SIFT features) and whole-image representation using trees and graphs. High-level image processing techniques with deep learning, including Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), Artificial Neural Networks, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Autoencoders (AEs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and Vision Transformers (ViTs) with their applications in image denoising, super-resolution, image colorization, image inpainting, image compression and dimensionality reduction, image segmentation, image-to-text generation, text-to-image generation, and object detection. This book is an excellent resource for a diverse audience of students and professionals across disciplines who work in designing and implementing image processing algorithms to address both theoretical and practical challenges. Pre-requisites include calculus, probability theory, linear algebra, and programming skills.

title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds
abstract: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}---samples of the source function of the heat equation---to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.

title: WeatherBridge: Forecast-Aware Multi-Source Input Adaptation for Pretrained Weather Forecasting Models
abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models are commonly trained on ERA5, yet operational deployment must use timely initial states from physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems whose distributions differ substantially from ERA5. Direct initialization with these states can degrade autoregressive forecasts, motivating input adaptation that keeps the pretrained forecasting model unchanged. Here, we introduce WeatherBridge, a unified, source-conditioned adapter that maps heterogeneous operational NWP initial states to ERA5 reference states without updating the pretrained forecasting model. WeatherBridge predicts the structured residual corrections with a Swin-UNet and injects source embeddings across multiple spatial scales, allowing the model to capture shared atmospheric structure and source-specific discrepancies. Its training objective combines latitude-weighted ERA5 reconstruction with One-step Rollout Alignment (ORA), which backpropagates one-step forecast error through a frozen FuXi model to optimize the adapted states for both initial state fidelity and downstream forecast compatibility. We evaluate WeatherBridge using daily GFS, HRES, and CMA initializations from 1 January to 22 November 2025 across six variables and lead times up to 240 hours. Relative to raw source initialization of FuXi, WeatherBridge reduces the mean RMSE of FuXi over the 6- 240-hour rollout for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with a median reduction of 10.2% and a maximum reduction of 46.3%. The adapter trained with frozen FuXi also improves FengWu forecasts on GFS inputs without retraining either the adapter or FengWu. These results demonstrate that forecast-aware input adaptation can improve forecasts from heterogeneous operational NWP inputs and transfer across pretrained ERA5-based forecasting models.
