title: A Self-Defining Operator for Distributed Applications
abstract: To operate distributed applications with high availability, operators must rapidly diagnose and mitigate any incident. LLM-based agents can help, but unlike experienced human operators they do not improve as they handle more incidents. Each investigation starts from scratch, re-deriving likely causes and re-testing hypotheses even when a similar fault was resolved in the past. We present a self-defining operator (SDO) that improves with time by updating its operational behavior and memory. When SDO resolves an incident, it distills that experience into playbooks, which describe reusable diagnostic instructions for future incidents with similar faults, and detectors, scripts that take application telemetry as input and output relevant playbook(s). SDO continuously runs the detectors and invokes LLMs only when one fires, so its token cost scales with incident count rather than with operational time. Across 11 open-source microservice applications, SDO cuts resolution time by 52% on recurring faults while keeping per-incident cost low. SDO is open source at https://github.com/self-defining-systems/sdo.

title: ELYON: Kernel-Verified Formalization and External Certification of the Claim1–Claim7 Chain
abstract: This publication documents the ELYON Claim1–Claim7 formal verification package, developed within the Axiomatic Theorem Kernel research program.The work presents a repository-scoped chain of seven formal claims, together with their associated Lean definitions, theorem dependencies, verification records, audit manifests, cryptographic checksums, and reproducibility procedures.The documented release includes Lean 4.19.0 and mathlib 4.19.0 verification records, with historical source and audit references preserved for independent inspection.The term external certification refers to the formally defined certificate endpoint within the Claim1–Claim7 development. It does not imply independent peer review or an unconditional resolution of the P versus NP problem.The publication aims to preserve the formal structure, verification scope, and provenance of the Claim1–Claim7 research artifact.

title: Evaluation of Online Voting System Towards Transmission of Secure Election Results
abstract: This is an undergraduate final-year project report (a B.Sc. thesis) in Cyber Security, submitted to the Department of Cyber Security at Federal University Dutse in October 2025 by Yunus Yahaya. It runs to 38 pages. The report evaluates, designs and builds a secure online voting system for Zaria Local Government Area in Kaduna State, Nigeria. The aim is to address the problems of paper-based voting: slow counting, fraud, disputed results, limited accessibility and high costs. The prototype uses PHP and MySQL, and the author developed it entirely on an Android smartphone. Its main features are three-factor voter authentication (voter card number, National Identification Number and an email one-time password), complete separation of voter identity from ballot choices, role-based admin access by ward, and audit logging. The report documents the system's design, implementation and testing, and concludes that secure online voting is technically feasible for Nigerian local government elections. It also notes that the system is a prototype that hasn't been tested in a real election. The document is formal and academic: a certification page, dedication, acknowledgements, table of contents, abstract, five chapters, and a reference list. It includes tables, an entity relationship diagram, a use case diagram and screenshots of the system's interfaces.

title: What Strict Point-wise F1 Actually Measures: Segment Saturation, Threshold Transfer, and Capacity Confounding in Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection — artefacts
abstract: Artefact archive for the paper “What Strict Point-wise F1 Actually Measures: Segment Saturation, Threshold Transfer, and Capacity Confounding in Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection”. The record contains two archives: tsad_zenodo_v4.65_full_20261010.zip — full package: code, run configurations, per-run metrics.json (825 runs), anomaly-score snapshots (817), all aggregated tables, diagnostic macros, manuscript sources and figures. Every reported number is recomputable offline without retraining. tsad_zenodo_v4.65_slim_20261010.zip — slim reading package: manuscript PDFs, aggregated tables, code and tools only. It contains no run records or score snapshots and therefore cannot reproduce the numbers. Each archive carries MANIFEST_SHA256.txt (per-file SHA-256) and TOOLS_MANIFEST_SHA256.txt. Reproduction commands and the portability note for metrics.json::scores_path are in the packaged ZENODO_README.md. Not included: third-party raw benchmarks (obtainable from their official sources; see DATA_PROVENANCE.md) and model checkpoints. Package layout. The full archive (139,582,766 bytes) is deposited as 67 parts of 2 MB (..._full_20261010.zip.q001 ... q067) because the authors' upload link dropped connections on transfers longer than about two minutes. Reassemble them with the commands in REJOIN.txt; the reassembled archive has SHA-256 5c0efb4ee49dad971527e18aae67d32d82f4fff1d87b450e7aec9b85caaf440b. The slim package is standalone. The manuscript PDFs in this snapshot are those frozen at deposit time; the version of record is the journal article.

title: ImageNet, RadiologyNET, or RadImageNet? Evaluating Pretraining Across CT, MRI, and X-Ray Classification
abstract: Due to the limited availability of annotated medical datasets, medical image classification typically relies on transfer learning from large-scale natural image datasets such as ImageNet. However, it remains unclear when domain-specific pretraining offers greater benefits. This study evaluates the impact of different pretrained weights on neural network performance in radiological image classification tasks. Four strategies were compared: ImageNet, RadiologyNET, and RadImageNet model fine-tuning against learning from randomly initialised weights (Baseline). Experiments were conducted over ten seed-paired runs using ResNet50, InceptionV3, DenseNet121, EfficientNet-B3, and MobileNetV3-Large on three classification tasks: multiclass Chest CT, multiclass BRISC brain MRI, and binary FracAtlas X-ray fracture classification. Pretraining generally improved performance over the Baseline, with the largest improvements observed on the Chest CT task. The Friedman tests identified significant differences between initialisation strategies for every architecture on all three tasks (all p≤0.0002). ImageNet achieved the best results in most architecture–task combinations, while RadiologyNET was comparable or superior in selected cases, including three of five architectures on Chest CT. RadImageNet showed less consistent transfer, particularly with DenseNet121. Pretrained models also generally reached high validation performance more rapidly than randomly initialised models. These results further support previous findings that ImageNet-pretrained models can perform comparably to or better than domain-specific radiological models when fine-tuned on sufficient downstream data, while the observed differences are consistent with possible effects of source–target alignment, downstream data availability, and network architecture.

title: PAT: A Personality-Driven Augmentation and Transfer Learning Framework for Depression Detection on Social Media
abstract: Depression is a prevalent mental disorder that affects millions worldwide, with early detection crucial for effective intervention. While exist?ing methods have achieved promising results in automated depression detection, they face two key limitations: (1) noise in post screening: symptom-based semantic screening is easily misled by superficial lexical patterns, thereby introducing false-positive posts; (2) weak op?timization of the post encoder: relying solely on coarse user-level supervision signals pre?vents models from capturing depressive cues within individual posts. To address these limita?tions, we propose PAT, a Personality-driven Augmentation and Transfer learning frame?work. In the first phase, PAT optimizes a post?level encoder via a fine-grained contrastive learning objective, utilizing LLM-based data augmentation driven by classic personality the?ories to alleviate data scarcity. In the second phase, the trained post-level scorer is deployed for high-quality post filtering, while its en?coder parameters are seamlessly transferred for user-level tasks. Extensive experiments demon?strate that PAT significantly outperforms exist?ing methods. Furthermore, PAT delivers multi?granular interpretability by tracing post-level mental-state trajectories and highlighting key symptoms, thereby offering reliable diagnostic evidence for clinical practice.

title: InfraWorld: Motion-Aware World Modeling for Roadside 4D Occupancy Forecasting
abstract: Roadside 4D occupancy forecasting predicts future semantic occupancy in a fixed infrastructure coordinate system. Roadside scenes are globally structured yet locally evolving, requiring comprehensive scene-level context while precisely modeling sparse localized motion. However, existing forecasting paradigms struggle to tackle both requirements. To address this limitation, we propose InfraWorld, a world model formulating roadside occupancy forecasting as selective state evolution. InfraWorld maintains a dense BEV state for the complete scene and persistent motion queries for moving regions, assigning complementary states to global context and local dynamics. Specifically, we propose Dynamic Query Initiation (DQI) to initialize queries in regions supported by motion in the observed history. During rollout, the dense state is updated through Long--Short Temporal Fusion (LST), which combines short-term adjacent-frame continuity with long-term motion trends to preserve stable context while capturing scene evolution. Motion-Aware Query Injection (MAQI) then refines the queries and injects confidence-weighted query information into corresponding BEV tokens, enabling targeted dynamic updates without perturbing global context. Together, InfraWorld concentrates predictive capacity on evolving traffic regions. Extensive experiments on the InfraOcc and Occ3D--nus datasets demonstrate that InfraWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance for roadside 4D occupancy forecasting while retaining its effectiveness under ego-centric settings. Code will be released.

title: Research Data and Reproducibility Package for Systematic Survey: Federated, Graph-Structured, and Verifiable RAG
abstract: This repository provides the open-access research data, double-coded classification matrices, reproducibility engine, and PRISMA 2020 protocol documentation for the systematic survey: "Federated, Graph-Structured, and Verifiable RAG: A Systematic Survey"(Submitted to Computer Science Review, Elsevier). Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds Large Language Models in external knowledge to curb hallucinations. However, enterprise deployment demands three interdependent capabilities that are currently isolated: data sovereignty (federated routing), relational reasoning depth (graph traversals), and retrieval integrity (cryptographic verification). Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines across six scientific databases (IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Scopus, arXiv, ScienceDirect, and DBLP), this survey evaluates a corpus of N = 154 primary studies (2021–2026) under the DFed–DGraph–DTrust three-axis framework (double-coded Cohen's kappa in [0.756, 0.809]). PACKAGE CONTENTS:1. 01_data/: Master coded dataset (corpus_154_studies.csv, corpus_154_studies.xlsx, and corpus_154_studies.json) with 27 extracted attributes per study, plus complete codebook and data dictionary (codebook_data_dictionary.md/.csv).2. 02_reproducibility_scripts/: Standalone Python verification script (reproduce_survey_analysis.py) that re-computes all manuscript tables (Tables 1–7), cross-tabulation ratios, Fisher's exact tests, and Cohen's kappa inter-rater reliability scores with 100% precision.3. 03_prisma_documentation/: Completed 27-item PRISMA 2020 Checklist (Word .docx and .md), high-resolution PRISMA 2020 Flow Diagrams (PNG, PDF, and LaTeX TikZ), and exact database search queries across all 6 databases.4. 04_figures/: Complete set of 8 high-resolution publication figures (300 DPI lossless PNG).5. 05_bibliographic_database/: Comprehensive 154-entry BibTeX citation database (References_corpus.bib) and tabular references catalog (references_summary.csv).6. 06_tables_and_synthesis/: CSV files for all synthesis tables from the manuscript. FAIR DATA PRINCIPLES & REPLICATION:All datasets are provided without proprietary format restrictions in RFC 4180 CSV, formatted multi-tab Excel, and JSON. To run the automated reproducibility suite:`python 02_reproducibility_scripts/reproduce_survey_analysis.py`

title: AraVISTA-Bench v1.1: Evidence-State Reasoning Benchmark for Selective Arabic RAG
abstract: AraVISTA-Bench v1.1 is a controlled Arabic benchmark developed for evaluating temporal evidence validity, pairwise evidence relations, query-conditioned evidence states, state-aware reranking, and selective actions in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The release contains 240 Arabic queries, 592 evidence passages, 960 construction-derived query-conditioned evidence-state (QCES) labels, and 592 construction-derived directed pairwise relation labels. It also includes the frozen BM25 and Dense-E5 predictions, evaluation split definitions, aggregate results, bootstrap confidence intervals, source provenance metadata, and the implementation-aligned frozen evaluation notebook. The benchmark covers temporal counterfactuals, Gregorian–Hijri calendar equivalence, controlled dialectal temporal variants, stale-evidence traps, co-temporal conflicts, and clarification/insufficient-evidence cases. The primary HELDOUT_NEW_CHAIN split contains 200 queries, and the separate CALENDAR_CHALLENGE split contains 40 queries. Benchmark instances were constructed from temporally ordered source chains grounded in publicly accessible official institutional webpages and dated official records. The released benchmark text consists of source-grounded paraphrases and controlled benchmark constructions; the linked original webpages remain third-party materials and are not relicensed by this dataset. Benchmark construction and initial labeling were AI-assisted under predefined source-chain structures, temporal scenarios, and ontology definitions. The resulting materials and labels were reviewed and refined by the authors. Human calibration was conducted separately for the action and pairwise-relation ontologies, and dialectal variants were reviewed by a native Arabic speaker for propositional and temporal equivalence. This dataset accompanies the manuscript “AraVISTA: Evidence-State Reasoning for Selective Arabic Retrieval-Augmented Generation”.

title: A four-qubit counterexample to first-excited parity in phase-shifted EPR-like Hamiltonians
abstract: This source-only preprint gives a four-qubit counterexample to the arbitrary-phase extension of the first-excited parity conjecture discussed in Wong, Bravyi, Gosset and Liu, Lee-Yang tensors and Hamiltonian complexity, arXiv:2602.03605v1, Section 5.6. For an unweighted four-cycle with phase pi on one edge and a common parameter 0 <= s < 1, it derives the complete 16-dimensional spectrum and an exact parity threshold. The rational value s = 2/3 is an explicit witness; a specified fixed-witness robustness interval is also proved. The original zero-phase conjecture and the general all-graph gap problem remain open. Ground-state uniqueness and the non-strict gap bound are known inputs, explicitly credited to Wei, arXiv:2609.26802v2, Corollary 5.8 and Section 5.4, and Bravyi, Gosset, Liu and Wong, arXiv:2607.14401v1, Theorem 1. The concrete phase counterexample, complete spectrum and threshold are distinguished from these known results. The primary-source comparison is dated and bounded; worldwide priority is not certified. Read the unchanged PHASE_EPR_FINAL_MANUSCRIPT_v0.1.3_R2_20261010.tex or .md first, together with the current public source/verification supplement and PUBLIC_RELEASE_NOTE. Older versions and administrative private-draft wording, if present as provenance, describe historical preparation stages and do not define this public version or its reviewed scope. Auxiliary six-qubit exploration is outside this paper's completed claim. Shunpei Shimizu initiated and directed this personal independent project, arranged verification, and coordinated the materials. No university or institutional affiliation is declared. AI systems performed research exploration, proof construction, computational checks, analytical review and manuscript preparation. The reviews are internal AI analyses; independent human verification of every proof, specialist human peer review and complete proof-assistant verification are not claimed. No PDF of editorial revision R2 has been generated or visually verified: the available compiler failed during environment setup. Editable TeX, a readable Markdown manuscript and verification materials are provided. This is a limited, unrefereed research preprint, released under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0.

title: A predictive uncertainty curve framework for membership inference attacks
abstract: Abstract Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) pose a notable privacy threat by determining whether specific samples were used to train a target model. Existing approaches primarily rely on static model outputs or computationally expensive shadow models, neglecting the dynamic stability of predictions under input perturbations. We propose a novel framework that systematically integrates Temperature Scaling, MC Dropout, and FGSM, shifting the attack paradigm from point-based observation to function-based uncertainty modeling. Through this multi-perturbation lens, PUC captures fine-grained memorization dynamics, enabling a comprehensive and efficient evaluation. We introduce a specialized curve feature engineering pipeline to extract geometric and statistical indicators from continuous response curves, quantifying prediction dynamic stability into compact feature vectors that enhance discriminative power. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and PathMNIST validate the framework’s effectiveness. Results demonstrate that PUC outperforms competing methods, particularly on ResNet-18, maintaining robust performance even at extremely low false positive rates. Specifically, it improves the AUC by 16.7 percentage points on CIFAR-10 and 4.2 percentage points on CIFAR-100 compared to LiRA.

title: Information-Theoretic Foundations of Online Temperature Sampling
abstract: Repetitive, degenerate generation is a persistent failure of LLM decoding, and the standard remedies (temperature, nucleus, and top-$k$ sampling) are static heuristics. By Kac's lemma and the AEP, a stationary source takes time exponential in its entropy to repeat a block. We therefore maximize the entropy of the sampling distributions under one cross-entropy budget that keeps the output plausible under the model. Offline, the solution is temperature sampling, with the inverse temperature as the budget's Lagrange multiplier. \emph{Our contribution is the online problem}: the conditionals $p_1, p_2, \dots$ are revealed one at a time, and the sampling distribution $q_t$ must be chosen causally from $p_1, \dots, p_t$ while the budget couples the entire horizon. The optimal temperature is thus a global shadow price that must be estimated from a prefix. We propose Entropic Online Sampling (EOS), which re-solves for the temperature on each prefix. We prove it loses $O(R\log n)$ entropy against the offline optimum while overshooting the budget by $O(R\log n)$, with $R$ an instance-dependent drift parameter. A budget-tightened variant is exactly feasible at the same rate. Conversely, every exactly feasible online algorithm must lose $Ω(R)$, so EOS is optimal up to a $\log n$ factor. When the conditionals are drawn from a finite mixture, $R=\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$. Experiments confirm that EOS tracks the offline temperature and beats fixed-temperature sampling in entropy.

title: Training-Free BioNEL-RAG: Advancing Biomedical Entity Linking through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Large Language Model
abstract: Biomedical Named Entity Linking (BioNEL) is the task of mapping mentions extracted from biomedical texts to canonical entities or concepts in the standardized knowledge base. Although existing methods have achieved remarkable performance in mapping accuracy, most rely on training with domain-specific datasets, which fundamentally limits their cross-domain adaptability. To address this limitation, we propose BioNEL-RAG, a novel training-free framework that combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with large language models (LLMs). Within this framework, the RAG module focuses on retrieving candidate entities, while the large language model module plays the role of selecting the most appropriate candidate for entity normalization, which is based on the analysis of the mention's context, with the aid of its remarkable text comprehension capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that BioNEL-RAG achieves performance comparable to existing methods without requiring training on subdomain datasets, whereas these methods necessitate fine-tuning on specific subdomains such as genes, diseases, or chemical compounds.

title: Are Multimodal Benchmarks Really Useful? Item-Level Multimodal Benchmark Diagnosis via Structure-Response Co-Calibration
abstract: Multimodal benchmarks are central to evaluating whether models can reason over information from multiple modalities. However, existing literature has revealed that some benchmarks may contain shortcut items that can be answered from a single modality or from answer-option regularities alone, thus failing to reflect models' true cross-modal inference ability. Existing methods for assessing benchmarks typically rely either on intrinsic item structure or extrinsic model response behavior, which are not adequate for a comprehensive diagnosis. To fill in this gap, we propose SRCoD, a structure-response co-calibrated diagnosis framework for item-level diagnosis of modality dependence in multimodal benchmarks. SRCoD estimates sample-wise multimodal information structure from benchmark content and target answers, and uses this signal as a soft structural anchor for modality-conditioned item response modeling. The learned model produces a calibrated item-level diagnostic profile that reflects how strongly an item depends on different forms of modality evidence, enabling fine-grained benchmark analysis beyond aggregate accuracy. SRCoD also provides interpretable attribution of the diagnosis results. Extensive experiments under two complementary protocols, i.e., benchmark-refinement oriented validation and human-labeled item validation, demonstrate that SRCoD outperforms state-of-the-art benchmark diagnosis methods.

title: HEAIN-SD-1.0: Policy-Governed Subtitling and Dubbing for Thai on Hybrid Edge AI Nodes
abstract: Automatic dubbing systems now produce intelligible speech, but professional subtitling and dubbing remain constrained by three problems that are seldom addressed together. Expressive delivery has to be directed by people who read the picture; profane or censorable content has to obey rules that differ by country and destination platform; and the recordings that make a system better are the personal data of identifiable voices. This paper introduces HEAIN-SD-1.0, an Application Profile that specifies how a Thai-centered subtitling and dubbing module runs as Layer 3 (Application AI) on HEAIN Core Protocol and the Hybrid Edge AI Node architecture. Four contributions are described. First, a policy-governed autonomy ladder (L0–L3): the system may learn everything about delivery and nothing about what is permitted, because content policy is a separately owned, fail-closed registry selected per destination. Second, a four-part decomposition of dubbed voice, in which timbre comes from the source performance, accent from the standard of professional dubbing teams in the target country, and emotion and rhythm from a producer's direction, realized as retrieval-prompted synthesis over a library of consented professional deliveries. Third, a protocol profile with a session model, a CORE/EDGE zone split, and an uplink whitelist that keeps media on the processing node and sends only records, scores, and small embeddings to the control node. Fourth, an evaluation plan with quality gates fixed before any experiment. The paper reports no experimental results: the profile is an unimplemented design, and every quantity marked as an estimate is a planning value. Keywords: Automatic Dubbing, Subtitling, Thai Language, Voice Cloning, Tonal Languages, Human-in-the-Loop, Content Policy, Edge Computing, Consent Management, Protocol Specification

title: Quantum Computing on the Sixty-Ring: Every Gate a Setting, Every Gradient a Quarter Turn, and a Checksum on the Classical Half
abstract: Every tool of quantum computing is one of three moves on two sliding rings marked with the sixty last digits of the Fibonacci numbers. A setting is a value read off one placement of the rings. A fold is a product turned into a sum by the half-angle law. A turn is a shift of position that carries a digit with it. Every gate is a setting, its entries cos(θ/2) and sin(θ/2) the half-distances of the rings at crossing separation θ, and the Hadamard, CZ and CNOT are quarter and half turns. Born's rule is the fold, amplitudes read at position k and expectation values at 2k. Every gradient is a quarter turn, because the parameter-shift rule is the ring's derivative law, its two shifts the ×7 and ×3 laws, with four eighth turns where a Givens gate needs them. A complete variational run is worked on a two-qubit number-conserving Hamiltonian. The energy is the ring shifted ten positions, the ground state the vesica setting at position 20, the optimizer three readings and a gnomon with nothing to tune, its convergence one line. Noise is the radius of the rings, and the square inside the ring, the stabilizer octahedron, says when the noise has cost a magic state. Phase estimation, Shor's classical end, Grover's search, Trotter chains, QAOA, Bell tests, teleportation, error mitigation, benchmarking and the [[4,2,2]] and [[5,1,3]] codes each reduce to the same three moves, forty tools on one page, and because every unitary is a finite product of rotation gates, the list is open and the three moves are closed. A checksum rides every classical number of the loop, the digits under the crossings on each setting, the addition law on each sum, the quarter-turn law on each gradient, the symmetry identity ⟨XX⟩ = ⟨YY⟩ on the measured data with its alarm threshold read off the setting, every one-, two- and three-bit upset of a 32-bit phase word and every burst of up to fifteen bits caught by three rings in lockstep, every corruption of any kind caught by the ladder, and the decoder table of the perfect code built on the four quarter turns of the net, any four simultaneous faults in an entry restored. The guard stands on every classical register of the loop, and the code space stands on the qubits. Thirty-one jobs on three IBM machines close the paper. A clean run on a 156-qubit machine had every compiled angle certified, the injected bit flip flagged at over a hundred standard errors, the clean checksum inside its line, the radius reading the noise, and the Bell value above 2, and one bit flipped in a phase word before submission, four ways, caught by the guard every time, turning the ground state into the top of its number sector and, from the entangler word, into the top of the whole spectrum when sent unguarded. The same words were corrupted up to all ten at once, by any change up to every bit inverted, and read both ways in four runs, unguarded and through the guard, and every setting word of a many-qubit tower was corrupted past any real error rate, caught and rebuilt in place, and read right on the machine. Every number is verified by the script in the appendix on explicit matrices and states, and the hardware readings are checked against the result files.

title: Sparsity Saves Compute, Not Samples: Oracle Inequalities for Dense and Sparse Mixture of Experts
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine specialized experts through an input-dependent routing mechanism, and their sparse variants underpin many modern large-scale systems. Yet the statistical cost of adaptive routing remains only partially understood. We study the estimation error of least-squares MoE estimators when both the experts and the gating network are Lipschitz in their parameters. We represent each MoE as a gate--expert pair in a Gated Hilbert Space, whose norm $\|\cdot\|_Δ$ separates the contributions of routing and expert discrepancies. Using its empirical representation, we derive an oracle inequality with a fast rate of order $\tilde{\mathcal O}\big((Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}+d_{\mathrm{pr},g})/n\big)$ for dense MoEs with $K$ experts. For sparse Top-$k$ and Top-$p$ routing, the selection map is discontinuous in the gating parameters. We handle this by partitioning the gating class according to the selection patterns it induces on the sample. The resulting bounds match the dense rate up to an additive routing cost governed by the Natarajan dimension of the selector. We show that such a routing-complexity condition cannot be dropped: Lipschitz continuity in the parameters alone does not suffice. For linear softmax gating, the routing cost is of the same order as the gating term. Finally, for linear experts, we establish a matching minimax lower bound of order $Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}/n$, showing that the rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors.

title: Contravariant Universe Subtyping, Formalized, Mechanized
abstract: In a type theory with a cumulative universe hierarchy, \emph{subtyping} is often incorporated to lift lower universe levels to higher ones. In practice, kernels of proof assistants typically implement universe subtyping conservatively: subtyping only propagates covariantly into the output types of $Π$ types, while input types must be equivalent. A full-blown subtyping relation also compares the input types contravariantly. However, contravariant subtyping is not justified by the existing set-theoretic model, and poses challenges in the development of a complete subtyping algorithm. To complete the verified pipeline for a type-checker, we give two complete and sound subtyping algorithms. The first one \emph{renormalizes} output types in every $Π$ iteration. Despite a simple completeness proof, this algorithm incurs additional computational cost. The second algorithm hence circumvents this cost by avoiding the renormalization at all. It simply recursively compares two already normalized types structurally. Nevertheless, a completeness proof of this algorithm in a semantic approach requires to reason about normalization in sub-contexts, a capability beyond what the current semantic gadget offers. Instead, we conduct a program equivalence proof through bisimulation relations. Using this technique, we prove that the NbE algorithm returns equal normal forms in sub-contexts up to universe levels, and successfully conclude the completeness of the subtyping algorithm.

title: Harmonic Reduction of Spin-Coupled Grover Walks on Hypercubes via Quantum Bernoulli Noises
abstract: We consider spin-coupled Grover walks on hypercubes within the framework of quantum Bernoulli noises (QBN). We identify parity-dependent harmonic subspaces generated by the central Hamming layers: in even dimension they give a fixed-point subspace, whereas in odd dimension the walk reduces on the harmonic subspace to an explicit eight-dimensional reduced dynamics. Using symmetric-group representation theory, we characterize the corresponding isotypic structure and determine the reduced spectrum. The harmonic reduction also yields explicit long-time probability behavior and shows that the resulting states may occupy an asymptotically vanishing fraction of the hypercube while still spanning its full Hamming diameter.

title: What Drives AI Citations? Content, Retrieval and Model Knowledge in Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)
abstract: Generative search engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity now decide which Web pages users see as sources, and a growing industry of generative engine optimization advises publishers on how to earn these citations. We study what shapes citation in two 90-day collections of answers to commercial questions in contrasting markets: 158,099 answers with 468,037 citations. Comparing pages of the same website, content matters in one way: pages whose title and paragraphs match the questions people ask are cited more, whereas FAQ blocks, structured data, summary boxes and page speed appear effective only across websites. Page properties nevertheless explain little of the variation between pages of a website. Replaying the questions through the engines' APIs shows why. Every page ChatGPT cites is one its own search retrieved, and which pages that search retrieves, for sub-queries the model rewrites on every answer and that rarely coincide with Google's or Bing's results, explains far more of the variation than page properties (32% against 2.8%). Content acts mainly through this step, by matching the engine's queries in meaning. The model's own knowledge shapes it too: ChatGPT writes brands it knows into its searches, prefers websites it knows, and names brands without any supporting page, and controlled experiments show that brand names reorder its rankings of products with identical facts. Pages are thus cited when searched; brands are also named when remembered. The findings replicate in a market of small B2B vendors. We release data and code.

title: Successful but Unsafe: An Analytical Benchmark for Revealing Collisions in Vision-and-Language Navigation
abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents are typically evaluated by whether they reach a target and how efficiently they follow an instructed route, yet these metrics provide little information about collision behavior. Moreover, continuous VLN evaluation commonly uses a sliding regime, where an agent can slide along obstacles after a collision, potentially masking the effect of unsafe actions on navigation performance. We introduce VLN-Safe, a benchmark for analyzing collision safety under two complementary evaluation regimes: sliding, reflecting common VLN evaluation practice, and blocking, where collision-inducing actions prevent forward motion and more directly expose their consequences. Across six published agents on R2R-CE, 38.5-56.8% of successful episodes contain contact under sliding, while switching to blocking decreases success rate by 11.7-36.1 percentage points. We further analyze signals for anticipating imminent collisions and find that depth geometry and recent movement history are more informative than policy-derived signals, while safe alternatives near the policy's preferred action are rarely available. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a training-free collision guard that vetoes risky forward actions, executes an escape maneuver, and returns control to the original policy. Under blocking, the guard reduces collision steps by 62-98% and improves success rate by 6.9-29.3 percentage points across five recurrent, topological, and vision-language-action agents. Under sliding, it leaves success rate unchanged while raising the share of collision-free successes by 4.1-12.4 points. These results reveal a substantial gap between task success and collision-safe navigation and show that lightweight collision-aware intervention can improve both safety and navigation performance.

title: Learn the Dynamics, Enforce the Physics: Generative Latent Operators for High-Dimensional Beam Evolution
abstract: Particle-in-cell (PIC) simulation is indispensable for modeling beam dynamics in particle accelerators, but its computational cost limits many-query workflows, such as configuration exploration, virtual diagnostics, and controller design. We introduce GLOBE, a physics-constrained Generative Latent Operator for Beam Evolution, modeling the nonlinear, control-dependent, multiscale evolution of 3D beam--field dynamics covering $10^7$ spatial cells. GLOBE compresses beam--field states into a compact latent space and factors their evolution into two components. A control-conditioned neural operator learns the dominant dynamics, while an amplitude-normalized generative model captures the residual distribution, recovering fine-scale structures and conditional variations. GLOBE enforces field constraints by regime-specific, parameter-free operators: a Poisson solve reconstructs the electric field in the electrostatic regime, and a spectral projection imposes Gauss's law and a divergence-free magnetic field in the electromagnetic regime. On two high-resolution 3D particle-accelerator benchmarks, bunched-beam transport and plasma-wakefield acceleration, GLOBE lowers relative-$L_2$ error by 9\% and 13\%, low-frequency spectral error by 69\% and 51\%, and mid-frequency spectral error by 54\% and 20\% relative to the strongest baseline (DPOT), satisfies field constraints, and reduces hours of PIC simulation to a minute per rollout.

title: Field Investigation Of Lithium And Associated Mineralization Potentials, Marafa Oja Environs, Kwara, North Central, Nigeria
abstract: Global demand for lithium resources is increasing rapidly, primarily due to its essential role in modern industrial, aerospace, defense, and especially lithium-ion battery technologies.Despite this surge, the lithium mineralization within the Nigerian Basement Complex remains significantly underexplored.Africa is recognized as a continent rich in mineral resources, including lithium, which is commonly found in rare-metal pegmatites.Historically, these pegmatites were mined sporadically for tin and tantalum across various regions.In recent years, Africa has emerged as a major focus for mining companies and international investors participating in the global "race" for lithium-often referred to as "white gold."Currently, Africa accounts for over 10% of the world's lithium production, with deposits of varying sizes and ore grades identified in several countries.This study examined the lithological features and lithium enrichment prospects of the Marafa Oja area in Kwara State, North-Central Nigeria.The field investigation involved detailed mapping and sampling, with an emphasis on analyzing the relationships among different rock units to assess their mineralization potential.Based on the findings, the local geology was established, and possible zones of mineralization were identified.Four distinct lithologies were identified in the area: biotite granite gneiss, amphibolite/amphibole schist, medium-grained granite, and pegmatite veins.The primary structural trends within the tenement run approximately NE/SW, with secondary trends in the NW/SE direction.Through systematic mapping and targeted sampling of suspected ore-bearing rocks, the study found the area is highly prospective for pegmatite-hosted mineralization, especially for minerals like muscovite and tantalite.Further evidence of local mining activities, combined with structural interpretations and observable field signatures, highlights areas with the greatest potential for future exploration.Overall, the research underscores the significance of the Marafa Oja area as a promising target for lithium and rare-metal exploration within Nigeria's broader mineral landscape.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Cybersecurity: Defensive Applications, Offensive Exploitation, Adversarial Risks, and Responsible Deployment
abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming cybersecurity by introducing advanced capabilities for threat detection, behavioral analysis, vulnerability management, malware classification, and incident response. At the same time, the increasing accessibility of machine learning and generative AI technologies creates new opportunities for malicious actors to enhance social engineering, automate elements of cyberattacks, and exploit weaknesses in AI-enabled systems. This technical review examines the dual-use nature of artificial intelligence in cybersecurity, focusing on its defensive applications, offensive misuse, adversarial machine learning threats, and operational security implications. It explores the integration of AI into Security Operations Centers (SOCs), Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) platforms, network monitoring, and threat intelligence workflows. It also discusses emerging risks, including AI-assisted phishing, synthetic content, prompt injection, data poisoning, model manipulation, and excessive reliance on automated security decisions. The study presents a comparative analysis of defensive and offensive AI capabilities and proposes a risk-aware framework for responsible AI adoption in cybersecurity operations. Particular attention is given to human oversight, model evaluation, data governance, privacy protection, and continuous security monitoring. The review concludes that AI can significantly support cybersecurity operations when implemented with appropriate safeguards, but it should complement rather than replace security professionals, established defensive controls, and evidence-based decision-making. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, Machine Learning, Generative AI, Threat Detection, Security Operations Center, SIEM, Adversarial Machine Learning, Prompt Injection, AI Security Governance.

title: Is the blind spot of a fixed evaluation a property of the question? A preregistered transfer test on fresh questions with independent exchanges
abstract: RIDI-PREDICT-v1 tests whether correctness changes in three small Qwen3 models under an independent grade-preserving retrieval exchange predict correctness changes in Qwen3-32B and OLMo-2-0325-32B-Instruct. Tokenizer-only preflight selected 800 fresh questions: 250 Natural Questions, 250 HotpotQA, and 300 FEVER. SciFact had no eligible fresh questions and was excluded under the prespecified rule. The design comprises 24 model-by-benchmark-by-draw units. No model responses have been generated for this study. Hypotheses, decision thresholds, exclusions, failure rules, and the analysis plan are specified in the attached protocol. The scientific lock will be published after registration and before generation. Parent registrations: https://osf.io/txwdv/, https://osf.io/ms4w8/, and https://osf.io/whjbs/.

title: InCLAD: A Continual Learning Benchmark for Industrial Visual Anomaly Detection
abstract: Industrial anomaly detection benchmarks have advanced rapidly, yet they remain largely static and therefore underrepresent deployment settings in which inspection systems must be extended from one industrial component to another over time. In our setting, continual industrial anomaly detection is framed as a task-incremental problem: each component defines a task, while the learning objective remains semi-supervised. The goal extends beyond conventional anomaly detection, since models should preserve their performance on all components as they are sequentially exposed to new components. This framing is especially relevant because many existing industrial pipelines either assume fully supervised defect labels or study only isolated datasets, leaving open the question of how semi-supervised anomaly detectors behave across a sequence of heterogeneous components. We address this gap by organizing the benchmark as a sequence of related component-level tasks and by defining multiple scenarios, including random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy. In addition to single-dataset continual scenarios, we propose challenging scenarios spanning across multiple datasets. We further evaluate continual performance from two complementary perspectives: image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localization. By recasting industrial anomaly detection as a continual benchmark rather than a static train/test problem, our work establishes a concrete path toward studying knowledge retention, adaptation, and generalization in evolving industrial environments.

title: MTFNet: A Lightweight Multi-Scale Time–Frequency Neural Network for Multi-Class Event Recognition in DAS-Based Perimeter Security
abstract: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) has emerged as a pivotal technology for perimeter security. However, existing DAS event recognition methods have inherent limitations. Single-domain modeling has limited feature representation, while conventional multi-domain fusion methods require converting one-dimensional signals into two-dimensional images. This conversion adds computational overhead and may discard part of the original phase and amplitude information. In addition, the robustness of lightweight recognizers under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions remains insufficiently examined. This paper proposes a lightweight multi-scale time–frequency network (MTFNet) for direct processing of one-dimensional DAS signals. The model adopts a parallel time–frequency dual-branch architecture. The time-domain branch utilizes a lightweight 1D Inception-ResNet variant to capture short-term impulse features and long-range temporal dependencies via multi-scale parallel convolutions and residual connections. The frequency-domain branch performs multi-scale segmented spectral analysis to extract complementary discriminative information at diverse time and frequency resolutions, followed by a lightweight attention-free fusion module for effective time–frequency feature fusion. Experimental results on a self-built dataset covering Wind, Facility Noise, Hammering, Sawing, and Walking events show that MTFNet achieves a recognition accuracy of 99.55% with 0.12 M parameters, outperforming SVM, 1D-CNN, TCN, MS 1D-CNN, CNN-BiLSTM, and attention-based multimodal fusion methods. It maintains an accuracy of 94.06% at an SNR of 0 dB, demonstrating its robustness against additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and practical engineering application potential.

title: Quantum Computing in Space: Engineering Challenges, Fundamental Limits, and Perspectives
abstract: Quantum computer deployment in space remains constrained by demanding hardware, environmental, and communications requirements. This paper reviews the opportunities and challenges of using quantum computing in space systems. It focuses on payload integration, radiation protection, quantum-memory stability, autonomous hybrid classical–quantum control, and quantum-network performance. The work is integrative, not novel in algorithms, architecture, optimization, or experiments. It organizes reviewed literature around system-level deployment barriers and highlights open research gaps. Compared with existing reviews, this paper adds a category taxonomy, a system-level constraint framing, updated coverage, and an integration of rate–loss fundamentals. The analysis highlights the need for standardized interfaces, autonomous classical–quantum control, and evolutionary qualification of subsystems in orbit. Modular, radiation-adaptive payloads and calibration-aware classical processing are identified as important strategies for improving reliability and mission resilience. The industrial outlook indicates a gradual transition from subsystem demonstrations toward standardized, interoperable, and vertically integrated quantum-communication services, including LEO QKD constellations, space-qualified protocol stacks, and CubeSat-scale photonic devices. Readiness claims are classified using a multi-stage ladder: launch, power-on, communication, calibration, quantum operation, and peer-reviewed useful computational performance. Fully fault-tolerant quantum computing in orbit remains a longer-term objective requiring advances in logical-qubit overhead, radiation tolerance, low-power control, memory performance, and repeater architectures.

title: Signal-to-noise problems in fault-tolerant quantum computation
abstract: Quantum computation offers a promising alternative to classical Monte Carlo methods by naturally avoiding sign problems through unitary evolution. A common misconception follows from this: because quantum simulation sidesteps the sign problem, it is often assumed to be an essentially perfect substitute for classical sampling. This is false---quantum measurements are intrinsically stochastic, and estimating observables often requires a number of samples that grows exponentially with system size, time separation, or inverse temperature, exactly as in the classical signal-to-noise problem. In this work, we analyze the origin and structure of signal-to-noise problems in quantum computation, drawing parallels with classical Monte Carlo, and demonstrate that such noise persists even in sign-problem-free regimes. We discuss strategies to mitigate it, in particular a quantum generalization of Stein control variates construction, in which unbiased estimators are built from operator commutators $[X,A]$ and their discrete diagonal counterparts, and validate the approach with exactly solvable numerical examples that quantify the achievable variance reduction. Our results underscore that variance reduction, not merely sign-problem avoidance, is required to make quantum algorithms practically viable for many-body physics.

title: Appearance Compensation in Volume Rendering
abstract: Can a volume that reproduces every external RGB view still have an incorrect density? We study this question in emission-absorption rendering with an independently parameterized, physically bounded effective source. Appearance compensates a density change by replacing the radiance that it removes from the rest of each ray. We characterize the surviving density information with a shared spatial appearance field. Our first result is an optimal density-only gain after finite-degree spherical-harmonic source refitting. A coupled tensor gauge and physical localized packets identify the sharp limiting nonlinear inverse coefficient as its reciprocal. Our second result realizes positive gain at every fixed finite degree for a residual set of isotropic spatial sources at one fixed density. At the same references, growing angular capacity hides a fixed nonzero density error while retaining physicality and any prescribed finite set of smoothness bounds. Local identifiability and the absence of a capacity-uniform recovery modulus therefore coexist. Our third result constructs an exact physical SH2 ambiguity: central density doubles and relative density $L^2$ error exceeds $14.52\%$, yet every external RGB ray is unchanged. We connect these continuum results to shared finite representations, continuous pixel measurements and density-sensitive acquisition. Complete-class certificates separate SH0, SH1 and SH2 fits at one learned density. Finite-camera results expose the distinct role of spatial capacity, and transmission measurements separate otherwise identical RGB fields. Controlled training tests and captured-smoke profiles supply mechanism evidence with explicit observation scopes. The results show why rendering accuracy alone cannot certify density: recovery also depends on appearance capacity, spatial resolution and measurement design.

title: How Should a Camera-First AI Agent Work?
abstract: Camera-first agents must act on the visual world as it unfolds. We argue that the central obstacle for future camera-first agents is not recognition ability - multimodal models (vision-language and live/streaming alike) generalize well through language and remain the right tool for semantic reasoning - but time. Many visual targets are ephemeral: they appear, are query-relevant, and leave within a short window. Binding memory to the same end-to-end path as reasoning means that by the time a monolithic pipeline completes, the evidence is gone. We formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and a Perceptual Deadline Contract separating a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, grounded in the bounded, passive nature of sensory and working memory. We propose a two-deadline architecture: an always-on, bounded, non-semantic fast path; an active remembering mechanism that commits a moment to durable memory before it is overwritten (event-driven in v1); and a deferred deliberation layer (multimodal model + tools). We instantiate the contract on real MOT17 track windows, a consistency check, and calibrate the single-path baseline from measured frontier-model latency: even a short answer takes 1.2-9.3 s, and an agentic identify-and-search longer. Answers can be late; evidence cannot be missed.

title: agents_Inc: A Model Ladder for Delegating and Verifying Work Across AI Agents
abstract: agents_Inc is a governed multi-agent dispatch and verification layer. It pools Claude, Codex, Gemini, Mistral and OpenRouter capacity behind one launcher, agents-inc, so a supervising agent can hand work to cheaper or specialised models without paying for a new API. You name models in plain English. A four-rung ladder (Executive, Orchestrator, Workhorse, Grunt) decides who manages whom, and every dispatch carries a 14-element prompt contract. A delegate never grades its own work: output passes deterministic checks, then a reviewer, and each decision lands in an append-only ledger. Main features One command, agents-inc dispatch, for Claude and Codex delegates, with prompt linting, a pre-run snapshot of the working tree and a verdict on return. Sandboxed Codex delegates that work like Claude subagents: tools, scoped write access, skills and built-in image generation. Model sync that detects new Claude and Codex models and promotes them with approval or pins. A credential-blind broker for nested runs, and a ledger that records every launched dispatch. Standard library only at runtime. Install with pip install agents-inc, then agents-inc install. New in 0.3.1 Opt-in network access for Codex delegates: the slot CODEX_NETWORK: yes or agents-inc run --network. Off by default. Codex tool commands get a private writable temp directory, so heredocs and scratch files work. A dispatched Codex delegate can run its own snapshot check. The snapshot check accepts allowed files inside a new directory. agents-inc report bug|feature drafts a GitHub issue; --submit files it. Sessions and agents-inc doctor say when a newer release is on PyPI. The full change list is in CHANGELOG.md. The project is experimental; the governed path is off by default. How to cite If you use agents_Inc in research or in published work, please cite it: Mattioli, D. O. title: Photon-number-resolved loss estimation using entanglement: Fisher information limits and accessible quantum advantage
abstract: Twin beams from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) enable sub-shot-noise transmission estimation, yet practical advantages are constrained by loss. We map joint photon-number-resolved (PNR) statistics to channel parameters using an exact, analytically solvable binomial-damping model for the lossy two-mode squeezed vacuum, removing the need for numerical master-equation integration. Benchmarking against an energy-matched coherent probe, we show the optimal linear estimator saturates the Cramer-Rao bound in closed form. For a fiber-coupled SPDC source interrogated with PNR superconducting nanowire detectors, we demonstrate that no quantum advantage survives at 14.7 to 23.5 dB signal loss and 14.8 dB idler loss. We conclude by providing a parameter-space design chart specifying the precise loss budget required for quantum-enhanced transmission estimation.

title: Calibration and drift thresholds for optical quantum biosensing under finite exposure budgets
abstract: Optical squeezing alone does not establish lower estimation error after calibration and drift. We optimize reference and sensing durations under a common deadline and specimen-exposure ceiling for a two-block Brownian-baseline model. Exact convex solutions identify exposure-limited operation, preparation-induced crossovers and drift-limited early completion. In an illustrative scenario, a noise-only variance gain of 2.5 becomes a protocol gain of 1.201 at 60 s and reverses below 35.953 s. Independent optimization and stochastic checks verify the calculations. The results define protocol-specific theoretical boundaries; no experimental or clinical validation is claimed.

title: Toward System One Clinical Intelligence: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Counterfactual Explainability of Decision Foundation Models
abstract: Automated disease classification from patient-reported symptoms requires balancing the speed of lightweight discriminative models against the contextual understanding and latency costs of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Decision foundation models offer an alternative by mapping representations directly to candidate classes without free-form text generation. We adapt Clef-Flash, a 9-billion-parameter decision model built on a Qwen3.5 backbone, for 24-class disease classification on the Symptom2Disease benchmark. Using 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) with differential learning rates and a stratified split of 960 training and 240 test cases, the model achieves 95.42% diagnostic accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.9551. This improves upon the reported zero-shot baselines of 61.67% for a remote API and 65.00% for a local unadapted initialization, and outperforms the ClinicalBERT baseline (90.90%). By evaluating candidate logits in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding, inference takes under 80 milliseconds per record on a single GPU, yielding a reported 31-fold speedup over generative LLM baselines. To examine symptom-level evidence, we introduce a Leave-One-Symptom-Out (LOSO) counterfactual perturbation framework. Removing disease-defining symptom clauses in a psoriasis example reduces predicted-class confidence from 100.00% to 0.12% and shifts the prediction to impetigo with 99.59% confidence, while removing secondary systemic symptoms produces less than 0.01% change in confidence. These findings suggest that decision-based architectures can combine the linguistic capabilities of large foundation models with low-latency inference and symptom-level interpretability for clinical triage.

title: Prior-Fitted and Frozen Scorers for Multimodal Contrastive Learning
abstract: Multimodal contrastive learning typically relies on manually specified scoring functions, such as cosine similarity, to quantify the similarity between representations from different modalities. Several such functions have been recently proposed to extend contrastive learning beyond two modalities. In principle, however, any function that assigns high compatibility to matched samples and low compatibility to mismatched ones could serve as a scorer. Motivated by this broader view, we instantiate the scorer with a Transformer and find that even a randomly initialized model, when kept frozen, can outperform strong handcrafted multimodal contrastive baselines, whereas optimizing the scorer jointly with the encoders is less effective. Building on this observation, we introduce the Prior-Fitted Scorer (PFS): a Transformer scorer pre-trained on synthetic multimodal data generated from structural causal model (SCM) priors before transferring it to real-world data. The SCM exposes the scorer to diverse dependency structures, including shared, pairwise, and private information, providing a structured prior over higher-order cross-modal similarity. Across four real-world datasets, frozen Transformer scorers are competitive to contrastive baselines, and prior-fitting further improves the random initialization. More broadly, our results suggest that multimodal contrastive learning need not rely on manual similarity functions: Transformers can provide strong inductive biases, while causal pretraining can further shape these biases.

Motivated by this broader view, we instantiate the scorer with a Transformer and find that even a randomly initialized model, when kept frozen, can outperform strong handcrafted multimodal contrastive baselines, whereas optimizing the scorer jointly with the encoders is less effective. Building on this observation, we introduce the Prior-Fitted Scorer (PFS): a Transformer scorer pre-trained on synthetic multimodal data generated from structural causal model (SCM) priors before transferring it to real-world data. The SCM exposes the scorer to diverse dependency structures, including shared, pairwise, and private information, providing a structured prior over higher-order cross-modal similarity. Across four real-world datasets, frozen Transformer scorers are competitive to contrastive baselines, and prior-fitting further improves the random initialization. More broadly, our results suggest that multimodal contrastive learning need not rely on manual similarity functions: Transformers can provide strong inductive biases, while causal pretraining can further shape these biases.

title: Verification granularity for authenticated medical-image archives: code and measurements
abstract: Code, specification and measurement outputs for the manuscript "Verification granularity for authenticated medical-image archives: a controlled same-host study of segmented and whole-object AEAD" (Mua'ad Alfarajat, submitted to the Journal of Cryptographic Engineering). The study compares one tag over a whole object with one tag per segment while each AEAD is held fixed (AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, AES-256-GCM-SIV and Ascon-AEAD128), measures archive reads from a file, and tests the receivers that the timings go through. One script runs every experiment and writes every number in the manuscript as a LaTeX macro; a second script checks each statement the text makes about those numbers. Contents: the specification of the experimental construction CLX-Duplex and of the per-segment AEAD wrapper, reference and vectorised implementations, a reimplementation of IDMM-SIV-H, the benchmark and receiver harnesses, the conformance suite (vectors, fuzzing corpora, regression inputs), the script that fetches and builds pinned third-party libraries, the outputs of the published run (exp/published) and MANIFEST.json, which gives the SHA-256 of every file and traces every reported value to the experiment that produced it. See README.md for requirements and how to run. CLX-Duplex and IDMM-SIV-H are experimental constructions measured as a case study; no security claim is made for them. Additional notes: Third-party libraries are not included; tools/build_deps.sh fetches pinned versions. The Springer LaTeX template files are under LPPL 1.3c. title: Replication artifact for "Responsibility bounds and representation sensitivity in monotone collusion models" (PRIMA 2026)
abstract: Replication artifact for "Responsibility bounds and representation sensitivity in monotone collusion models" by Florian A. D. Burnat, accepted as a full paper at PRIMA 2026 (Springer Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence, to appear). The archive contains exact, standard-library Python checkers and their generated outputs: regression tests of the paper's void characterization, the tight 1/m responsibility floor and the original/updated Halpern–Pearl pivotal-profile formulas over enumerated finite model classes; an all-context, both-definition enumeration of the five locked structural variants M0–M4 in reduced and expanded representations; the definition-split and mediator boundary examples. make all (Python 3.10 or later, no third-party packages) reruns every checker, validates the locked counts and regenerates the transcripts, JSON results, LaTeX outputs and a SHA-256 verification manifest. make package builds a clean archive from a committed snapshot. The finite checks corroborate the stated results over their declared ranges; they do not replace the paper's proofs or validate any structural equation as an empirical model of an auction. The three generated TeX inputs used by the camera-ready paper are included and are byte-identical to the paper's copies. No paper PDF or data is included. The code is released under the MIT License.

title: Inference Burden in Mathematical Tasks: A Scope-Sensitive Proof-Theoretic Analysis
abstract: 抄録 Mathematical tasks impose inferential demands that cannot be identified with the length of a calculation or the number of inference steps. We define inference burden as a scope-sensitive structural profile of first-order natural-deduction certificates, relative to a fixed interface of certified mathematical operations. The profile separates rule occurrences from quantifier and case depth, temporary assumptions, eigenparameter scope, witness support, and quantifier–case interaction. The separation from theory-level work is a measurement boundary: unrestricted background reasoning would collapse logical costs, whereas linear background refinement preserves the profile. The central discrimination result constructs proofs of the same sequent whose rule histograms and all seven other structural coordinates agree, but whose quantifier–case interaction differs by an arbitrarily large amount. Thus the interaction coordinate is not recoverable from the remaining aggregate indicators. At task level, feasible-budget sets define a resource preorder without psychological weights. We prove Pareto computation correct for finite acyclic scoped proof grammars and exhibit a three-case grammar with exactly four incomparable frontier profiles. Secondary-school algebra examples cover all four quantifier rules, parameter conditions, uniqueness, and attained minima. A reproducible checker validates 115 certificates and rejects 12 invalid inputs. The framework supplies a formal basis for subsequent cognitive and instructional studies; it neither predicts learner performance by definition nor claims a new distinction between deduction and computation. title: Training-Free Multi-Agent Cooperative Embodied Search from Uncertain Vision-Language Priors
abstract: Real-world Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to act under partial observability, where map structure, semantic cues, and target locations may be incomplete or incorrectly inferred by foundation models. This paper presents a lightweight, training-free, and uncertainty-aware framework for cooperative multi-agent multi-target search in mapless environments. Instead of learning an end-to-end navigation policy, the framework separates high-level semantic reasoning from low-level execution through a scalable graph-optimization backbone. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serve only as hypothesis generators, proposing semantic zones, target-location cues, and possible navigable connections. These outputs are treated as uncertain priors and further refined using online observations and graph-context evidence. Cooperative navigation is then formulated as a rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear program with a lexicographic objective that first maximizes target-directed reward and then reduces travel distance, uncertain-edge use, and repeated visits. Experiments derived from 100 Matterport3D test cases show that the proposed framework improves target coverage and search efficiency over representative baseline methods, while shared information and joint planning enable more balanced workloads across agents. By operating on an abstract graph without relying on embodiment-specific policy parameters, the framework scales across varying numbers of agents and targets, generalizes to unseen environments, and accommodates different perception modules and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.

title: Who Receives Respect? A Counterfactual Benchmark for Honorific Allocation Bias in Bengali
abstract: Bengali has no grammatical gender, but honorificity is obligatory: every third-person reference must choose ordinary or respectful register. English has no such signal, so the system must choose a level of deference that the source never specified. We use this property to measure how large language models (LLMs) allocate respect in English--Bengali translation. Our evaluation set contains 2{,}016 sentences across 72 occupations. Each appears in seven sentence frames under four pronoun conditions. Masculine and feminine versions differ by one word, forming counterfactual pairs. We report a single Honorific Bias Score (HBS) for each model on a 0--100 scale, covering both the gender and occupation axes. A lower score means that respect is allocated more evenly. For the occupation analysis, we compute each occupation's honorific rate across the seven no-pronoun sentence frames. The standard deviation of these 72 occupation-level rates ranges from 17.2 to 35.5 percentage points across models, showing substantial variation in how honorifics are allocated across occupations. Occupation is associated with 3.2\% to 51.5\% of the variance in register choice, compared with at most 1.2\% for gender. Gender effects are much smaller overall: only two of the nine models show significant directional gender gaps, and they favor opposite genders. HBS ranges from 19.9 to 70.1 across the nine models, showing substantial variation in how evenly the models allocate respect.

title: ScienceBuddy-PV: A Verifier-Governed Recursive Improvement Protocol for Panvascular Intervention Research
abstract: ScienceBuddy-PV adapts the ScienceBuddy recursive-in-recursive design to panvascular intervention research through a structured evidence ledger, device-vessel ontology, abstention contract and retained failure bank. Recursive harness optimization and outer-loop model learning, including reinforcement learning, are specified but not executed. We audit a fixed component, rather than the complete agent system, using separate ARCADE syntax and stenosis tasks (1,000 training, 200 validation and 300 test images per task). A shared task-masked convolutional model was trained once per representation setting; its parameters and the heuristic support gate were then held fixed, with the stenosis threshold selected on validation data. On the locked test sets, syntax Dice was 0.475 (95% CI 0.459-0.490) and stenosis Dice was 0.231 (95% CI 0.214-0.249). Stenosis pixel AUROC was 0.957 and AUPRC was 0.180 at prevalence 0.00975. The gate accepted 76.7% of stenosis-frame outputs versus 100% for a score-only comparator. In a constructed mask audit, it accepted 44.3% of reference candidates and rejected 55.7%, exposing the cost of abstention. Acceptance does not establish correctness or clinical safety. This public-data component audit makes support and abstention measurable and provides a reproducible protocol for future collaborative agent studies. It does not demonstrate recursive improvement, patient-level validity or clinical device recommendations.

title: Shared Memory Is Not Enough for LLM-Agent Teams
abstract: Teams of artificial intelligence agents can share records to preserve knowledge when their members change. Completing a task requires new members to find relevant information and coordinate its use. We examine where this process breaks down in simulated teams controlled by large language models. One agent delivers a component and another performs a repair. After replacing all agents that knew which component was needed, we keep the task and record unchanged and vary how and when replacements receive that fact. Here we show that correct shared records can survive replacement without supporting timely, coordinated action. Some agents never read freely available records. Showing the fact before action sped up pickup. Information received after a route choice delayed pickup when agents had already committed to an unhelpful path. The same delay mattered little when the next useful step did not depend on the fact. Even with information available before action, some teams failed to coordinate delivery and repair. Shared memory should be evaluated through the decisions and task outcomes it supports. Its usefulness depends on timely access and coordination between agents with different capabilities.

title: Expand the digital commons: human-curated and AI-generated defensive publication
abstract: Language is the substrate of the patent system, and that substrate is arithmetizable. The claim is the invention's true text, and what can be written can be enumerated, varied, and generated. First, we argue that the patent system's foundations are empirically failing on their own evidence: search does not find, the inventive step does not discriminate, and classification silos conceal from the examiner the analogical transfers that drive real invention. Second, we argue that doctrine itself supplies the remedy's mechanism. Prior art turns on accessibility and enablement, not on authorship or readership: hidden but published is doctrine. This creates a decisive asymmetry: machines cannot invent, but they can anticipate. Third, we argue that generative models, today devoted almost entirely to the production of exclusivity, can be turned toward the opposite end, the digital commons: distributed, timestamped, enabling defensive publication at scale, with the human contribution quantified and placed on record. The service txtcraft proposes a concrete implementation. Copyleft was built on top of copyright. Generative patentleft can now be instrumented. Where copyleft used copyright's own lever to guarantee freedom, patentleft-by-publication needs only patent law's own definition of novelty. Four ideas carry the argument: the arithmetization of the claim, the asymmetry theorem, patentleft-by-publication, and the spread between accessibility, which the law pays out on, and attention, which the economy pays out on. One major research question is whether generative models augmented with scarce human curation can multiply the defensive value and the retrievability of contents, without multiplying noise and verification costs at the same rate. Machines now make claims and disclosures cheap to write on both sides. They can also check them. World models and AI systems can test enablement in silico, automated laboratories may test it in reality, and humans and machines may audit the results afterwards. A commons that publishes prior art together with the means to check claims against it could become a public verification layer for the patent system. This paper is also a call for help: its theses are provisional, and researchers, practitioners and institutions are invited to test and correct them, and to measure what the approach achieves. Preprint, not peer-reviewed. English is the reference text. Version 1.0. The text is released under CC0 1.0

title: Shared Persistence Ceiling, Divergent Failure Mode: Source-to-Successor Comparisons
abstract: Source to successor model updates can change how a model fails without changing whether it fails. This paper presents matched-probe comparisons across three source/successor pairs from different providers, evaluated at four temperatures using the MTCP correction-sequence protocol (200 probes, 800 pooled probe-pairs per comparison). Two of three pairs show failure-mode divergence: the successor triggers safety hard stops at 2-3.6x the source rate, with 95% confidence intervals excluding zero at every temperature including greedy decoding (t=0.0). In one pair, this divergence occurs while the persistence ceiling is statistically indistinguishable. A third pair does not replicate. The finding is that the persistence ceiling alone is not a sufficient safety characterisation. Two models can share a ceiling and present different risk profiles. The failure mode must be measured per model, per pair, per deployment context.

title: Identication and Estimation of Nonsymmetric Determinantal Point Processes
abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) provide tractable distributions for nite random sets, but the usual symmetric-kernel specication imposes nonpositive pairwise dependence. Statistical research on nonsymmetric DPPs, which can accommodate positive dependence, remains limited. We study identication and estimation for this class. First, we establish the equivalence of two sucient conditions for a nonsymmetric kernel to dene a valid DPP. Second, we develop the identication theory for nonsymmetric DPPs. Third, we develop cardinality-truncated maximum-likelihood estimation and estimation by averaged stochastic gradient descent. Under suitable identication and regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality for both estimators. Simulations examine identication, the eects of truncation, and the nite-sample performance of the estimators. We illustrate the methods with two cyber applications at markedly dierent sampling frequencies: weekly sector-by-breach data and second-by-second enterprise authentication data with more than ve million set observations.

title: Beyond Domain-Routed Supervision: Cross-Teacher Guarding for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends on-policy distillation (OPD) by routing domain-specific data to specialized teachers, integrating their capabilities through dense token-level supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, domain routing only distinguishes the supervision sources for different domains; updates from all domains still act on shared parameters. When teachers differ substantially in response style and domain expertise, supervision that is effective in isolation may still lead to persistent gradient conflicts and capability degradation during joint optimization. To address this challenge, we propose Cross-Teacher Guarding for MOPD (Road MOPD), which introduces non-routed teachers as auxiliary cross-domain critics on the same student trajectories and coordinates multi-teacher supervision through token-level credit assignment and gradient updates. Specifically, cross-teacher-guided credit assignment uses teacher agreement to strengthen token-level corrections jointly supported by the teachers and attenuate conflicting signals; preventive multi-teacher gradient projection uses auxiliary gradients from the same trajectories to constrain potentially conflicting updates and adaptively controls projection strength to retain target-domain learning signals.
